| Immunoglobulin G antibody (Fc portion) | Fcγ receptors |
| C3b and its breakdown product iC3b (complement) | Complement receptors (including MAC-1 / CR3) |
| Plasma lectins: mannose-binding lectin and collectins | Lectin receptors |
| Acute-phase proteins such as C-reactive protein and serum amyloid A | Bind microbial walls and fix complement |

**Mechanism.** Antibody binds through its Fab region to a microbial antigen and presents the Fc tail to Fc receptors; complement activation by the classical, alternative or lectin pathways deposits C3b covalently on the microbial surface; mannose-binding lectin binds microbial sugars. The bridge formed between the microbe and the phagocyte receptor triggers signalling that leads to engulfment and also activates the phagocyte.

**Significance.** Opsonisation is the mechanism by which adaptive immunity (antibodies) and innate immunity (complement, lectins) direct phagocytes against microbes. Deficiencies of antibody or complement (and, clinically, absence of the spleen) predispose to infections with encapsulated bacteria. Opsonin-coated microbes are also recognised by macrophages through opsonin-independent receptors such as the mannose and scavenger receptors, but with lower efficiency.

**Chemical Mediators of Inflammation**

**Chemical mediators**


## Name the chemical mediators of inflammation.

The chemical mediators of inflammation are either cell-derived (vasoactive amines such as histamine and serotonin, arachidonic acid metabolites, platelet-activating factor, cytokines and chemokines, reactive oxygen species, nitric oxide, lysosomal enzymes, neuropeptides) or plasma-derived (the complement system, kinins and the coagulation system).

The most important mediators of acute inflammation are vasoactive amines, lipid products (prostaglandins and leukotrienes), cytokines including chemokines, and products of complement activation.

| Origin | Mediators | Principal sources | Principal actions |
|---|---|---|---|
| Cell-derived, preformed | Histamine | Mast cells, basophils, platelets | Vasodilation, increased permeability, endothelial activation |
| | Serotonin | Platelets, neuroendocrine cells | Vasoconstriction (importance uncertain) |
| | Lysosomal enzymes | Neutrophils, macrophages | Microbial killing, tissue damage |
| Cell-derived, newly synthesised | Prostaglandins | Mast cells, leukocytes | Vasodilation, pain, fever |
| | Leukotrienes | Mast cells, leukocytes | Permeability, chemotaxis, leukocyte adhesion and activation, bronchospasm |
| | Platelet-activating factor | Leukocytes, mast cells | Vasodilation, permeability, leukocyte adhesion, chemotaxis, degranulation, oxidative burst |
| | Cytokines (TNF, IL-1, IL-6), chemokines | Macrophages, endothelial cells, mast cells | Endothelial activation, fever, leukocyte recruitment |
| | Nitric oxide, reactive oxygen species | Macrophages, neutrophils, endothelium | Killing, vasodilation, tissue damage |
| | Neuropeptides (substance P) | Sensory nerves | Pain transmission, increased permeability |
| Plasma-derived | Complement (C3a, C5a, C3b, MAC) | Plasma (liver) | Chemotaxis, anaphylatoxin, opsonisation, lysis |
| | Kinins (bradykinin) | Plasma (liver) | Increased permeability, vasodilation, smooth muscle contraction, pain |
| | Coagulation and fibrinolytic products | Plasma | Link between clotting and inflammation |


## General principles of action of chemical mediators.

Mediators are produced only in response to offending stimuli, are either cell-derived or plasma-derived, usually act briefly, and can stimulate the release of other mediators, with considerable redundancy in their actions.

1. The vascular and cellular reactions are triggered by soluble factors that are produced by cells or derived from plasma proteins, and are generated or activated in response to the inflammatory stimulus.
2. **Cell-derived mediators** are sequestered in intracellular granules and rapidly secreted by exocytosis (for example histamine in mast cell granules), or synthesised de novo (prostaglandins, leukotrienes, cytokines). The main producers are sentinel cells (macrophages, dendritic cells, mast cells), but platelets, neutrophils, endothelium and epithelia may also elaborate them.
3. **Plasma-derived mediators** (complement, kinins) are produced mainly in the liver and circulate as inactive precursors that must be activated by a series of proteolytic cleavages.
4. **Active mediators are produced only in response to stimuli** such as microbial products and substances released from necrotic cells, which ensures that inflammation is triggered only when and where it is needed.
5. **Most mediators are short lived.** They decay quickly, are inactivated by enzymes (for example kininase for bradykinin), scavenged or inhibited, giving a system of checks and balances.
6. **One mediator can stimulate the release of others.** For example, complement products stimulate histamine release and TNF stimulates endothelial cells to produce IL-1 and chemokines. Such cascades amplify or, in some instances, counteract the initial action.
7. There is **redundancy**: several mediators act on the same target, so the response is robust and not readily subverted; yet their actions are sufficiently distinct that inhibiting each has been therapeutically useful.
8. Most mediators act by binding to specific receptors, usually G protein-coupled, on target cells; some have direct enzymatic activity (lysosomal proteases) or mediate oxidative damage (ROS).


## Principal actions of arachidonic acid metabolites.

Arachidonic acid metabolites (eicosanoids) are produced by cyclooxygenases (prostaglandins and thromboxane) and lipoxygenases (leukotrienes and lipoxins); prostaglandins cause vasodilation, pain and fever, leukotrienes cause chemotaxis, increased permeability and bronchospasm, and lipoxins inhibit inflammation.

Arachidonic acid (AA), a 20-carbon polyunsaturated fatty acid, is released from membrane phospholipids by phospholipase A₂ in response to mechanical, chemical or physical stimuli or mediators such as C5a. It is metabolised along two pathways.

| Action | Eicosanoid |
|---|---|
| Vasodilation | PGI₂ (prostacyclin), PGE₁, PGE₂, PGD₂ |
| Vasoconstriction | Thromboxane A₂, leukotrienes C₄, D₄, E₄ |
| Increased vascular permeability | Leukotrienes C₄, D₄, E₄ (PGD₂ and PGE₂ potentiate oedema) |
| Chemotaxis and leukocyte adhesion | LTB₄, 5-HETE (PGD₂ for neutrophils) |
| Platelet aggregation | Thromboxane A₂ (promotes); PGI₂ (inhibits) |
| Pain and fever | PGE₂ (hyperalgesia; resets hypothalamic set point) |
| Bronchospasm | LTC₄, LTD₄, LTE₄ |
| Anti-inflammatory | Lipoxins (inhibit neutrophil chemotaxis and adhesion); resolvins |

COX-1 is constitutive (gastric cytoprotection, renal function), while COX-2 is induced at inflammatory sites. Aspirin and NSAIDs inhibit cyclooxygenases; corticosteroids reduce transcription of COX-2 and phospholipase A₂; leukotriene receptor antagonists and 5-lipoxygenase inhibitors are used in asthma.


## Name some important cytokines in inflammation.

The important cytokines in acute inflammation are TNF, IL-1, IL-6, chemokines such as IL-8, and IL-17; in chronic inflammation IL-12 and IFN-γ are prominent, and IL-10 and TGF-β are anti-inflammatory.

| Cytokine | Principal sources | Principal actions in inflammation |
|---|---|---|
| TNF | Macrophages, dendritic cells, mast cells, T cells | Endothelial adhesion molecule expression, secretion of other cytokines, systemic effects (fever, cachexia, shock) |
| IL-1 | Macrophages, dendritic cells, some epithelial cells | Similar to TNF; greater role in fever; requires inflammasome for activation |
| IL-6 | Macrophages, other cells | Systemic effects, acute-phase response |
| Chemokines (IL-8/CXCL8, MCP-1, eotaxin) | Macrophages, endothelium, T cells, mast cells | Recruitment and activation of leukocytes |
| IL-17 | Th17 cells | Recruitment of neutrophils and monocytes |
| IL-12 | Dendritic cells, macrophages | Increases IFN-γ production (Th1 differentiation) |
| IFN-γ | T cells, NK cells | Classical macrophage activation |
| IL-4, IL-13, IL-5 | Th2 cells | Alternative macrophage activation, IgE; IL-5 recruits eosinophils |
| IL-10, TGF-β | Macrophages, T cells | Terminate inflammation; TGF-β promotes fibrosis |


## Write the functions of vasoactive amines.

The vasoactive amines are histamine and serotonin; they are preformed and stored in cells, so they are among the first mediators released, and they cause vasodilation and increased vascular permeability, with histamine the principal mediator of the immediate transient phase of increased permeability.

**Sources.** Histamine is richest in mast cells located in connective tissue adjacent to blood vessels, and is also found in basophils and platelets. Serotonin (5-hydroxytryptamine) is present in platelets and in neuroendocrine cells such as those in the gastrointestinal tract, where its primary function is as a neurotransmitter.

**Release.** Histamine is released from mast cell granules by degranulation in response to (1) physical injury (trauma, cold, heat), (2) binding of antigen to IgE antibodies on mast cell surfaces (immediate hypersensitivity), (3) the anaphylatoxins C3a and C5a, and (4) neuropeptides such as substance P and cytokines (IL-1, IL-8).

**Functions of histamine.**

- Dilates arterioles and increases the permeability of venules by producing interendothelial gaps in postcapillary venules; it is the principal mediator of the immediate transient phase of increased permeability (15 to 30 minutes), leading to redness, warmth and swelling.
- Contracts some smooth muscles (for example bronchial).
- Activates endothelium (P-selectin expression).
- Acts mainly through H1 receptors on microvascular endothelium. Four receptor types exist (H1 in allergic responses, H2 in gastric acid secretion, H3 in neurotransmitter modulation, H4 in immune function), all G protein-coupled; H1 blockers treat allergy, H2 blockers reduce gastric acid.

**Functions of serotonin.** Serotonin is a vasoconstrictor, but its importance in inflammation is unclear. It is released from platelets during aggregation and contributes to increased permeability in some species.


## How is the complement system activated?

The complement system is activated by three pathways, classical (antigen-bound IgM or IgG), alternative (microbial surfaces without antibody) and lectin (mannose-binding lectin), all of which converge on C3 convertase, which cleaves C3 into C3a and C3b; C3b leads to C5 convertase, and the late components form the membrane attack complex.

The complement system consists of more than 20 plasma proteins, some numbered C1 to C9, present as inactive precursors and activated in an enzymatic cascade capable of great amplification. The critical step is proteolysis of C3, the most abundant component.

- **Classical pathway:** triggered by binding of C1 to antibody (IgM or IgG) that has combined with antigen, followed by sequential binding of C4 and C2 and formation of a multiprotein enzyme (C3 convertase).
- **Alternative pathway:** triggered by microbial surface molecules (endotoxin/LPS), complex polysaccharides, cobra venom and other substances in the absence of antibody; spontaneous C3 cleavage is amplified and stabilised on the microbe.
- **Lectin pathway:** plasma mannose-binding lectin binds microbial carbohydrates and activates a C1-homologous protease; subsequent steps are those of the classical pathway.

C3 convertase splits C3 into C3a (released) and C3b (deposited on the microbe). More C3b binds to form C5 convertase, which cleaves C5 into C5a (released) and C5b, which binds C6 to C9 to form the membrane attack complex (MAC), made of multiple C9 molecules.

Activation is controlled by regulatory proteins on host cells and in plasma: C1 inhibitor (deficiency causes hereditary angioedema), decay-accelerating factor (CD55) and CD59 (GPI-anchored; deficiency causes paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria), and factor H (defects cause atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome and are linked to macular degeneration).


## What chemical mediators are responsible for the vascular events/features of acute inflammation?

The vascular events of acute inflammation (vasodilation, increased vascular permeability, and the later endothelial activation that promotes leukocyte adhesion) are driven by several mediators with overlapping actions, which ensures a robust response (Table 3.5).

**Vasodilation** (cause of redness and warmth):

- **Histamine**, acting on H1 receptors of vascular smooth muscle, is the principal early mediator.
- **Prostaglandins** PGI₂ (prostacyclin), PGE₁, PGE₂ and PGD₂ are vasodilators; PGD₂ is the major prostaglandin of mast cells.
- **Nitric oxide**, produced by endothelial and inducible NOS, relaxes vascular smooth muscle.
- **Bradykinin** (kinin system), **PAF** (at low concentrations), and the anaphylatoxins **C3a and C5a** (by releasing histamine from mast cells) contribute.

**Increased vascular permeability** (cause of oedema):

- **Histamine and serotonin**, the immediate transient response through endothelial contraction.
- **Bradykinin**, which has effects similar to those of histamine, and is rapidly inactivated by kininase.
- **Leukotrienes C₄, D₄ and E₄**, produced by 5-lipoxygenase in mast cells and leukocytes.
- **C3a and C5a**, by liberating vasoactive amines from mast cells.
- **PAF**, **substance P** and prostaglandins (which potentiate permeability).
- **Cytokines (TNF, IL-1)** and **reactive oxygen species and lysosomal enzymes** from leukocytes mediate delayed and sustained leakage by endothelial activation and injury.

**Vasoconstriction** (transient, minor): thromboxane A₂, leukotrienes C₄, D₄, E₄ and serotonin.

**Leukocyte adhesion and recruitment:** TNF and IL-1 induce E-selectin and the integrin ligands ICAM-1 and VCAM-1; histamine and thrombin mobilise P-selectin; chemokines, C5a and LTB₄ attract and activate leukocytes.

| Reaction | Principal mediators |
|---|---|
| Vasodilation | Histamine, prostaglandins, NO, bradykinin |
| Increased permeability | Histamine, serotonin, C3a, C5a, leukotrienes C₄/D₄/E₄, bradykinin, PAF |
| Endothelial activation | TNF, IL-1 |


## List the molecules and cytokines involved in inflammation.

A large number of molecules mediate the steps of inflammation, grouped as follows.

| Category | Molecules |
|---|---|
| Recognition receptors | Toll-like receptors, NOD-like receptors and inflammasome, mannose-binding lectin, collectins, Fc and complement receptors |
| Adhesion molecules | Selectins (L, E, P), integrins (LFA-1, MAC-1, VLA-4, α4β7), ICAM-1, VCAM-1, CD31 (PECAM-1), sialyl-Lewis X |
| Vasoactive amines | Histamine, serotonin |
| Arachidonic acid metabolites | Prostaglandins (PGE₂, PGD₂, PGI₂), thromboxane A₂, leukotrienes (LTB₄, LTC₄, LTD₄, LTE₄), lipoxins, resolvins |
| Other lipid mediator | Platelet-activating factor |
| Plasma proteases | Complement (C3a, C5a, C3b, MAC), kinins (bradykinin), coagulation and fibrinolytic proteins (thrombin, plasmin) |
| Cell-derived effectors | Reactive oxygen species, nitric oxide, lysosomal enzymes |
| Neuropeptides | Substance P, neurokinin A |
| Pro-inflammatory cytokines | TNF, IL-1, IL-6, IL-12, IL-17, IL-18, IFN-γ, HMGB1 |
| Chemokines | CXCL8 (IL-8), MCP-1 (CCL2), eotaxin (CCL11), MIP-1α (CCL3), lymphotactin (XCL1), fractalkine (CX3CL1) |
| Th2 cytokines | IL-4, IL-5, IL-13 |
| Anti-inflammatory cytokines | IL-10, TGF-β |
| Acute-phase proteins | C-reactive protein, fibrinogen, serum amyloid A, hepcidin |


## State the consequences of complement activation.

Activation of the complement system through the classical, alternative or lectin pathways yields cleavage products that have three principal biological effects, and its dysregulation causes disease.

1. **Inflammation.** C5a, C3a and, to a lesser extent, C4a are anaphylatoxins: they stimulate histamine release from mast cells and thereby cause increased vascular permeability and vasodilation. C5a is also a chemotactic agent for neutrophils, monocytes, eosinophils and basophils, and activates the lipoxygenase pathway of arachidonic acid metabolism in neutrophils and monocytes, leading to further release of mediators.
2. **Opsonisation and phagocytosis.** C3b and its inactive product iC3b, fixed to microbial cell walls, act as opsonins and promote phagocytosis by neutrophils and macrophages, which bear receptors for these fragments.
3. **Cell lysis.** The membrane attack complex (C5b to C9, with multiple C9 molecules) makes cells permeable to water and ions and causes osmotic lysis, important in killing microbes with thin cell walls such as Neisseria; deficiency of terminal components predisposes to Neisseria infection.

**Pathological consequences.** Complement activation by antibodies or antigen-antibody complexes deposited on host cells and tissues is an important mechanism of tissue injury in autoimmune and immune-complex disease. Inherited deficiencies of complement proteins increase susceptibility to infection, and deficiency of regulators produces excess activation: C1 inhibitor deficiency causes hereditary angioedema; deficiency of DAF and CD59 causes paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria; defects in factor H cause atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome and are associated with age-related macular degeneration. Inhibitors of C5 and C3 activation are now approved for several of these disorders.


## Which chemical mediators are responsible for pain and swelling?

**Pain (dolor).** The mediators responsible for pain are:

- **Prostaglandins**, especially PGE₂, which are hyperalgesic: they sensitise sensory nerve endings so that the skin becomes hypersensitive to painful stimuli such as histamine and bradykinin. This explains why NSAIDs relieve inflammatory pain.
- **Bradykinin**, which produces pain when injected into the skin, in addition to increasing vascular permeability.
- **Substance P**, a neuropeptide released by sensory nerves, which transmits pain signals and increases vascular permeability.
- Other contributors are histamine and cytokines (IL-1, TNF), as well as distension of tissue by oedema and direct injury by leukocyte-derived enzymes and oxygen radicals.

**Swelling (tumour).** Swelling is produced mainly by oedema due to increased vascular permeability of venules, together with vasodilation that increases the hydrostatic pressure. The responsible mediators are:

- **Histamine** and **serotonin** (immediate transient phase).
- **Bradykinin**.
- **Leukotrienes C₄, D₄ and E₄**.
- **C3a and C5a**, by releasing histamine and other amines from mast cells.
- **PAF**, **substance P**, and **prostaglandins** (PGE₂ and PGD₂, which potentiate oedema formation).
- **TNF and IL-1**, and leukocyte products (ROS and lysosomal enzymes), which sustain leakage by injuring the endothelium.

| Reaction | Principal mediators (Robbins) |
|---|---|
| Pain | Prostaglandins, bradykinin, substance P |
| Swelling (increased permeability) | Histamine and serotonin, C3a and C5a, leukotrienes C₄/D₄/E₄ |

**Morphology, Outcomes and Systemic Effects**

**Morphological patterns**


## Morphological types / patterns of acute inflammation.

The morphological patterns of acute inflammation are serous, fibrinous, purulent (suppurative, including abscess) and ulcerative inflammation.

The morphological hallmarks of acute inflammation are dilation of small blood vessels and accumulation of leukocytes and fluid in the extravascular tissue, but special patterns are superimposed depending on the severity of the reaction, its aetiology and the tissue involved. Recognising these patterns often provides clues to the underlying cause.

| Pattern | Characteristic |
|---|---|
| Serous | Exudation of cell-poor, serum-like fluid into spaces or body cavities |
| Fibrinous | Greater permeability: fibrinogen leaks out and fibrin is deposited, typically on serosal surfaces |
| Purulent (suppurative) | Pus (neutrophils, necrotic debris, oedema fluid) from pyogenic bacteria; abscess is a localised collection |
| Ulcer | Local defect of an epithelial surface from sloughing of inflamed necrotic tissue |

Other descriptive terms used in practice include catarrhal (mucous), pseudomembranous (a membrane of fibrin, necrotic epithelium and leukocytes as in diphtheria) and haemorrhagic inflammation.


## One example of each morphological type.

Serous inflammation is exemplified by a skin blister from a burn; fibrinous inflammation by fibrinous pericarditis; purulent inflammation by acute appendicitis or an abscess; and ulcerative inflammation by a peptic ulcer.

- **Serous:** a skin blister due to a burn or viral infection, with fluid accumulating beneath the epidermis; effusions in the pleural, pericardial or peritoneal cavity from irritation.
- **Fibrinous:** fibrinous pericarditis (bread-and-butter appearance), fibrinous pleuritis, and meningitis; the lining of body cavities is characteristically involved.
- **Purulent (suppurative):** acute appendicitis; a staphylococcal skin abscess; bronchopneumonia with abscesses.
- **Ulcer:** peptic ulcer of the stomach or duodenum, in which acute and chronic inflammation coexist; also ulcers of the mouth and intestine, and diabetic or venous ulcers of the lower limb.


## What is an ulcer?

An ulcer is a local defect or excavation of the surface of an organ or tissue, produced by the sloughing of inflamed necrotic tissue.

Ulceration can occur only when tissue necrosis and resultant inflammation exist on or near a surface. It is most common in (1) the mucosa of the mouth, stomach, intestines and genitourinary tract, and (2) the skin and subcutaneous tissue of the lower extremities in individuals with disorders that predispose to vascular insufficiency, such as diabetes, sickle cell anaemia and peripheral vascular disease. Ulcers are best exemplified by peptic ulcer of the stomach or duodenum, in which acute and chronic inflammation coexist: in the acute stage there is intense polymorphonuclear infiltration and vascular dilation at the margins of the defect, and with chronicity the margins and base develop fibroblastic proliferation, scarring, and accumulation of lymphocytes, macrophages and plasma cells. An ulcer may be considered as a discontinuity in an epithelium with underlying acute and chronic inflammation. Chronic ulcers of the leg include venous, arterial, diabetic ulcers and pressure sores.


## Define abscess.

Abscesses are localised collections of pus caused by suppuration buried in a tissue, an organ, or a confined space; they are produced by seeding of pyogenic bacteria into a tissue.

Pus is an exudate of neutrophils, the liquefied debris of necrotic cells, and oedema fluid. It is produced when infection with pyogenic bacteria, such as staphylococci, causes liquefactive necrosis. The abscess has a central liquefied region composed of necrotic leukocytes and tissue cells, a zone of preserved neutrophils around this focus, and, outside this, vascular dilation with parenchymal and fibroblastic proliferation indicating chronic inflammation and repair. In time the abscess may be walled off by a fibrous capsule (pyogenic membrane) and ultimately replaced by connective tissue. The fate of an abscess includes rupture and drainage with healing, formation of a sinus or fistula, spread, or chronic abscess formation with scarring and, occasionally, calcification. Abscesses are treated by drainage and antibiotics, since antibiotics penetrate the avascular pus poorly.


## Describe the morphological patterns of acute inflammation.

The morphological hallmarks of acute inflammation are dilation of small vessels and accumulation of leukocytes and fluid in the extravascular tissue. Superimposed on these are special patterns that depend on the severity of the reaction, its cause, and the tissue and site involved, and which often give clues to the cause.

**1. Serous inflammation.** Serous inflammation is marked by exudation of cell-poor, serum-like fluid into spaces created by cell injury or into body cavities lined by peritoneum, pleura or pericardium. The fluid usually contains no microbes and few leukocytes. The skin blister resulting from a burn or viral infection is a collection of serous fluid within or beneath the damaged epidermis. In body cavities the fluid may derive from plasma, owing to increased vascular permeability, or from secretions of mesothelial cells, owing to local irritation; accumulation is called effusion (effusions also occur in noninflammatory conditions, such as heart failure).

**2. Fibrinous inflammation.** With a greater increase in vascular permeability, large molecules such as fibrinogen leak from vessels and, if there is a local procoagulant stimulus, fibrin is formed and deposited in the extracellular space. It is characteristic of inflammation in the lining of body cavities such as the meninges, pericardium and pleura. Histologically fibrin is an eosinophilic meshwork of threads or an amorphous coagulum. Fibrinous exudates may be dissolved by fibrinolysis and cleared by macrophages; if not removed, they stimulate the ingrowth of fibroblasts and blood vessels (organisation) and lead to scarring, with opaque fibrous thickening of the pericardium and, if extensive, obliteration of the pericardial space.

**3. Purulent (suppurative) inflammation and abscess.** This is characterised by the production of pus, an exudate of neutrophils, liquefied debris of necrotic cells and oedema fluid. It is most often caused by pyogenic (pus-producing) bacteria, such as staphylococci, that cause liquefactive necrosis. Acute appendicitis is a common example. An abscess is a localised collection of pus buried in tissue, with a central liquefied region, a surrounding zone of preserved neutrophils, and an outer zone of vascular dilation and fibroblastic proliferation; in time it is walled off and replaced by connective tissue.

**4. Ulcers.** An ulcer is a local defect of the surface of an organ or tissue produced by the sloughing of inflamed necrotic tissue; it occurs only where necrosis and inflammation exist on or near a surface. It is common in the mucosa of the mouth, stomach, intestines and genitourinary tract and in the skin and subcutaneous tissue of the legs in patients with vascular insufficiency (diabetes, peripheral vascular disease). Peptic ulcer is the classic example, with acute inflammation at the margins and chronic inflammation and fibrosis in the base.


## Beneficial effects of acute inflammation.

Acute inflammation is beneficial because it delivers leukocytes, antibodies, complement and fibrin to the site of injury, dilutes toxins, destroys microbes and necrotic tissue, and initiates repair.

- **Dilution of toxins** by oedema fluid, and delivery of plasma proteins (antibodies, complement, clotting factors) to the injured site.
- **Fibrin formation**, which forms a meshwork that traps microbes, limits spread and provides a scaffold for repair.
- **Delivery of leukocytes**, which phagocytose and kill microbes and clear necrotic debris.
- **Drainage** of fluid and antigens through lymphatics to lymph nodes, which initiates the adaptive immune response, and delivery of antimicrobial drugs to the site.
- **Fever**, which may be a protective host response.
- **Initiation of repair**: macrophages produce growth factors and cytokines that promote angiogenesis, fibroblast proliferation and healing.

Without inflammation, infections would go unchecked and wounds would never heal.


## Harmful effects of acute inflammation.

The harmful effects of acute inflammation include tissue damage from leukocyte enzymes and oxygen radicals, swelling of vital structures in confined spaces, scarring and adhesions, fluid loss, and systemic effects such as septic shock.

- **Digestion and injury of normal tissue** by lysosomal enzymes and reactive oxygen species of leukocytes released into the extracellular space.
- **Swelling in vital or confined areas:** oedema of the epiglottis may obstruct the airway; brain oedema in meningitis may raise intracranial pressure and cause herniation.
- **Fibrinous exudates** may organise to form scars and adhesions, causing, for example, constrictive pericarditis or intestinal obstruction.
- **Massive fluid loss** in severe burns.
- **Inappropriate or exaggerated reactions**: hypersensitivity (anaphylaxis, asthma), autoimmune diseases, and diseases in which leukocytes are the principal cause of injury such as ARDS and glomerulonephritis.
- **Systemic effects** of high levels of cytokines: sepsis, septic shock, DIC and multiorgan failure.
- **Progression to chronic inflammation** with fibrosis and loss of function.


## Outcomes of acute inflammation.

Acute inflammation has three possible outcomes: complete resolution, healing by connective tissue replacement (scarring or fibrosis), or progression to chronic inflammation.

1. **Complete resolution.** The site is restored to normal. This is the usual outcome when injury is limited or short-lived, there has been little tissue destruction, and the damaged parenchymal cells can regenerate.
2. **Healing by connective tissue replacement (scarring/fibrosis).** This follows substantial tissue destruction, injury to tissues incapable of regeneration, or abundant fibrin exudation in tissue or serous cavities that cannot be adequately cleared. Connective tissue grows into the area of damage or exudate and converts it into a mass of fibrous tissue, a process called organisation.
3. **Progression to chronic inflammation.** This occurs when the acute response cannot be resolved because of persistence of the injurious agent or interference with healing.

Abscess formation is a pattern of purulent inflammation that may drain, heal by scar, or become chronic.


## How does (complete) resolution occur?

Complete resolution occurs when the injurious agent is removed, mediators are neutralised and leukocyte emigration stops, macrophages clear debris and microbes, lymphatics reabsorb oedema fluid, and the damaged tissue regenerates.

Resolution is favoured when the injury is limited or brief, tissue destruction is slight, and the parenchymal cells are capable of regeneration (labile and stable cells). The sequence is as follows:

- The stimulus is removed, and the production of mediators ceases; the mediators are short-lived and are degraded.
- Vascular permeability returns to normal and leukocyte emigration ends.
- Neutrophils die by apoptosis within hours to days after leaving the blood.
- Active termination signals operate: switch from pro-inflammatory leukotrienes to anti-inflammatory lipoxins (and resolvins), release of TGF-β and IL-10, and cholinergic inhibition of TNF.
- Macrophages remove the cellular debris, apoptotic neutrophils and microbes.
- Oedema fluid and protein are reabsorbed by lymphatics and venules; fibrin is dissolved by fibrinolysis.
- The damaged parenchyma regenerates from surviving cells or stem cells, and the normal architecture is restored, as in lobar pneumonia.


## What are the systemic effects of inflammation?

The systemic effects of inflammation, mediated by cytokines (TNF, IL-1, IL-6), include fever, leukocytosis, the acute-phase response with elevated acute-phase proteins such as CRP, and, in severe infection, septic shock.

Even localised inflammation is associated with cytokine-induced systemic reactions, as anyone who has had influenza will recognise.

**1. Fever.** Elevation of body temperature by 1 to 4 °C is one of the most prominent manifestations. Pyrogens are exogenous (bacterial products such as LPS) or endogenous (IL-1 and TNF). Exogenous pyrogens stimulate immune cells to release IL-1 and TNF, which upregulate cyclooxygenases in vascular and perivascular cells of the hypothalamus; the resulting PGE₂ stimulates neurotransmitter production, resetting the thermostat to a higher level by reducing heat loss (vasoconstriction) and increasing heat generation (brown fat, skeletal muscle). NSAIDs reduce fever by inhibiting prostaglandin synthesis.

**2. Leukocytosis.** The count usually rises to 15,000 to 20,000/μL, sometimes 40,000 to 100,000 (a leukaemoid reaction). It results initially from accelerated release of granulocytes from the marrow (due to TNF and IL-1), with a rise in mature and immature neutrophils (a "shift to the left"), and later from marrow proliferation due to colony-stimulating factors. Bacterial infections cause neutrophilia; viral infections (infectious mononucleosis, mumps, rubella) cause lymphocytosis; allergies and helminth infections cause eosinophilia; typhoid and some viral, rickettsial and protozoal infections cause leukopenia.

**3. Acute-phase response.** The liver synthesises acute-phase proteins, whose plasma concentration can rise several hundredfold. C-reactive protein (CRP) and fibrinogen are induced by IL-6, and serum amyloid A (SAA) by IL-1 and TNF. CRP and SAA bind microbial walls, act as opsonins and fix complement. Fibrinogen causes red cell rouleaux and accelerates the erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR). Hepcidin sequesters iron and causes the anaemia of chronic inflammation; thrombopoietin is upregulated and may cause thrombocytosis. Prolonged SAA production may cause secondary amyloidosis, and raised CRP is a marker of cardiovascular risk.

**4. Other manifestations.** Increased pulse and blood pressure, decreased sweating (redirection of blood from skin), rigors, chills, anorexia, somnolence and malaise, due to the action of cytokines on the brain; TNF-induced cachexia in chronic disease.

**5. Septic shock.** In severe bacterial infection, enormous quantities of TNF and IL-1 produce DIC, hypotensive shock and metabolic disturbances (insulin resistance, hyperglycaemia).


## Common investigations usually done in inflammatory conditions.

The common investigations in inflammation are a complete blood count with differential leukocyte count, ESR and C-reactive protein, culture and Gram stain of pus or blood, and, where needed, imaging and histopathology.

The tests reflect the systemic response and identify the cause:

- **Complete blood count and differential:** neutrophilic leukocytosis with a shift to the left in bacterial infection (and toxic granulation); lymphocytosis in viral infection; eosinophilia in allergy and helminthiasis; anaemia of chronic disease and thrombocytosis in chronic inflammation.
- **Acute-phase reactants:** ESR (raised because fibrinogen promotes rouleaux formation) and C-reactive protein; procalcitonin in sepsis.
- **Microbiology:** Gram stain, culture and sensitivity of pus, aspirates, blood, urine or other fluid; acid-fast stains, culture or PCR for tuberculosis; serology (for example for syphilis).
- **Imaging:** ultrasonography, radiography, CT or MRI to locate an abscess or involved bone.
- **Cytology and histopathology:** fine-needle aspiration or biopsy to demonstrate the type of inflammation (suppurative, granulomatous), with special stains for organisms.
- **Immunological tests** (autoantibodies, immunoglobulins) when immune-mediated disease is suspected.

**Chronic and Granulomatous Inflammation**

**Chronic inflammation**


## Define chronic inflammation.

Chronic inflammation is a prolonged host response to persistent stimuli, in which inflammation, tissue injury and attempts at repair coexist.

It may follow acute inflammation or may begin insidiously, as a prolonged response without a preceding acute reaction. It is a response to agents that are difficult to eradicate, such as tubercle bacilli, certain viruses, fungi and parasites, and to self antigens and environmental antigens. It is characterised by infiltration with mononuclear cells (macrophages, lymphocytes and plasma cells), tissue destruction induced by the persistent agent or the inflammatory cells, and attempts at healing by connective tissue replacement through angiogenesis and fibrosis.


## Causes of chronic inflammation.

Chronic inflammation arises from persistent infections by organisms difficult to eradicate, immune-mediated diseases (autoimmune and allergic), prolonged exposure to toxic agents, and unresolved acute inflammation.

1. **Persistent infections** by microorganisms that are difficult to eradicate, such as mycobacteria and certain viruses, fungi and parasites. These often evoke a T-lymphocyte reaction, delayed-type hypersensitivity, and sometimes a granulomatous reaction. Unresolved acute inflammation, such as a lung abscess following bacterial pneumonia, may evolve into chronic inflammation.
2. **Hypersensitivity (immune-mediated) diseases**, in which immune responses develop against the individual's own tissues (autoimmune diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis and multiple sclerosis), against microbes in an unregulated way (inflammatory bowel disease), or against common environmental substances (bronchial asthma). Repeated bouts of inflammation produce mixed acute and chronic patterns, with fibrosis in the late stage.
3. **Prolonged exposure to toxic agents**, exogenous (non-degradable particulate silica causing silicosis) or endogenous (excess cholesterol and lipids causing atherosclerosis).

Foreign bodies that persist impede healing by perpetuating chronic inflammation.


## Morphological features of chronic inflammation.

Chronic inflammation shows infiltration by mononuclear cells (macrophages, lymphocytes, plasma cells), tissue destruction, and attempts at healing by angiogenesis and fibrosis.

In contrast to acute inflammation, which is manifested by vascular changes, oedema and neutrophilic infiltration, chronic inflammation is characterised by:

1. **Infiltration by mononuclear cells**: macrophages, lymphocytes and plasma cells. Eosinophils, mast cells and sometimes neutrophils may also be present, and lymphoid follicles (tertiary lymphoid structures) may form.
2. **Tissue destruction**, induced by the persistent offending agent or by the inflammatory cells (their enzymes, oxygen radicals and cytokines). In the lung, for example, normal alveoli are replaced by spaces lined by cuboidal epithelium.
3. **Attempts at healing by connective tissue replacement**, through proliferation of small blood vessels (angiogenesis) and especially fibrosis.

Granulomatous inflammation, with epithelioid cells, giant cells and often necrosis, is a distinctive pattern.


## Common examples of chronic inflammation.

Common examples of chronic inflammation are tuberculosis, leprosy, chronic osteomyelitis, rheumatoid arthritis, chronic peptic ulcer, inflammatory bowel disease, silicosis and atherosclerosis.

- **Chronic infections:** tuberculosis, leprosy, syphilis, chronic osteomyelitis, chronic lung abscess, chronic viral hepatitis, fungal infections.
- **Immune-mediated:** rheumatoid arthritis, multiple sclerosis, Hashimoto thyroiditis, Crohn disease and ulcerative colitis, bronchial asthma (chronic form), psoriasis.
- **Toxic and particulate agents:** silicosis, asbestosis, smoking-related lung injury, atherosclerosis.
- **Unresolved acute inflammation:** chronic peptic ulcer, chronic cholecystitis, chronic pyelonephritis, chronic bronchitis.
- **Foreign-body reactions** and gout (urate crystals).


## Macrophage is the central cell of chronic inflammation / role of macrophage in chronic inflammation.

The macrophage is the dominant cell of chronic inflammation because it phagocytoses microbes and dead tissue, secretes cytokines and growth factors, presents antigen to T cells and interacts with them in a self-perpetuating cycle, and initiates repair and fibrosis, but the same products cause tissue destruction.

**Origin.** Macrophages are tissue cells derived from bone-marrow haematopoietic stem cells (via blood monocytes, which have a half-life of about 1 day) in postnatal life and, for tissue-resident populations such as Kupffer cells, microglia and alveolar macrophages, from yolk-sac and foetal liver progenitors in embryonic life. Tissue macrophages live months to years. In inflammation monocytes emigrate early, and within 48 hours may predominate. Macrophage accumulation persists through continuous recruitment and local proliferation.

**Functions in chronic inflammation.**

1. Like neutrophils, they ingest and destroy microbes and dead tissue.
2. They initiate tissue repair and take part in scar formation and fibrosis, secreting growth factors (PDGF, FGF, TGF-β) and cytokines that stimulate fibroblast and endothelial proliferation.
3. They secrete mediators of inflammation (TNF, IL-1, chemokines and eicosanoids), thereby initiating and propagating the response.
4. They display antigens to T lymphocytes and respond to T-cell signals, forming a feedback loop. Macrophages produce IL-12, which promotes Th1 cells; Th1 cells release IFN-γ, which activates macrophages; T cells also secrete TNF, IL-17 and chemokines that recruit more monocytes. This bidirectional cycle sustains chronic inflammation and leads to granuloma formation.

**Activation pathways.**

| | Classical (M1) | Alternative (M2) |
|---|---|---|
| Inducers | Microbial products (LPS), IFN-γ, crystals | IL-4, IL-13 |
| Products | NO, ROS, lysosomal enzymes, inflammatory cytokines | Growth factors, TGF-β; anti-inflammatory |
| Role | Kill microbes and promote inflammation | Terminate inflammation, tissue repair and fibrosis |

In reality most reactions contain both types, and intermediate phenotypes exist.

**Fate.** If the irritant is eliminated macrophages die off or pass into lymphatics; if not, they accumulate and may become epithelioid cells or fuse into giant cells. The same arsenal of mediators that destroys microbes causes much of the tissue injury of chronic inflammation, so tissue destruction is one of its hallmarks.


## Define granuloma with an example.

A granuloma is a focal collection of activated macrophages (epithelioid cells), usually with a surrounding collar of lymphocytes and often with multinucleate giant cells and sometimes central necrosis, formed as a cellular attempt to contain an agent that is difficult to eradicate; the classic example is the tubercle of tuberculosis.

Granulomatous inflammation is a form of chronic inflammation characterised by collections of activated macrophages, often with T lymphocytes, and sometimes associated with necrosis. The name derives from the granular macroscopic appearance of the foci. It represents an attempt to wall off an offending agent that is resistant to eradication, and involves strong activation of macrophages and T lymphocytes, which can injure normal tissue.

**Morphology.** In H&E sections the activated macrophages have abundant pink granular cytoplasm and indistinct cell boundaries, resembling epithelial cells (epithelioid cells). Aggregates of epithelioid cells are surrounded by a collar of lymphocytes, and older granulomas have a rim of fibroblasts and connective tissue. Multinucleate giant cells 40 to 50 μm across, formed by fusion of activated macrophages, are frequently found (Langhans giant cells). In granulomas associated with certain organisms, most classically Mycobacterium tuberculosis, a central zone of caseous necrosis develops, from hypoxia and free radical injury; it appears as amorphous, structureless, eosinophilic granular debris without cellular outlines. Healing is accompanied by fibrosis.

**Example: tuberculosis.** The tubercle is a caseating granuloma: central caseous necrosis surrounded by epithelioid cells, Langhans giant cells, a peripheral rim of lymphocytes and fibroblasts, and acid-fast bacilli demonstrated by the Ziehl-Neelsen stain. Other examples are leprosy, syphilis, sarcoidosis (noncaseating), Crohn disease and foreign-body reactions.


## How is a granuloma formed?

A granuloma forms when a persistent antigen or inert foreign body cannot be eliminated; in immune granulomas, antigen-presenting macrophages activate CD4⁺ T cells, which secrete IFN-γ that further activates macrophages, transforming them into epithelioid cells and giant cells.

1. A persistent microbe or other chronic stimulus is engulfed by macrophages and dendritic cells, which present its antigens to T cells.
2. Macrophages secrete IL-12 (and other cytokines), which drives Th1 differentiation.
3. Th1 cells secrete IFN-γ, which activates macrophages by the classical pathway; TNF, IL-17 and chemokines recruit more monocytes.
4. Activated macrophages become epithelioid cells; some fuse to form multinucleate giant cells.
5. Lymphocytes form a surrounding collar; with time, fibroblasts and connective tissue form a rim.
6. In tuberculosis, hypoxia and free radical-mediated injury cause central caseous necrosis.

In foreign-body granulomas, macrophages cannot ingest a large inert particle (talc, suture), so epithelioid cells and giant cells are applied to its surface without a T-cell immune response. In schistosomiasis, granulomas are associated with Th2 responses and eosinophils.


## Types of granuloma.

There are two types of granuloma: foreign-body granulomas, which form around inert material without T-cell involvement, and immune granulomas, which result from persistent T cell-mediated immune responses.

| | Foreign-body granuloma | Immune granuloma |
|---|---|---|
| Stimulus | Inert, non-immunogenic foreign body too large for phagocytosis (talc, suture, fibres) | Persistent microbe or chronic stimulus that activates T cells |
| Mechanism | Inflammation without a specific T cell-mediated response | Th1 response, IFN-γ-activated macrophages (Th2 and eosinophils in schistosomiasis) |
| Morphology | Epithelioid and giant cells against the foreign body, which may be seen within giant cells, refractile in polarised light | Epithelioid cells, giant cells, lymphocyte collar; caseation in tuberculosis |

Granulomas are also divided morphologically into caseating (tuberculosis) and noncaseating (sarcoidosis, Crohn disease, foreign-body reactions).


## Examples of granulomatous inflammation.

Examples of granulomatous inflammation are tuberculosis, leprosy, syphilis, cat-scratch disease, sarcoidosis and Crohn disease, as well as foreign-body reactions and schistosomiasis.

| Disease | Aetiology | Tissue reaction |
|---|---|---|
| Tuberculosis | Mycobacterium tuberculosis | Caseating granulomas (tubercles): epithelioid cells, Langhans giant cells, lymphocytes, central caseous necrosis, acid-fast bacilli |
| Leprosy | Mycobacterium leprae | Acid-fast bacilli within macrophages; noncaseating granulomas |
| Syphilis | Treponema pallidum | Gumma: central coagulative necrosis with preserved cell outlines, surrounded by histiocytes and plasma cells |
| Cat-scratch disease | Bartonella henselae | Stellate granuloma with central granular debris and neutrophils; giant cells uncommon |
| Sarcoidosis | Unknown | Noncaseating granulomas with abundant activated macrophages |
| Crohn disease | Immune reaction against intestinal bacteria, possibly self-antigens | Occasional noncaseating granulomas in the intestinal wall |
| Foreign-body reactions | Talc, suture, silica | Noncaseating foreign-body granulomas |
| Schistosomiasis | Helminth eggs | Granulomas with eosinophils (Th2) |

Tuberculosis should always be excluded when granulomas are seen.


## Morphological features of chronic granulomatous inflammation.

Chronic granulomatous inflammation shows aggregates of epithelioid macrophages with multinucleate giant cells, surrounded by a collar of lymphocytes and sometimes a rim of fibroblasts, with central caseous necrosis in tuberculosis.

- **Grossly,** the foci are granular; caseous necrosis has a granular, cheesy appearance.
- **Epithelioid cells:** activated macrophages with pink granular cytoplasm and indistinct cell boundaries.
- **Giant cells:** multinucleate, 40 to 50 μm, Langhans type (nuclei arranged peripherally), formed by fusion of macrophages.
- **Lymphocytes** (mainly T cells) form a collar around the aggregate; plasma cells may be present.
- **Fibroblasts and connective tissue** rim in older lesions; healing by fibrosis, which may be extensive.
- **Necrosis:** central caseous necrosis, with amorphous, structureless, eosinophilic granular debris and complete loss of cellular detail, as in tuberculosis. Crohn disease, sarcoidosis and foreign-body reactions are noncaseating.
- Organisms may be seen with special stains (acid-fast for tubercle bacilli), and foreign material may be seen in polarised light.


## Write a short note on granulomatous inflammation.

**Definition.** Granulomatous inflammation is a distinctive form of chronic inflammation characterised by collections of activated macrophages, often with T lymphocytes, and sometimes with necrosis. A granuloma is a cellular attempt to contain an offending agent that is difficult to eradicate.

**Types and pathogenesis.** Foreign-body granulomas form around inert materials (talc, suture, fibres) too large for phagocytosis and are not immunogenic, so there is no T-cell response. Immune granulomas are caused by agents that induce a persistent T cell-mediated response. Antigen-presenting macrophages stimulate Th1 cells through IL-12; Th1 cells produce IFN-γ, which activates macrophages; and a macrophage-T-cell cycle sustains the reaction. In schistosomiasis a Th2 response with eosinophils is seen.

**Morphology.** Activated macrophages with abundant pink cytoplasm resemble epithelium (epithelioid cells), are surrounded by a collar of lymphocytes, and may fuse into Langhans giant cells (40 to 50 μm). Older granulomas have a rim of fibroblasts. Hypoxia and free radical injury produce central caseous necrosis in tuberculosis; granulomas of Crohn disease, sarcoidosis and foreign-body reactions are noncaseating. Healing causes fibrosis.

**Causes.** Tuberculosis, leprosy, syphilis, cat-scratch disease, fungal and parasitic infections, sarcoidosis, Crohn disease, foreign materials.

**Significance.** The limited number of causes (some life-threatening) makes recognition important; tuberculosis must always be excluded, and the aetiologic agent should be identified by special stains (acid-fast), culture, PCR or serology. Activation of macrophages and T cells may itself cause tissue damage, and TNF antagonists can reactivate tuberculosis by impairing granuloma maintenance.


## Mention the types/etiological classification of granuloma with examples.

Granulomas are classified by pathogenesis into foreign-body and immune types, and by aetiology as follows (Table 3.9).

| Aetiological group | Examples | Type of granuloma |
|---|---|---|
| Bacterial | Tuberculosis (caseating), leprosy (noncaseating, bacilli in macrophages), syphilis (gumma), cat-scratch disease (stellate), brucellosis | Immune |
| Fungal | Histoplasmosis, cryptococcosis, blastomycosis, coccidioidomycosis | Immune |
| Parasitic | Schistosomiasis (egg granuloma with eosinophils; Th2) | Immune |
| Foreign bodies / chemical | Talc, suture material, silica, beryllium, urate crystals (gout) | Foreign-body (beryllium is immune) |
| Idiopathic or immune-mediated | Sarcoidosis, Crohn disease | Immune (noncaseating) |

Morphologically they are separated into **caseating** granulomas (tuberculosis, with central amorphous eosinophilic granular necrosis) and **noncaseating** granulomas (sarcoidosis, Crohn disease, foreign-body reactions, leprosy). Syphilitic gumma shows coagulative necrosis with preserved cell outlines.


## Draw and label a tubercular (typical) granuloma.

The following schematic shows a typical tuberculous granuloma (tubercle) in cross-section, with concentric zones from the centre outward.

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
╱ Fibroblasts / collagen rim (outermost) ╲
│ ┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│ ╱ Collar of lymphocytes (mostly T cells) ╲ │
│ │ ┌────────────────────────────────────┐ │ │
│ │ ╱ Epithelioid cells (activated ╲ │ │
│ │ │ macrophages) + Langhans giant cells │ │ │
│ │ │ ┌──────────────────────────────┐ │ │ │
│ │ │ │ CENTRAL CASEOUS NECROSIS │ │ │ │
│ │ │ │ (amorphous, granular, │ │ │ │
│ │ │ │ eosinophilic debris; │ │ │ │
│ │ │ │ AFB seen with ZN stain) │ │ │ │
│ │ │ └──────────────────────────────┘ │ │ │
│ │ ╲ ╱ │ │
│ ╲ └────────────────────────────────────┘ ╱ │
│ └─────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
╲ ╱
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

**Labels.**

1. **Central zone of caseous necrosis**: structureless, granular, eosinophilic debris with complete loss of cellular outlines (cheesy on gross); acid-fast bacilli may be demonstrated with the Ziehl-Neelsen stain.
2. **Epithelioid cells**: activated macrophages with abundant pink granular cytoplasm and indistinct cell boundaries, arranged around the necrosis (palisading).
3. **Langhans giant cells**: large multinucleate cells (40 to 50 μm) with nuclei arranged in a horseshoe or peripheral ring, formed by the fusion of macrophages.
4. **Lymphocytes** (a collar of mainly CD4⁺ T cells) at the periphery of the epithelioid zone.
5. **Fibroblasts and connective tissue** rim in older granulomas, indicating healing by fibrosis.


## How does immune granuloma form?

An immune granuloma is the result of a persistent T cell-mediated immune (delayed-type hypersensitivity) response to a microbe or other chronic stimulus that cannot be eliminated. It is the typical consequence of prolonged interaction between T cells and macrophages. The steps are as follows.

1. **Antigen uptake and presentation.** Macrophages and dendritic cells ingest the persistent agent (for example tubercle bacilli), process it, and display its peptides to CD4⁺ T lymphocytes, together with costimulators.
2. **T-cell activation and differentiation.** Macrophages produce IL-12 and other cytokines, which drive differentiation of naive CD4⁺ cells into Th1 cells (in some parasitic infections, such as schistosomiasis, strong Th2 responses with eosinophils; Th17 cells contribute through IL-17, which recruits neutrophils and monocytes).
3. **Macrophage activation.** Th1 cells secrete IFN-γ, which activates macrophages by the classical pathway, enhancing their ability to kill microbes (NO, ROS, lysosomal enzymes). TNF, IL-17 and chemokines recruit further monocytes from the blood.
4. **Feedback loop.** Activated macrophages again present antigen and secrete IL-12, stimulating more T cells, which produce more cytokines; this bidirectional cycle propagates and sustains the reaction.
5. **Formation of epithelioid and giant cells.** Strongly activated macrophages acquire abundant cytoplasm and resemble epithelial cells (epithelioid cells); some fuse into multinucleate giant cells.
6. **Organisation of the granuloma.** Lymphocytes cluster around the macrophage mass; with time, fibroblasts deposit connective tissue around it.
7. **Necrosis and healing.** In tuberculosis, hypoxia and free radical injury cause central caseous necrosis. Healing is accompanied by fibrosis which may be extensive.

Granuloma formation is therefore a protective attempt to wall off an agent resistant to eradication, but it can injure normal tissue and cause fibrosis.


## Give the immunopathogenesis of TB granuloma.

Mycobacterium tuberculosis is inhaled in droplets and ingested by alveolar macrophages, in which it survives by inhibiting phagosome-lysosome fusion and thereby multiplies in the first weeks. Infected macrophages and dendritic cells transport antigen to regional lymph nodes, and after about 2 to 4 weeks a cell-mediated immune response (delayed-type hypersensitivity) develops.

1. Antigen-presenting macrophages and dendritic cells secrete **IL-12**, which drives differentiation of CD4⁺ **Th1** cells.
2. Th1 cells secrete **IFN-γ**, which activates macrophages: phagosome-lysosome fusion is restored, and macrophages produce nitric oxide, reactive oxygen species and lysosomal enzymes that kill or inhibit the bacilli. **TNF** secreted by macrophages and T cells recruits monocytes and is essential for maintaining the granuloma; patients treated with TNF antagonists may reactivate latent infection.
3. Activated macrophages transform into **epithelioid cells** and fuse into **Langhans giant cells**; lymphocytes form a surrounding collar and fibroblasts, a rim.
4. **Caseous necrosis** develops centrally because of hypoxia, free radical injury and the cytotoxic effect of T-cell and macrophage products; it limits bacillary growth because of its low oxygen tension and low pH.
5. The primary lesion, with involved hilar nodes, forms the Ghon complex, which heals by fibrosis and calcification. Failure of immunity (HIV infection, malnutrition, immunosuppression, TNF blockade) allows progressive disease, and reactivation or reinfection produces secondary tuberculosis.

The same immune response that controls the infection causes tissue destruction through caseation, which is why the host response contributes more to the pathology than the organism itself.


## Define a giant cell.

A giant cell is a large multinucleate cell; inflammatory giant cells are formed by the fusion of activated macrophages in granulomatous inflammation.

They are seen in granulomas and contain a large mass of cytoplasm and many nuclei. Langhans giant cells, 40 to 50 μm across, derive from the fusion of multiple activated macrophages. Other physiological multinucleate cells include osteoclasts and syncytiotrophoblast, and giant cells may be seen in some tumours, but the term "inflammatory giant cell" refers to those derived from macrophages.


## Names / types of inflammatory giant cells with examples.

The main inflammatory giant cells are the Langhans type, with nuclei arranged at the periphery in a horseshoe, seen in tuberculosis, and the foreign-body type, with randomly scattered nuclei, seen in foreign-body granulomas; Touton giant cells are seen in lipid-rich lesions.

| Type | Nuclear arrangement | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| Langhans giant cell | Nuclei peripheral, horseshoe or ring | Tuberculosis, sarcoidosis, other immune granulomas |
| Foreign-body giant cell | Nuclei scattered haphazardly | Foreign-body reactions (suture, talc, silica); also seen in tuberculosis, sarcoidosis, fat necrosis |
| Touton giant cell | Ring of nuclei around a central homogeneous cytoplasm with foamy peripheral cytoplasm | Xanthoma, fat necrosis, xanthogranuloma |
| Aschoff giant cell | Large cells with "owl-eye" or caterpillar nuclei | Rheumatic carditis (Aschoff nodule) |
| Warthin-Finkeldey cell | Multinucleate cells in lymphoid tissue | Measles |


## How are inflammatory giant cells formed?

Inflammatory giant cells form by fusion of multiple activated macrophages (epithelioid cells) under the influence of cytokines, in response to persistent stimuli that cannot be phagocytosed.

Monocytes recruited to a site of chronic inflammation differentiate into macrophages, which, when strongly and persistently activated by IFN-γ from Th1 cells (or by other cytokines such as IL-4 and IL-13 in foreign-body reactions), become epithelioid cells with abundant cytoplasm. Some of these cells fuse, through membrane fusion proteins, to form multinucleate giant cells. The stimulus is a large indigestible particle or a persistent microbe (frustrated phagocytosis), which the macrophage cannot engulf singly. The nuclei result from fusion of cells, not from nuclear division without cytokinesis. The giant cell has a large mass of cytoplasm and many nuclei, and in foreign-body granulomas the foreign material may be seen within the giant cell. In tuberculosis the peripheral arrangement of nuclei gives the Langhans pattern; in foreign-body reactions the nuclei are randomly distributed.

**Tissue Repair and Wound Healing**

**Regeneration and repair**


## Define regeneration.

Regeneration is the process by which some tissues replace the damaged components and essentially return to a normal state, by proliferation of surviving cells or from tissue stem cells.

Some tissues can replace the damaged components and essentially return to a normal state. Regeneration may occur by proliferation of differentiated cells that survive the injury and retain the capacity to proliferate, such as hepatocytes in the liver, or, particularly in the epithelia of the skin and intestines, by tissue stem cells and their progenitors, which live in specialised niches. It is driven by growth factors and depends critically on the integrity of the extracellular matrix. Regeneration occurs readily in labile tissues (as long as the stem cell pool is preserved) and in stable tissues (the liver being the model), but mammals have a limited capacity to regenerate most organs.


## Define repair.

Repair, also called healing, is the restoration of tissue architecture and function after injury, which occurs by regeneration of the parenchymal cells and by scarring, the deposition of connective tissue.

Repair is the response that follows inflammation, and the inflammatory response to microbes and injured tissue sets repair in motion. If the injured tissue is incapable of regeneration, or if the supporting framework is damaged, repair occurs by laying down fibrous tissue (scar). A fibrous scar is not normal tissue, but it usually gives enough structural stability for the tissue to function. In most injuries both regeneration and scarring contribute in varying degrees. Both processes involve cell proliferation and close interactions between cells and extracellular matrix.


## What is healing?

Healing is the body's response to injury in which damaged tissue is restored by regeneration of surviving cells and by filling of the defect with connective tissue (scar), so as to restore the integrity and function of the tissue; by convention "repair" is used for parenchyma and connective tissue and "healing" for surface epithelia, but the terms are used interchangeably.

Healing is critical to survival. The sequence in skin wounds, which is the best-studied model, includes:

1. **Haemostasis and inflammation.** Within minutes a platelet haemostatic plug and clot form; over 6 to 48 hours neutrophils and then monocytes clear the offending agents and debris.
2. **Cell proliferation (up to about 10 days).** Epithelial cells migrate over the wound; endothelial cells proliferate to form new vessels (angiogenesis); fibroblasts migrate in and lay down collagen. Together with macrophages they form granulation tissue.
3. **Deposition and remodelling of connective tissue.** Granulation tissue is replaced by collagen to form a stable fibrous scar, and remodelling by matrix metalloproteinases, balanced by their tissue inhibitors, increases tensile strength; scars contract through myofibroblasts.

Wounds heal by first intention (primary union) if clean and approximated, with epithelial regeneration and minimal scarring, or by second intention (secondary union) if larger or infected, with granulation tissue, scarring and contraction. Healing can be impaired by infection, diabetes, malnutrition, steroids, poor perfusion and mechanical factors.


## Types of cells on the basis of regenerating capability, with examples.

On the basis of regenerative capacity, cells are divided into labile (continuously dividing), stable (quiescent) and permanent (non-dividing) cells.

| Type | Behaviour | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| Labile (continuously dividing) | Continuously lost and replaced by stem cells and mature cell proliferation; regenerate readily if the stem cell pool is preserved | Haematopoietic cells of marrow; surface epithelia (stratified squamous epithelium of skin, mouth, oesophagus, vagina, cervix; cuboidal epithelium of ducts; columnar epithelium of gastrointestinal tract, uterus, fallopian tubes; transitional epithelium of urinary tract) |
| Stable (quiescent) | In G₀ with minimal proliferation normally, but divide in response to injury; limited regeneration except in liver | Parenchyma of liver, kidney, pancreas; endothelial cells, fibroblasts, smooth muscle cells |
| Permanent | Terminally differentiated, non-proliferative after birth; repair by scarring | Most neurons, cardiac muscle cells; skeletal muscle (limited regeneration by satellite cells) |


## What do you mean by regeneration and repair?

**Repair** (healing) refers to the restoration of tissue architecture and function after injury. It occurs by two processes: **regeneration**, which restores normal cells and structures, and **scarring** (fibrosis), the deposition of connective tissue.

**Regeneration** is the replacement of injured cells by cells of the same type, restoring normal tissue. It may occur by proliferation of surviving differentiated cells that retain proliferative capacity (hepatocytes), or by development of mature cells from tissue stem cells and progenitors in their niches (the epithelia of skin and intestine). It is driven by growth factors (HGF, TGF-α, EGF) and signals from the extracellular matrix and integrins, and it requires an intact connective tissue framework. The liver is the classic example: after partial hepatectomy, up to 90% can regenerate by proliferation of residual hepatocytes, primed by IL-6 from Kupffer cells and driven by HGF and TGF-α; when hepatocyte proliferation is impaired, as in chronic injury, progenitor cells in the canals of Hering contribute. Labile tissues regenerate readily, stable tissues can regenerate to a limited extent (except the liver), and permanent tissues (neurons, cardiac muscle) cannot.

**Repair by scarring** occurs when injury is severe or chronic, when the tissue is made of permanent or stable cells with limited proliferative capacity, or when the connective tissue framework is damaged. Its steps are clot formation, inflammation, angiogenesis with formation of granulation tissue, proliferation and migration of fibroblasts, collagen synthesis, and remodelling. Scar "patches" rather than restores tissue; for example, the replacement of necrotic myocardium after infarction by collagen.

| | Regeneration | Scarring |
|---|---|---|
| Result | Restitution of tissue | Replacement by connective tissue |
| Tissue | Labile, stable cells, intact framework | Permanent cells, damaged framework, severe injury |
| Example | Liver after hepatectomy; skin epithelium | Myocardial infarct; healing of a deep wound |


## What is granulation tissue?

Granulation tissue is formed by migration and proliferation of fibroblasts and deposition of loose connective tissue, together with new thin-walled vessels and interspersed mononuclear leukocytes, during healing; it is not to be confused with a granuloma.

Granulation tissue is formed by migration and proliferation of fibroblasts and deposition of loose connective tissue, together with the new vessels and interspersed mononuclear leukocytes. The name derives from the pink, soft, granular gross appearance, as seen beneath the scab of a skin wound. The amount formed depends on the size of the defect and the intensity of inflammation.

**Histology.** Proliferating fibroblasts and myofibroblasts; new, thin-walled, delicate capillaries (angiogenesis) with endothelial sprouts, perpendicular to the surface; loose, oedematous extracellular matrix; and inflammatory cells, mainly macrophages, with some lymphocytes, plasma cells and, early, neutrophils. Mature collagen is minimal at first.

**Formation.** Macrophages (mainly of the M2 type) clear debris and release growth factors (PDGF, FGF-2, TGF-β) and VEGF, which stimulate fibroblast proliferation and angiogenesis.

**Functions.** It fills the tissue defect, provides a scaffold and nutrients for repair, and is progressively replaced by collagen to form a scar with regression of vessels. Myofibroblasts bring about wound contraction.

**Abnormalities.** Excessive granulation tissue protruding above the surrounding skin (exuberant granulation, "proud flesh") blocks re-epithelialisation and must be cauterised or excised.


## Morphological features of granulation tissue.

Grossly granulation tissue is pink, soft and granular, and microscopically it shows proliferating fibroblasts and delicate new capillaries in a loose, oedematous matrix with macrophages and other inflammatory cells.

**Gross:** pink to red, soft, moist, granular surface ("granules" correspond to loops of new capillaries), friable and bleeds easily; painless because it has no nerve fibres; seen beneath a scab or in the floor of an ulcer.

**Microscopic:**

- Numerous new thin-walled capillaries lined by plump endothelial cells, often oriented perpendicular to the wound surface.
- Proliferating fibroblasts (and myofibroblasts) in a loose extracellular matrix of fibronectin, proteoglycans and early (type III) collagen; mature collagen minimal (seen with trichrome stain).
- Oedema.
- Inflammatory cells, mainly macrophages, with lymphocytes, plasma cells and occasional neutrophils.
- With time, more collagen is deposited, the number of vessels and cells decreases, and the tissue becomes a pale avascular scar.


## Define wound healing.

Wound healing is the complex, orderly process by which an injured tissue, most commonly skin, repairs itself through haemostasis and inflammation, cell proliferation with granulation tissue formation, and deposition and remodelling of connective tissue.

Skin wound healing illustrates the principles of repair by regeneration and scarring because it can be observed and defined precisely. The main phases are inflammation, formation of granulation tissue (epithelial migration, angiogenesis, fibroblast proliferation), and extracellular matrix remodelling. It is orchestrated by growth factors and cytokines from platelets, macrophages and other cells, and the final result is a fibrous scar covered by epithelium. Healing may occur by primary or secondary union.


## Classify wound healing.

Skin wound healing is classified into healing by first intention (primary union) and healing by second intention (secondary union), according to the extent of tissue injury and the dominant mechanism of healing.

| Feature | First intention (primary union) | Second intention (secondary union) |
|---|---|---|
| Wound | Clean, uninfected, surgically incised with edges approximated (sutured) | Large, gaping wound with tissue loss, infected, or with wide edges |
| Clot/necrosis | Minimal | Abundant fibrin clot and debris |
| Inflammation | Mild | Intense |
| Granulation tissue | Scanty | Abundant |
| Mechanism | Mainly epithelial regeneration | Regeneration and scarring |
| Wound contraction | Minimal | Marked (myofibroblasts) |
| Scar | Thin | Large, may cause contracture |
| Time | Short | Prolonged |

Third intention (delayed primary closure) refers to closure of a wound by suturing after infection has been controlled and the wound cleaned.


## Factors that influence wound healing / tissue repair.

Wound healing is influenced by local and systemic factors: infection, diabetes, glucocorticoids, nutritional deficiency (protein and vitamin C), ageing, poor perfusion, mechanical factors, foreign bodies, and the type and location of the injury.

Variables that modify repair may be extrinsic or intrinsic to the injured tissue, and local or systemic:

- **Infection** is clinically one of the most important causes of delayed healing; it prolongs inflammation and increases local tissue injury.
- **Diabetes** compromises repair in many ways and is one of the most important systemic causes of abnormal wound healing.
- **Glucocorticoids** have anti-inflammatory effects and may weaken scars by inhibiting TGF-β production and fibrosis (this effect is sometimes desirable, as in corneal infection).
- **Nutritional status:** protein deficiency and vitamin C deficiency inhibit collagen synthesis and retard healing.
- **Ageing** reduces the capacity to heal.
- **Mechanical factors:** excessive mobility interferes with apposition of wound edges (fractures, skin grafts); increased local pressure or torsion may pull wounds apart.
- **Poor perfusion** from peripheral vascular disease, atherosclerosis, diabetes or obstructed venous drainage (varicose veins).
- **Foreign bodies** (steel, glass, bone fragments) perpetuate chronic inflammation.
- **Type and extent of tissue injury, and character of the tissue:** complete restoration occurs only in tissues of stable and labile cells; permanent cells result in scarring.
- **Location:** inflammation in tissue spaces (pleura, peritoneum, synovium) produces large exudates; these may undergo resolution, or granulation tissue may grow in (organisation).


## Mention the complications of wound healing.

The complications of wound healing include defective healing (chronic wounds, infection, dehiscence), excessive scarring (hypertrophic scar, keloid, exuberant granulation), and contracture; other complications are haematoma, adhesions, fistula or sinus, traumatic neuroma, implantation cyst and malignant change.

Complications of tissue repair can arise from abnormalities in any of the basic components of the process: deficient scar formation, excessive formation of the repair components, and formation of contractures.

**1. Defects in healing (deficient repair)**

- **Chronic wounds and ulcers**, caused by local and systemic factors:
- Venous leg ulcers in elderly people with chronic venous hypertension (varicose veins, congestive heart failure), with haemosiderin deposition and chronic inflammation; they do not heal because of poor oxygen delivery.
- Arterial ulcers from peripheral atherosclerosis, especially in diabetes: ischaemia causes atrophy and necrosis; they are painful.
- Diabetic ulcers of the feet, due to vascular disease causing ischaemia, neuropathy and secondary infection; histologically epithelial ulceration with extensive granulation tissue.
- Pressure sores from prolonged compression against bone with local ischaemia.
- **Wound infection**, delaying healing and increasing tissue injury.
- **Wound dehiscence** is reopening of a surgical incision, internally or externally; risk factors are obesity, malnutrition, infection, vascular insufficiency and mechanical factors (in abdominal wounds, vomiting and coughing). Evisceration and incisional hernia are associated complications.

**2. Excessive formation of the components of repair**

- **Hypertrophic scar:** a raised scar from excess collagen with abundant myofibroblasts, confined to the wound boundary, often after thermal or traumatic injury involving the deep dermis; tends to regress over several months.
- **Keloid:** scar tissue growing beyond the boundaries of the original wound, which does not regress and recurs after excision; individual predisposition (more common in dark-skinned individuals).
- **Exuberant granulation ("proud flesh"):** excess granulation tissue protruding above the skin and blocking re-epithelialisation; requires cautery or excision.
- **Desmoid (aggressive fibromatosis):** rarely, exuberant fibroblastic proliferation after incisional scars or trauma that recurs after excision; a benign neoplasm.

**3. Contracture.** Exaggeration of wound contraction causes deformity of the wound and surrounding tissues and compromises joint movement; particularly prone are the palms, soles and anterior thorax, notably after serious burns.

**4. Other complications.** Haematoma or seroma formation; adhesions after peritoneal or pleural inflammation; fistula or sinus; epidermal implantation (inclusion) cyst; traumatic neuroma; changes in pigmentation; and malignant transformation in chronic scars or ulcers (Marjolin ulcer).


## How does diabetes mellitus impair wound healing?

Diabetes impairs wound healing by causing vascular disease with ischaemia, neuropathy, increased susceptibility to infection from defective leukocyte function, and impaired growth-factor-driven angiogenesis and collagen synthesis.

Diabetes is a metabolic disease that compromises tissue repair for many reasons and is one of the most important systemic causes of abnormal wound healing. The mechanisms are:

- **Vascular disease.** Atherosclerosis of large vessels and microangiopathy (thickened basement membranes) reduce blood flow and oxygen delivery, causing ischaemia and poor healing.
- **Neuropathy.** Loss of sensation, particularly in the feet, allows repeated unnoticed trauma and pressure; autonomic neuropathy reduces perfusion and sweating.
- **Infection.** Hyperglycaemia impairs neutrophil function (chemotaxis, phagocytosis and killing), so infection is frequent and prolongs inflammation.
- **Impaired repair responses.** Defective growth factor production and endothelial dysfunction reduce angiogenesis; fibroblast proliferation and collagen synthesis are decreased and ECM turnover abnormal, in part because of advanced glycation end-products.
- **Consequence.** Diabetic ulcers, particularly of the feet, show tissue necrosis, chronic inflammation, failure to heal, and are a major cause of gangrene and amputation.


## What is angiogenesis?

Angiogenesis is the formation of new blood vessels, which in tumours takes the form of neoangiogenesis, the sprouting of new vessels from pre-existing capillaries; it is essential for tumour growth beyond 1 to 2 mm in diameter.

A solid tumour, even if it carries all the genetic aberrations required for malignant transformation, cannot enlarge beyond 1 to 2 mm unless it can induce a blood supply, since this distance is the maximum across which oxygen, nutrients and waste products can diffuse from existing vessels. Early in their development most tumours do not induce angiogenesis and remain small or in situ, possibly for years, until an "angiogenic switch" terminates this stage of quiescence. Angiogenesis is controlled by a balance between angiogenesis promoters and inhibitors, and in tumours this balance is tilted in favour of the promoters. Angiogenesis is therefore an essential requirement for malignancy.

Angiogenesis is also critical in healing at sites of injury and in the development of collateral circulation at sites of ischaemia.

**Steps.** In tissue repair angiogenesis occurs mainly by sprouting:

1. Vasodilation in response to nitric oxide and increased permeability induced by vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF).
2. Separation of pericytes from the abluminal surface and breakdown of the basement membrane by matrix metalloproteinases to allow formation of a vessel sprout.
3. Migration of endothelial cells toward the area of tissue injury.
4. Proliferation of endothelial cells just behind the leading "tip" cell.
5. Remodelling into capillary tubes.
6. Recruitment of periendothelial cells (pericytes for small capillaries, smooth muscle cells for larger vessels) to form the mature vessel.
7. Suppression of endothelial proliferation and migration and deposition of the basement membrane.

**Mediators.** VEGF-A (mainly) stimulates endothelial migration and proliferation, the "angiogenic switch", promotes vasodilation through NO and helps form the lumen. FGF-2 stimulates endothelial proliferation and the migration of macrophages and fibroblasts. Angiopoietins 1 and 2 contribute to the structural maturation of vessels. PDGF recruits smooth muscle cells, and TGF-β suppresses endothelial proliferation and enhances ECM production, thereby stabilising the vessel. The Notch pathway regulates sprouting and branching so that new vessels are properly spaced. Matrix metalloproteinases degrade ECM to permit extension of the vessel, and integrin-ECM interactions provide scaffold.

**Angiogenesis in tumours.** Growing cancers stimulate neoangiogenesis, in which new vessels sprout from capillaries. A solid tumour cannot enlarge beyond 1 to 2 mm unless it induces angiogenesis, and early in their development most tumours do not do so until an "angiogenic switch" occurs. Hypoxia stabilises HIF1α, which activates the transcription of VEGF and bFGF. Tumour vessels are leaky, dilated and haphazardly connected, and angiogenesis also contributes to metastasis.


## Mention the factors influencing/delaying wound healing.
