Wound healing may be delayed or impaired by factors that are intrinsic or extrinsic to the injured tissue, and local or systemic.

| Factor | Effect on healing |
|---|---|
| **Infection** | One of the most important causes of delayed healing; prolongs inflammation and increases tissue injury |
| **Diabetes mellitus** | Vascular disease, neuropathy, impaired leukocyte function and infection, impaired angiogenesis and collagen synthesis |
| **Glucocorticoids** | Anti-inflammatory; inhibit TGF-β production and fibrosis, weakening the scar |
| **Nutritional deficiency** | Protein deficiency and vitamin C deficiency inhibit collagen synthesis; (zinc deficiency also delays healing) |
| **Ageing** | Reduced capacity to heal injured tissue |
| **Poor perfusion** | Peripheral vascular disease, atherosclerosis, varicose veins and obstructed venous drainage reduce oxygen and nutrients |
| **Mechanical factors** | Excessive mobility, increased local pressure or torsion pull wound edges apart (fractures, skin grafts, abdominal wounds) |
| **Foreign bodies** | Fragments of steel, glass or bone, or suture material perpetuate chronic inflammation |
| **Type, size and extent of injury** | Larger defects require more granulation tissue; extensive necrosis and crush injury delay healing |
| **Tissue type** | Labile and stable tissues regenerate; permanent cells heal by scarring |
| **Location** | Wounds over joints and areas of tension, and inflammation in body cavities, heal differently |
| **Other** | Obesity, smoking, uraemia, radiation, cytotoxic drugs, haematoma, oedema |


## Mention the sequential steps of healing by first intention (primary union).

Healing by first intention occurs when a clean, uninfected surgical incision has its edges well approximated, so that there is only a minimal gap to fill, scarring is minimal and restitution occurs mainly by epithelial regeneration. The sequence is as follows.

1. **Immediately after injury (first hours).** The incision space fills with blood containing fibrin and blood cells; dehydration of the surface forms a scab that covers the wound. Haemostasis is secured by platelet plug and clot.
2. **Within 24 hours.** Neutrophils appear at the margins of the incision and migrate toward the fibrin clot (acute inflammation). Epithelial cells at the edges begin to proliferate and migrate.
3. **24 to 48 hours.** Epithelial cells from both edges migrate and grow along the dermis beneath the scab, fusing in the midline to form a thin continuous epithelial layer.
4. **Day 3.** Neutrophils are replaced largely by macrophages; granulation tissue progressively invades the incision space. Collagen fibres appear at the margins but do not yet bridge the incision. Epithelial proliferation continues, thickening the epidermal layer.
5. **Day 5.** Neovascularisation reaches its peak and granulation tissue fills the incisional space. Collagen fibrils become abundant and begin to bridge the incision. The epidermis recovers its normal thickness and differentiation, with surface keratinisation.
6. **Week 2.** There is continued accumulation of collagen and proliferation of fibroblasts. The leukocyte infiltrate, oedema and increased vascularity substantially disappear; the long process of "blanching" begins, accomplished by increasing collagen deposition within the incisional scar and regression of vascular channels.
7. **End of the first month.** The scar is composed of a cellular connective tissue largely devoid of inflammatory infiltrate, covered by intact epidermis. The dermal appendages destroyed in the line of incision are permanently lost. Tensile strength of the wound increases with time (about 10% of normal at the end of the first week, and reaching about 70% to 80% by about 3 months) as type III collagen is replaced by type I and the matrix is remodelled by metalloproteinases.


## Write a short note on keloid.

**Definition.** A keloid is an exuberant scar formed by excessive deposition of collagen, which grows beyond the boundaries of the original wound, does not regress, and tends to recur after excision.

**Aetiopathogenesis.** Keloid formation seems to be an individual predisposition, with a familial tendency and higher incidence in dark-skinned individuals (African, Asian), and in young adults. It follows trauma, surgical incision, burns, vaccination, acne or ear piercing. It arises from excessive activity of fibroblasts, with overproduction of TGF-β and other growth factors, increased collagen synthesis and deficient collagen degradation (imbalance of MMPs and their inhibitors). Typical sites are the earlobes, sternum, shoulders, upper back and face.

**Morphology.** Grossly it is a firm, raised, shiny, sometimes pruritic or tender scar with claw-like extensions, which may be erythematous in light skin and hyperpigmented in dark skin. Microscopically there is a thick mass of hyalinised, glassy, eosinophilic, haphazardly arranged collagen bundles in the dermis, with few fibroblasts and a flattened epidermis, and absence of adnexa.

**Comparison with hypertrophic scar.**

| | Hypertrophic scar | Keloid |
|---|---|---|
| Extent | Remains within wound boundary | Extends beyond wound |
| Onset | Soon after injury, grows rapidly | Months after injury |
| Regression | Regresses over months | Does not regress |
| Recurrence after excision | Uncommon | Frequent |
| Predisposition | Deep dermal injury | Genetic; dark skin |
| Cells and collagen | Many myofibroblasts, thin parallel collagen | Thick, hyalinised collagen bundles |

**Treatment** includes intralesional corticosteroids, pressure and silicone sheeting, cryotherapy, surgical excision combined with radiotherapy or steroids, and laser.


## A 30y African-American lady has a raised scar larger than the incision, recurring after excision. What is your probable diagnosis?

The probable diagnosis is **keloid**.

The scar is raised and extends beyond the boundaries of the original incision, which distinguishes keloid from hypertrophic scar (confined to the wound margins and tending to regress over several months). Recurrence after excision and an individual predisposition, seen especially in dark-skinned people, are characteristic. Keloids result from excessive production of collagen (an imbalance in the repair process with excess ECM deposition, with TGF-β and fibroblast overactivity). Histology shows thick, hyalinised, eosinophilic collagen bundles in the dermis. The condition is benign but cosmetically disfiguring, and may be itchy or tender. Treatment is by intralesional steroids, silicone, pressure, cryotherapy, or excision combined with adjuvant radiotherapy or steroids.

**Clinical Scenarios**

**Inflammation cases**


## Painful, red, warm swelling (leg in a 15-year-old girl) / pain and swelling in the right inguinal region of a 10-year-old boy for 7 days — Likely diagnosis? Chemical mediators responsible for the signs (pain and swelling)?

This is acute inflammation, most probably an acute suppurative infection (cellulitis or abscess of the leg, and acute lymphadenitis with possible abscess in the inguinal region), with pain due to prostaglandins, bradykinin and substance P, and swelling due to histamine, bradykinin, leukotrienes and other permeability-increasing mediators.

**Diagnosis.** A painful, red, warm swelling is the combination of the cardinal signs of acute inflammation: dolor, rubor, calor and tumour. In the 15-year-old girl, with a swollen leg, the likely diagnosis is acute pyogenic inflammation (cellulitis or an early abscess) due to bacterial infection, usually staphylococcal or streptococcal, through a break in the skin. In the 10-year-old boy with a 7-day painful inguinal swelling, the likely diagnosis is acute (suppurative) lymphadenitis of the inguinal lymph nodes, secondary to infection in the lower limb, perineum or genitalia, which may progress to abscess; the inflamed nodes are enlarged because of hyperplasia of lymphoid follicles and increased numbers of lymphocytes and macrophages, and red streaks of lymphangitis may be visible. An obstructed or strangulated inguinal hernia and acute osteomyelitis would be considered in the differential diagnosis.

**Mediators of the signs.**

- **Pain:** prostaglandins (PGE₂ sensitises nerve endings), bradykinin, and substance P, together with distension of tissue by oedema and injury by leukocyte products.
- **Swelling:** vasodilation and increased permeability of venules caused by histamine and serotonin, bradykinin, leukotrienes C₄, D₄ and E₄, C3a and C5a, PAF; PGE₂ and PGD₂ potentiate oedema, and TNF and IL-1 and leukocyte products sustain leakage.


## 8-year-old boy with right iliac fossa pain for 2 days / 15-year-old boy with RIF pain, rebound tenderness and fever — Most probable diagnosis? Expected histological findings? Positive haematological findings expected?

The most probable diagnosis is acute appendicitis; histology shows neutrophilic infiltration of the muscularis propria with mucosal ulceration and a fibrinopurulent serosal exudate, and the blood shows neutrophilic leukocytosis with a shift to the left.

**Diagnosis.** Pain in the right iliac fossa for a day or two, with rebound tenderness (peritoneal irritation) and fever in a child or adolescent, indicates acute appendicitis, the classic example of acute suppurative inflammation. It is usually initiated by luminal obstruction (fecalith, lymphoid hyperplasia) with bacterial invasion.

**Histological findings.** The diagnostic criterion is neutrophilic infiltration of the muscularis propria. In early disease there is mucosal congestion, oedema and neutrophilic exudate in the mucosa and submucosa, with neutrophils in the lumen and mucosal ulceration. In established disease there is a transmural neutrophilic infiltrate, with vascular congestion and a fibrinopurulent exudate on the serosa (acute suppurative appendicitis). Severe cases show abscess formation, haemorrhagic necrosis of the wall and gangrene, with a risk of perforation and peritonitis.

**Haematological findings.** Neutrophilic leukocytosis (usually 12,000 to 20,000/μL) with a shift to the left (increased immature forms) and toxic granulation; raised ESR and C-reactive protein.


## Discharging sinus in the shin of the leg with radiological involucrum (sclerosis) — Most probable diagnosis?

The most probable diagnosis is chronic suppurative osteomyelitis of the tibia, in which a sinus discharges pus from infected necrotic bone (sequestrum) surrounded by a sheath of new bone (involucrum).

Pyogenic osteomyelitis, usually staphylococcal and often haematogenous, begins as acute suppuration in the metaphysis. If untreated or inadequately treated, necrotic bone (sequestrum) forms within the pus; the periosteum lays down new reactive bone around it (involucrum), which appears radiologically as sclerosis; and pus tracks through gaps in the involucrum (cloacae) to the skin as a discharging sinus. Chronic bacterial infection of bone shows a persistent neutrophilic exudate for months, along with chronic inflammatory cells (lymphocytes, plasma cells, macrophages), granulation tissue and fibrosis. The shin (tibia) is a common site. Tuberculous osteomyelitis is a differential diagnosis. Management requires removal of sequestrum and antibiotics, and complications include pathological fracture, secondary amyloidosis and, rarely, squamous cell carcinoma in the sinus tract.


## Non-healing ulcer on the chest wall; scraping cytology shows epithelioid cells and Langhans-type giant cells — Most probable diagnosis?

The most probable diagnosis is tuberculosis, in the form of a tuberculous (granulomatous) ulcer of the chest wall, because epithelioid cells and Langhans giant cells indicate a granulomatous inflammation, of which tuberculosis is the prototype.

The finding of epithelioid cells and Langhans-type giant cells indicates granulomatous inflammation, and tuberculosis should always be excluded as the cause when granulomas are identified. A chronic non-healing ulcer on the chest wall suggests cutaneous tuberculosis (scrofuloderma from underlying rib or lymph node disease, with a cold abscess breaking down through the skin). Confirmation requires acid-fast stain (Ziehl-Neelsen) of the smear, culture, PCR, and histology demonstrating caseating granulomas, together with chest radiography and Mantoux or interferon-gamma release assays. Other causes of granulomatous ulcers (fungal infection, leprosy, sarcoidosis) must be considered.


## 50-year-old woman with gum lesion (fibroblast proliferation and angiogenesis), long history of betel nut chewing — What type of inflammation occurs? What might be the complication?

Chronic inflammation with repair by granulation tissue and fibrosis is occurring because of persistent irritation by betel nut, and the important complications are submucous fibrosis and malignant transformation to oral squamous cell carcinoma.

Fibroblast proliferation with angiogenesis (granulation tissue) is the hallmark of the repair phase accompanying chronic inflammation. Chronic inflammation is characterised by mononuclear cell infiltration, tissue destruction and healing by angiogenesis and fibrosis, and occurs through prolonged exposure to a toxic agent, here betel nut and its additives (areca nut alkaloids, tobacco, lime). Continued injury and repair lead to excessive collagen deposition (oral submucous fibrosis with trismus), epithelial dysplasia and leukoplakia, and the complication of greatest importance is oral squamous cell carcinoma. Chronic inflammation is also a setting for persistent ulceration. Biopsy is required to exclude dysplasia or carcinoma.


## Raised/fleshy scar or mass at a surgical incision site, recurring after excision — Most probable diagnosis?

The most probable diagnosis is a keloid, an exuberant scar caused by excessive collagen deposition that extends beyond the boundaries of the original wound, does not regress, and recurs after excision.

A raised scar at an incision site that recurs after excision indicates keloid rather than hypertrophic scar. Hypertrophic scars contain abundant myofibroblasts and excess collagen but remain within the boundary of the wound and tend to regress over several months; keloids grow beyond the boundary of the wound, do not regress and recur. Keloid formation seems to be an individual predisposition (higher in dark-skinned people), and microscopically shows thick hyalinised collagen bundles in the dermis. TGF-β-driven fibroblast activity and an imbalance between collagen synthesis and degradation underlie it. Rarely, a recurring exuberant fibroblastic proliferation after incision or trauma may represent a desmoid (aggressive fibromatosis), a benign neoplasm, which also recurs after excision; histology distinguishes them. Treatment is intralesional steroids, pressure or silicone, or excision with adjuvant radiotherapy or steroids.


## A 15y girl has pain, redness, swelling of forearm after trauma. What is the likely diagnosis?

The likely diagnosis is **acute inflammation** of the forearm (post-traumatic acute inflammation, which may be complicated by cellulitis or an early abscess if infection supervenes). Pain (dolor), redness (rubor) and swelling (tumour), with heat and loss of function, are the cardinal signs of acute inflammation, and trauma is a recognised cause because it produces tissue necrosis, which elicits inflammation regardless of cause. Mediators released from injured cells and sentinel cells (histamine, prostaglandins, bradykinin, cytokines) produce vasodilation (redness, heat), increased permeability (swelling) and pain. If fever, a fluctuant swelling or neutrophilic leukocytosis is present, a pyogenic infection should be suspected. A fracture should be excluded by radiograph.


## Same girl: why does the swelling occur?

The swelling is due to **inflammatory oedema (exudation)** together with the accumulation of inflammatory cells. Trauma damages cells and tissue and releases mediators (histamine from mast cells, bradykinin, leukotrienes, prostaglandins, cytokines). Vasodilation increases blood flow and the hydrostatic pressure in capillaries, and contraction of endothelial cells and direct endothelial injury in postcapillary venules open interendothelial gaps so that plasma proteins and fluid escape into the interstitium. The loss of protein from the plasma and its accumulation in the tissue abolishes the osmotic gradient that normally retains water within the vessels, and the lymphatics cannot drain the fluid as fast as it forms. Fluid, fibrin and emigrated leukocytes (neutrophils, later macrophages) accumulate in the tissue and produce visible swelling. Haemorrhage from damaged vessels may add to it.


## A 9y girl has a red, painful arm swelling with raised local temperature. What is the likely diagnosis?

The likely diagnosis is **acute inflammation**, most probably acute pyogenic (suppurative) inflammation such as cellulitis or an early abscess of the arm, usually due to Staphylococcus aureus or streptococci entering through a break in the skin. Redness, pain, swelling and raised local temperature are the cardinal signs of acute inflammation (rubor, dolor, tumour, calor). Redness and heat are caused by vasodilation and increased blood flow; swelling is caused by exudation of protein-rich fluid; and pain is caused by prostaglandins, bradykinin and substance P and by tissue distension. If pus has collected, a fluctuant swelling forms, which is an abscess, and the regional nodes may be tender (lymphadenitis). Investigation includes a total and differential leukocyte count (neutrophilia), Gram stain and culture of pus, and ultrasonography.


## A 10y boy has pain and swelling in the right inguinal region for 7 days. What is the likely diagnosis?

The likely diagnosis is **acute inflammation of the right inguinal lymph nodes (acute suppurative lymphadenitis)**, which may progress to an inguinal abscess; it is usually secondary to a pyogenic infection in the area drained, such as the lower limb, buttock, perineum or external genitalia.

Lymphatic vessels and lymph nodes filter the extravascular fluid and clear microbes, and are involved in acute inflammation; inflamed nodes are enlarged and painful because of hyperplasia of lymphoid follicles and increased numbers of lymphocytes and macrophages (reactive or inflammatory lymphadenitis). Red streaks on the skin represent lymphangitis. After 7 days with pain and swelling the nodes may have suppurated, forming a fluctuant abscess. The pain is due to prostaglandins, bradykinin and substance P, and the swelling to oedema and cellular infiltration. Differential diagnoses include a strangulated inguinal hernia, tuberculous lymphadenitis, and, less commonly, lymphoma. Investigation includes a leukocyte count, aspiration with Gram stain and culture, and ultrasound.


## A 7y boy has sudden red painful thigh swelling with raised local temperature. What is your probable diagnosis?

The probable diagnosis is **acute inflammation of the thigh**, most likely acute pyogenic (suppurative) inflammation, such as cellulitis, pyomyositis or an abscess of the soft tissue (acute osteomyelitis of the femur must be excluded in a child). The sudden onset of a red, painful, warm swelling reflects the cardinal signs of acute inflammation, due to vasodilation (redness, heat), exudative oedema (swelling), and prostaglandins and bradykinin (pain). Neutrophils predominate in the infiltrate and, if the organisms are pyogenic (staphylococci), there is liquefactive necrosis and pus formation (abscess). Investigations include leukocyte count, ESR and CRP, aspiration of pus for Gram stain and culture, ultrasonography and radiography or MRI of the bone.


## A 10y boy has fever, local swelling and pain. What is your provisional diagnosis?

The provisional diagnosis is **acute suppurative (pyogenic) inflammation**, most likely an abscess or cellulitis at the site of swelling. Fever (a systemic effect due to IL-1, TNF and PGE₂), together with local swelling and pain, indicates acute inflammation with bacterial infection. The fever reflects the systemic response to cytokines, and is usually accompanied by neutrophilic leukocytosis. If the swelling is over a bone, acute osteomyelitis should be considered, and if it is in the inguinal or cervical area, acute lymphadenitis. Treatment consists of antibiotics and drainage of any pus.


## How will you confirm this diagnosis (10y boy, fever, local swelling)?

Confirmation rests on demonstrating acute inflammation and identifying the causative organism:

1. **Clinical examination** for the cardinal signs and fluctuation, which indicates pus.
2. **Complete blood count with differential:** neutrophilic leukocytosis with a shift to the left and toxic granulation; raised **ESR** and **C-reactive protein** (acute-phase proteins).
3. **Aspiration of pus** (needle aspiration or incision and drainage) with **Gram stain** and **culture and sensitivity**; **blood culture** if fever is high or sepsis is suspected.
4. **Fine-needle aspiration cytology or biopsy** showing abundant neutrophils, necrotic debris and bacteria, or granulomas if the lesion is chronic.
5. **Imaging**: ultrasound to demonstrate a fluid collection or abscess; radiography, CT or MRI if bone is involved.
6. Special stains and cultures (acid-fast) if tuberculosis is suspected.

**Ch 4 · Haemodynamic Disorders, Thromboembolic Disease, and Shock**

95 questions

**Oedema and Effusions**

**Oedema**


## Define edema.

Oedema is the accumulation of excess fluid in the interstitial tissue spaces, resulting from a net movement of water from the vasculature into the extravascular space; when the fluid collects in a body cavity it is called an effusion.

Under normal conditions, as blood passes through capillary beds, plasma proteins are retained within the vasculature, and there is little net movement of water and electrolytes into the tissues. The tendency of vascular hydrostatic pressure to push water and salts out of capillaries into the interstitium is nearly balanced by the plasma colloid osmotic pressure, which pulls them back. There is a small net movement of fluid into the interstitium, which drains into lymphatic vessels and returns to the bloodstream through the thoracic duct, keeping the tissues "dry". Elevated hydrostatic pressure or diminished colloid osmotic pressure disrupts this balance. If the net rate of fluid efflux exceeds the capacity of lymphatic drainage, fluid accumulates.

The fluid may be an **exudate** (protein-rich, resulting from increased vascular permeability in inflammation) or a **transudate** (protein-poor, from hydrostatic or osmotic imbalance without altered permeability). The causes of oedema are increased hydrostatic pressure, reduced plasma osmotic pressure, increased vascular permeability, lymphatic obstruction, and sodium and water retention.

Morphologically, oedema is recognised as clearing and separation of the extracellular matrix with subtle cell swelling. It is most common in subcutaneous tissue, lungs and brain, and is often dependent (legs when standing, sacrum when recumbent). Pressure over markedly oedematous subcutaneous tissue leaves a depression (**pitting oedema**). In renal disease it appears first in loose tissues such as the eyelids (periorbital oedema). Pulmonary oedema produces lungs two to three times the normal weight with frothy, blood-tinged fluid; brain oedema produces narrowed sulci and distended gyri.

Clinically, subcutaneous oedema signals possible cardiac or renal disease and impairs wound healing and clearance of infection; pulmonary oedema impairs gas exchange and predisposes to infection; brain oedema may cause herniation and death.


## Important causes of edema formation.

The important causes of oedema are increased hydrostatic pressure (for example heart failure), reduced plasma osmotic pressure from hypoalbuminaemia (nephrotic syndrome, cirrhosis, malnutrition), increased vascular permeability (inflammation), lymphatic obstruction, and sodium and water retention.

| Category | Examples |
|---|---|
| **Increased hydrostatic pressure** | Impaired venous return: congestive heart failure, constrictive pericarditis, ascites (cirrhosis), venous obstruction or compression (thrombosis, external pressure, tumour mass), lower-extremity inactivity with prolonged dependency. Arteriolar dilation: heat, neurohumoral dysregulation |
| **Reduced plasma osmotic pressure (hypoproteinaemia)** | Protein-losing glomerulopathies (nephrotic syndrome), liver cirrhosis (reduced albumin synthesis), malnutrition, protein-losing gastroenteropathy |
| **Lymphatic obstruction** | Inflammatory (filariasis), neoplastic, postsurgical, postirradiation |
| **Sodium and water retention** | Excessive salt intake with renal insufficiency, increased tubular reabsorption of sodium, renal hypoperfusion, increased renin-angiotensin-aldosterone secretion |
| **Inflammation** | Acute and chronic inflammation, angiogenesis (increased permeability) |


## What is anasarca?

Anasarca is severe, generalised oedema with widespread, profound swelling of the subcutaneous tissues, often accompanied by effusions in the body cavities.

It is the generalised form of oedema in which fluid accumulates diffusely in the subcutaneous tissues and all serous cavities (ascites, pleural and pericardial effusions). It occurs when the mechanisms of oedema are severe and systemic, most typically in nephrotic syndrome (massive proteinuria and hypoalbuminaemia, with secondary salt and water retention), severe congestive heart failure, advanced cirrhosis with hypoalbuminaemia, and severe protein malnutrition (kwashiorkor). The face and eyelids (loose connective tissue) swell, and the dependent parts show pitting oedema. Pulmonary oedema may be present. The pathogenesis involves a fall in plasma oncotic pressure or a rise in venous pressure, together with renal retention of sodium and water through activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone axis.


## What is effusion?

An effusion is the accumulation of excess fluid in a body cavity, such as the pleural, pericardial or peritoneal cavity; it may be an exudate or a transudate.

When oedema fluid involves a serosal surface, fluid accumulates within the adjacent body cavity as an effusion. Effusions involving the pleural cavity are called hydrothorax, the pericardial cavity hydropericardium, and the peritoneal cavity hydroperitoneum or ascites. Transudative effusions are typically protein-poor, translucent and straw-coloured; an exception is chylous effusion (peritoneal effusion due to lymphatic blockage), which is milky from lipids absorbed from the gut. Exudative effusions are protein-rich and often cloudy due to white cells; if pus is present, the term empyema is used (pleural), and blood in the cavity is haemothorax or haemopericardium. Effusions occur in inflammatory and in noninflammatory conditions (heart failure, liver failure, renal disease, malnutrition). Pleural effusions may compress the lung and compromise gas exchange, and ascites is prone to bacterial seeding (spontaneous bacterial peritonitis).


## Diseases where edema occurs due to increased hydrostatic pressure.

Oedema from increased hydrostatic pressure occurs in diseases that impair venous return, chiefly congestive heart failure, constrictive pericarditis, cirrhosis with portal hypertension, deep vein thrombosis and venous obstruction.

Increases in hydrostatic pressure are mainly caused by disorders that impair venous return. If the impairment is localised, for example deep vein thrombosis in a lower extremity, the oedema is confined to the affected part; conditions leading to systemic venous hypertension are associated with widespread oedema. Examples:

- Congestive heart failure (right-sided failure causes systemic oedema, ascites and effusions; left-sided failure causes pulmonary oedema), and mitral stenosis.
- Constrictive pericarditis.
- Cirrhosis of the liver, with portal hypertension and ascites.
- Thrombosis of veins (DVT), external compression of veins by masses, varicose veins, and superior vena cava obstruction.
- Lower-extremity inactivity with prolonged dependency, and pregnancy (venous compression).
- Arteriolar dilation (heat, neurohumoral dysregulation) raises capillary hydrostatic pressure.


## State the pathophysiologic categories / classify edema.

Oedema is classified according to the pathophysiologic mechanism (Table of pathophysiologic categories) and also according to the nature of the fluid and its distribution.

| Category | Mechanism | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| **Increased hydrostatic pressure** | Impaired venous return (localised or systemic), arteriolar dilation | Congestive heart failure, constrictive pericarditis, cirrhotic ascites, venous thrombosis, external pressure, lower-extremity inactivity; heat, neurohumoral dysregulation |
| **Reduced plasma osmotic pressure (hypoproteinaemia)** | Reduced albumin synthesis or increased albumin loss | Nephrotic syndrome, cirrhosis, protein malnutrition, protein-losing gastroenteropathy |
| **Lymphatic obstruction** | Impaired clearance of interstitial fluid | Inflammatory (filariasis), neoplastic, postsurgical, postirradiation |
| **Sodium and water retention** | Increased intravascular volume (increased hydrostatic pressure, diluted proteins) | Renal failure, excessive salt intake with renal insufficiency, increased renin-angiotensin-aldosterone secretion |
| **Inflammation** | Increased vascular permeability | Acute and chronic inflammation, angiogenesis |

By the nature of the fluid, oedema is either a **transudate** (protein-poor; the first four categories) or an **exudate** (protein-rich; inflammation). By distribution, it is **localised** (venous or lymphatic obstruction, inflammation) or **generalised** (anasarca; cardiac, renal, hepatic or nutritional).


## Give in brief the mechanisms of edema formation.

Fluid movement across the capillary wall depends on the balance between vascular hydrostatic pressure, which pushes fluid out of the vessel, and plasma colloid osmotic pressure, which retains it; the small amount that escapes is returned by lymphatic drainage. Oedema forms when this balance is upset, by the following mechanisms.

1. **Increased hydrostatic pressure**, due to impaired venous return (heart failure, venous thrombosis, constrictive pericarditis, cirrhosis) or arteriolar dilation. Fluid is forced out of the capillary.
2. **Reduced plasma colloid osmotic pressure**, due to hypoalbuminaemia from decreased synthesis (cirrhosis, protein malnutrition) or increased loss (nephrotic syndrome, protein-losing enteropathy). The fall in intravascular volume causes renal hypoperfusion and secondary hyperaldosteronism, whose retention of salt and water does not correct the deficit and aggravates the oedema.
3. **Increased vascular permeability**, in inflammation: protein-rich fluid escapes and the osmotic gradient is lost.
4. **Lymphatic obstruction**, from trauma, fibrosis, invasive tumours, surgery, irradiation, and filariasis, which produces lymphoedema (elephantiasis in filariasis).
5. **Sodium and water retention**, due to renal disease or reduced renal perfusion with activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone axis; retained fluid increases hydrostatic pressure and dilutes plasma proteins.


## Explain the mechanism of edema in nephrotic syndrome.

Oedema in nephrotic syndrome is primarily due to reduced plasma colloid osmotic pressure from loss of albumin in the urine, aggravated by secondary retention of sodium and water.

1. **Massive proteinuria.** In nephrotic syndrome the glomerular capillaries are abnormally permeable, and albumin leaks into the urine (more than 3.5 g/day in adults).
2. **Hypoalbuminaemia.** Urinary loss exceeds hepatic synthesis, so plasma albumin falls and with it the colloid osmotic pressure of plasma (albumin accounts for almost half of the plasma protein).
3. **Fluid shift.** The reduced oncotic pressure allows fluid to move from the vessels into the interstitium, producing oedema and reducing the intravascular volume.
4. **Secondary hyperaldosteronism.** The reduced intravascular volume causes renal hypoperfusion, which activates the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone axis (and antidiuretic hormone), causing renal salt and water retention. This does not correct the plasma volume deficit, since the primary defect (low plasma protein) persists; the retained fluid merely leaks into the tissues and exacerbates the oedema.
5. A contribution from primary renal sodium retention is also recognised in some patients.

The oedema is generalised, soft and pitting; it appears first in loose connective tissue, notably the periorbital region (eyelids), and may progress to anasarca with ascites and pleural effusions.


## Write the mechanism of edema in nephritic syndrome.

Oedema in nephritic syndrome (acute glomerulonephritis) is predominantly due to **retention of sodium and water** by the kidneys because of reduced glomerular filtration, and is therefore an "overfill" type of oedema, in contrast to the "underfill" oedema of nephrotic syndrome.

1. Inflammation and proliferation of the glomerular capillary endothelial and mesangial cells, with infiltration of leukocytes, reduce the glomerular filtration rate.
2. The reduced filtration and increased tubular reabsorption of sodium cause salt and water retention, with expansion of the plasma and extracellular volume.
3. Increased intravascular volume raises capillary hydrostatic pressure and dilutes plasma proteins (lowering colloid osmotic pressure), so fluid moves into the interstitium; the process is aided by activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone axis and hypertension.
4. Proteinuria is mild to moderate, so hypoalbuminaemia is not marked, and the contribution of reduced oncotic pressure is small.

The oedema is mild to moderate and appears first in loose connective tissue (periorbital, face), and is associated with oliguria, haematuria, azotaemia and hypertension. Heart failure and pulmonary oedema may develop from volume overload.


## How does edema due to cardiac failure develop?

Oedema in congestive heart failure results from increased hydrostatic pressure due to impaired venous return, combined with sodium and water retention through renal hypoperfusion.

1. **Venous congestion.** When the heart fails, blood is not pumped forward effectively and venous pressure rises (backward failure). Right-sided failure raises systemic venous pressure and thereby capillary hydrostatic pressure, causing dependent pitting oedema of the legs (or sacrum when recumbent), hepatic congestion, ascites and pleural effusion. Left-sided failure raises pulmonary venous pressure and causes pulmonary oedema.
2. **Reduced cardiac output and renal hypoperfusion.** Decreased cardiac output reduces renal perfusion, which activates the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone axis and raises antidiuretic hormone and sympathetic tone. In early failure this is beneficial: salt and water retention, increased vascular tone and other adaptations improve cardiac output and restore renal perfusion.
3. **Vicious circle.** As failure worsens and cardiac output diminishes, the retained fluid merely increases the hydrostatic pressure further, leading to oedema and effusions.
4. **Additional factors.** In advanced failure, hepatic congestion and protein-losing enteropathy may lower plasma albumin and colloid osmotic pressure, adding to the oedema.


## Important diseases where transudates occur.

Transudates occur in noninflammatory conditions such as congestive heart failure, cirrhosis of the liver, nephrotic syndrome and protein malnutrition.

Noninflammatory oedema and effusions, which are protein-poor transudates, occur in many disorders:

- **Congestive heart failure** (ascites, pleural effusion, oedema) and constrictive pericarditis, through increased hydrostatic pressure.
- **Liver failure and cirrhosis**, through reduced albumin synthesis and portal hypertension (ascites).
- **Renal disease**, particularly nephrotic syndrome (loss of albumin) and renal failure (salt and water retention).
- **Malnutrition** (kwashiorkor) and protein-losing enteropathy.
- Venous obstruction (thrombosis, compression).
- Others: hypothyroidism, Meigs syndrome, peritoneal dialysis.


## How are exudates and transudates formed?

An exudate forms in inflammation because increased vascular permeability allows protein-rich fluid to leak from vessels, whereas a transudate forms from increased hydrostatic pressure or decreased colloid osmotic pressure without any increase in vascular permeability.

At the arterial end of a capillary, hydrostatic pressure is about 32 mm Hg and at the venous end about 12 mm Hg; the mean colloid osmotic pressure is about 25 mm Hg, equal to the mean capillary pressure, so the net flow is nearly nil.

- **Exudate:** chemical mediators and endothelial injury widen the interendothelial spaces, and plasma proteins escape, causing loss of the osmotic gradient. The fluid has high protein content and may contain cells and debris.
- **Transudate:** fluid leaks out because of increased hydrostatic pressure (venous outflow obstruction, as in heart failure) or decreased colloid osmotic pressure (decreased protein synthesis as in liver disease, increased protein loss as in kidney disease, malnutrition). The endothelium remains intact; the fluid is an ultrafiltrate of plasma with little protein (mostly albumin) and little cellular material.


## Define exudate and transudate.

An exudate is an extravascular fluid with a high protein concentration, which may contain cellular debris or cells and implies increased vascular permeability due to inflammation; a transudate is a low-protein, essentially cell-free ultrafiltrate of plasma that forms without increased vascular permeability.

An **exudate** is an inflammatory extravascular fluid with high protein concentration (above about 3 g/dL), specific gravity above 1.020, containing cellular debris and often leukocytes and sometimes red cells; its presence implies increased permeability of small blood vessels. A special exudate is pus, rich in neutrophils, dead cell debris and often microbes. A **transudate** is a fluid with low protein content (mostly albumin; below about 3 g/dL), specific gravity below 1.012, and little or no cellular material, produced by osmotic or hydrostatic imbalance across an intact vessel wall. Both are forms of oedema when they accumulate in tissue or serous cavities.


## Differences between exudate and transudate.

An exudate is protein-rich, cellular, cloudy, and arises from increased vascular permeability in inflammation; a transudate is protein-poor, nearly cell-free, clear, and arises from hydrostatic or osmotic imbalance.

| Feature | Exudate | Transudate |
|---|---|---|
| Mechanism | Increased vascular permeability | Increased hydrostatic or decreased osmotic pressure |
| Cause | Inflammation (infection, infarct, malignancy) | Heart failure, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome, hypoproteinaemia |
| Protein content | High (above about 3 g/dL; fluid/serum ratio above 0.5) | Low (below about 3 g/dL; mostly albumin) |
| Specific gravity | Above 1.020 | Below 1.012 |
| Cells | Many (neutrophils, lymphocytes, red cells), debris | Few or none |
| Appearance | Cloudy, turbid, may be bloody or purulent | Clear, translucent, straw-coloured |
| Clotting | Often clots spontaneously (fibrinogen present) | Does not clot |
| LDH (pleural) | Fluid/serum ratio above 0.6 | Below 0.6 |
| Rivalta test | Positive | Negative |
| Significance | Implies inflammatory process | Noninflammatory |


## Name the body fluids commonly examined in the laboratory.

The body fluids commonly examined in the laboratory include blood, urine, cerebrospinal fluid, pleural, peritoneal (ascitic) and pericardial fluids, synovial fluid, semen and sputum.

| Fluid | Common indication |
|---|---|
| Cerebrospinal fluid | Meningitis, encephalitis, subarachnoid haemorrhage, demyelination, malignancy |
| Pleural fluid | Pleural effusion: heart failure, tuberculosis, pneumonia, malignancy |
| Peritoneal (ascitic) fluid | Ascites: cirrhosis, peritonitis, tuberculosis, malignancy |
| Pericardial fluid | Pericardial effusion, pericarditis, tamponade |
| Synovial fluid | Arthritis: infection, gout (crystals), rheumatoid arthritis |
| Urine | Renal and urinary tract disease, diabetes |
| Semen | Infertility |
| Others | Sputum, bronchoalveolar lavage, gastric juice, bile, amniotic fluid |


## Tests performed for examination of body fluid.

Body fluid examination comprises physical, chemical, cytological and microbiological tests, to distinguish transudate from exudate and to determine the cause.

1. **Physical examination:** volume, colour, turbidity or clarity (clear, cloudy, bloody, purulent, chylous), odour, clotting, viscosity (synovial fluid), specific gravity.
2. **Chemical examination:** protein (total, and fluid-to-serum ratio), glucose (low in infection, tuberculosis, rheumatoid arthritis), lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), amylase (pancreatitis, oesophageal rupture), cholesterol and triglycerides (chylous effusion), pH, adenosine deaminase (tuberculosis), and in ascites the serum-ascites albumin gradient (above 1.1 g/dL indicates portal hypertension). Light's criteria separate pleural exudate (fluid/serum protein above 0.5, fluid/serum LDH above 0.6, or pleural LDH above two-thirds the upper normal serum value) from transudate.
3. **Cytology and cell counts:** total and differential cell counts (neutrophils in bacterial infection, lymphocytes in tuberculosis), red cells; cytology for malignant cells; crystals in synovial fluid under polarised light (urate, calcium pyrophosphate); Rivalta test.
4. **Microbiological examination:** Gram stain, acid-fast stain, culture and sensitivity, PCR, fungal stains, India ink for cryptococcus (CSF).
5. **Immunological and other tests:** tumour markers (CEA), rheumatoid factor, antinuclear antibody, serology.

**Hyperaemia and Congestion**

**Hyperaemia and congestion**


## What is hyperemia?

Hyperaemia is an active process in which arteriolar dilation increases blood flow to a tissue, making it red (erythema) because of increased delivery of oxygenated blood.

It is seen at sites of inflammation and in skeletal muscle during exercise; other examples are blushing, the flushing of the skin in fever or in a warm environment, and menopausal hot flushes. It is physiological in exercising muscle, the gastrointestinal tract after a meal and the skin during heat, and pathological in inflammation. The tissue is warm and red, and the blood flowing through is oxygenated, not deoxygenated; venous outflow is not impaired.


## What is congestion?

Congestion is a passive process resulting from reduced venous outflow of blood from a tissue; the tissue becomes blue-red (cyanosis) from accumulation of deoxygenated haemoglobin.

Congestion may be systemic, as in cardiac failure, or localised, as in isolated venous obstruction. Congested tissues are dusky and blue-red, cool, and oedematous because of the increased hydrostatic pressure. In long-standing chronic passive congestion, chronic hypoxia may result in ischaemic tissue injury and scarring (fibrosis). Capillary rupture can produce small haemorrhagic foci, and breakdown of extravasated red cells leaves clusters of haemosiderin-laden macrophages. Acute pulmonary congestion shows engorged alveolar capillaries, septal oedema and focal intra-alveolar haemorrhage; chronic pulmonary congestion shows thickened fibrotic septa and haemosiderin-laden macrophages ("heart failure cells"). In the liver, acute congestion distends the central vein and sinusoids, and chronic passive congestion yields the "nutmeg liver" with red-brown, slightly depressed centrilobular areas against the tan, uncongested periportal zones, with centrilobular haemorrhage and necrosis.


## Differences between hyperemia and congestion.

Hyperaemia is an active process of increased arterial inflow producing a red, warm tissue, whereas congestion is a passive process of reduced venous outflow producing a blue-red, cyanotic tissue.

| Feature | Hyperaemia | Congestion |
|---|---|---|
| Nature | Active | Passive |
| Mechanism | Arteriolar dilation, increased inflow | Impaired venous outflow |
| Blood | Oxygenated | Deoxygenated haemoglobin accumulates |
| Colour | Red (erythema) | Blue-red (cyanosis) |
| Temperature | Increased | Normal or decreased |
| Oedema | Present in inflammation, otherwise not | Common, due to increased hydrostatic pressure |
| Consequences | Usually none | Chronic hypoxia, fibrosis, haemorrhage, haemosiderin deposition |
| Examples | Inflammation, exercise, blushing | Heart failure, venous obstruction |


## Common examples of each.

Examples of hyperaemia are the redness of acute inflammation and exercising muscle; examples of congestion are chronic passive congestion of the lung and liver in heart failure.

- **Hyperaemia (physiological):** skeletal muscle during exercise, blushing, skin in a hot environment, gastrointestinal mucosa after a meal. **(Pathological):** acute inflammation (erythema), fever.
- **Congestion (systemic):** left heart failure producing chronic pulmonary congestion with brown induration (heart failure cells) and right heart failure producing nutmeg liver, splenomegaly and peripheral oedema. **(Localised):** deep vein thrombosis causing a swollen, cyanotic limb, hepatic venous obstruction (Budd-Chiari syndrome), portal vein obstruction, strangulated hernia or torsion of testis.

**Thrombosis**

**Normal haemostasis**


## Describe briefly the role of platelets in normal haemostasis.

Platelets are disk-shaped, anucleate cell fragments shed from megakaryocytes. They form the primary haemostatic plug that initially seals vascular defects and provide a phospholipid surface that binds and concentrates activated coagulation factors. Their function depends on glycoprotein receptors, a contractile cytoskeleton, and two types of granules: α-granules (P-selectin on the membrane; fibrinogen, factors V and XI, vWF, fibronectin, platelet factor 4, PDGF and TGF-β) and dense (δ) granules (ADP, ATP, ionised calcium, serotonin, epinephrine).

1. **Adhesion.** After endothelial disruption, platelets adhere to subendothelial matrix. GpIb on the platelet binds von Willebrand factor (vWF) bound to collagen (vWF acts as a bridge under high shear); platelets also bind collagen through GpIa/IIa and GpVI. Deficiency of vWF (von Willebrand disease) or GpIb (Bernard-Soulier syndrome) causes bleeding.
2. **Activation.** Platelets change shape from disks to spiky "sea urchins" with greater surface area; GpIIb/IIIa changes conformation, increasing its affinity for fibrinogen; negatively charged phospholipids (phosphatidylserine) are translocated to the surface and, with calcium, nucleate assembly of coagulation factor complexes. Secretion (release reaction) of granule contents follows. Activation is triggered by thrombin (through PAR-1) and ADP (through P2Y₁ and P2Y₁₂), and ADP release recruits more platelets. Activated platelets synthesise thromboxane A₂, a potent aggregating agent and vasoconstrictor (inhibited by aspirin).
3. **Aggregation.** Fibrinogen bridges adjacent platelets by binding GpIIb/IIIa, forming the primary haemostatic plug (inherited deficiency causes Glanzmann thrombasthenia).
4. **Consolidation.** Thrombin, generated locally by tissue factor, further activates platelets, causes irreversible platelet contraction and converts fibrinogen into fibrin, "cementing" the platelets into the definitive secondary haemostatic plug. Leukocytes adhere to platelet P-selectin.
5. Platelet growth factors (PDGF, TGF-β) contribute to wound healing.

Drugs that inhibit platelet function include aspirin (COX inhibition), P2Y₁₂ antagonists, and PAR-1 antagonists.


## What are the antithrombotic properties of endothelial cells?

The balance between antithrombotic and prothrombotic activities of endothelium determines whether clot formation, propagation or dissolution occurs. Normal, intact endothelium expresses many factors that inhibit platelets and coagulation and augment fibrinolysis, so that thrombosis is prevented and clotting is restricted to sites of vascular injury.

**1. Platelet inhibitory effects.** Intact endothelium shields platelets from subendothelial vWF and collagen. It also releases **prostacyclin (PGI₂)**, **nitric oxide (NO)** and **adenosine diphosphatase**, which degrades ADP and inhibits platelet activation and aggregation. PGI₂ (formed through COX-1) and NO (formed by eNOS) production is regulated by blood flow.

**2. Anticoagulant effects.**

- Normal endothelium shields coagulation factors from tissue factor in the vessel wall.
- **Thrombomodulin** binds thrombin; in this complex thrombin loses its ability to activate coagulation factors and platelets, and instead activates **protein C** (with the **endothelial protein C receptor, EPCR**), which with its cofactor **protein S** inactivates factors Va and VIIIa.
- **Heparin-like molecules** on the endothelial surface bind and activate **antithrombin III**, which inhibits thrombin and factors IXa, Xa, XIa and XIIa.
- **Tissue factor pathway inhibitor (TFPI)** binds and inhibits tissue factor/factor VIIa complexes.

**3. Fibrinolytic effects.** Endothelial cells synthesise **tissue plasminogen activator (t-PA)**, which converts plasminogen to plasmin, to degrade fibrin.

With injury or activation (by inflammatory cytokines, microbes, haemodynamic stress), the endothelium loses these properties: thrombomodulin, protein C and TFPI are downregulated, t-PA falls, and plasminogen activator inhibitors (PAI) rise, shifting the balance toward thrombosis.

**Thrombosis**


## Define thrombus.

A thrombus is a solid mass formed in the living circulation, within an intact blood vessel or the chambers of the heart, from the components of blood (platelets, fibrin, red cells and leukocytes).

Haemostasis is the process by which blood clots form at sites of vascular injury; in thrombotic disorders, blood clots (thrombi) form within intact vessels or within the heart chambers. A thrombus is thus an inappropriate, pathological haemostatic plug. It is attached to the vessel wall at its point of origin, and usually shows laminations (lines of Zahn). The process is called thrombosis. A thrombus differs from a clot formed in a test tube or after death in that it forms in flowing blood during life.


## Virchow's triad.

Virchow's triad consists of the three primary abnormalities that lead to thrombosis: endothelial injury, abnormal blood flow (stasis or turbulence), and hypercoagulability of the blood.

- **Endothelial injury** is the dominant influence and can by itself lead to thrombosis (for example over ulcerated atherosclerotic plaques, damaged heart valves, or after endothelial activation by hypertension, toxins, inflammation and metabolic products).
- **Stasis or turbulence of blood flow** contributes to arterial and cardiac thrombosis (turbulence) and to venous thrombosis (stasis).
- **Hypercoagulability** is any alteration of the coagulation pathways that predisposes to thrombosis; it is primary (genetic) or secondary (acquired).

The three factors may act independently or together, and endothelial injury can alter local flow and coagulability while abnormal flow can in turn injure endothelium.


## Why does prolonged bed rest result in pulmonary embolism?

Prolonged bed rest causes stasis of blood in the deep veins of the legs, because lack of muscle contraction removes the milking action on the veins, so deep vein thrombi form, and fragments of these thrombi break off, travel to the right heart and lodge in the pulmonary arteries as emboli.

Bed rest and immobilisation reduce the pumping action of the leg muscles, which normally propels blood toward the heart; blood in the deep veins of the calf and thigh becomes stagnant (stasis), and stasis is a major contributor to venous thrombosis. Stasis allows platelets to contact endothelium, prevents washout and dilution of activated clotting factors, and promotes endothelial activation. The underlying illness, surgery, trauma or heart failure that caused the bed rest often adds hypercoagulability and endothelial injury (Virchow triad). Deep vein thrombosis at or above the knee (popliteal, femoral, iliac veins) is serious because such thrombi readily embolise; they are often asymptomatic, so that approximately 50% of DVTs are recognised only after embolisation. The propagating portion of a venous thrombus is poorly attached and may fragment; the fragments are carried through progressively larger veins and the right side of the heart to impact in the pulmonary arterial tree. About 70% to 80% of pulmonary emboli arise from leg DVT.


## What are mural thrombi?

Mural thrombi are thrombi that form in the heart chambers or in the aortic lumen and are attached to the wall without completely occluding the lumen.

They arise where there is abnormal myocardial contraction (arrhythmias such as atrial fibrillation, dilated cardiomyopathy, myocardial infarction with dyskinetic myocardium) or endomyocardial injury (myocarditis, catheter trauma), and, in the aorta, over ulcerated atherosclerotic plaques and in aneurysmal dilations, where turbulence and stasis exist. Left ventricular thrombi overlie infarcts, and atrial thrombi form in dilated, fibrillating left atria (rheumatic mitral stenosis). They are laminated and friable, and are prone to embolisation, a common source of systemic emboli (80% of systemic emboli arise from intracardiac mural thrombi); the brain, kidneys and spleen are particularly likely targets.


## Differences between thrombus and post-mortem clot.

A thrombus forms in life, is firm, dry and attached to the vessel wall, with lines of Zahn; a postmortem clot forms after death, is soft and gelatinous, shows a dark red lower portion and a yellow "chicken fat" upper portion, and is not attached to the wall.

| Feature | Thrombus (antemortem) | Postmortem clot |
|---|---|---|
| Formation | In flowing blood during life | After death, in stagnant blood |
| Attachment | Attached to the vessel wall at point of origin | Not attached |
| Consistency | Firm, friable, dry | Soft, gelatinous, rubbery |
| Surface | Rough, dull, granular | Smooth, glistening |
| Lines of Zahn | Present (alternating pale platelet-fibrin and dark red cell layers) | Absent (not laminated) |
| Colour | Mixed, red and gray; red cell-rich in veins | Dark red dependent portion (settled red cells) with yellow "chicken fat" upper portion |
| Shape | May be occlusive or mural; cast of vessel in veins | Conforms to the lumen; may be a cast but not attached |
| Microscopy | Fibrin, platelets, red cells and leukocytes, with lamination | Sedimented red cells and fibrin without lamination |


## What is thrombosis?

Thrombosis is the inappropriate formation of a blood clot (thrombus) within an intact blood vessel or within the chambers of the heart during life. Haemostasis, the process by which blood clots form at sites of vascular injury, is essential for life, and thrombosis represents its pathological counterpart, in which the haemostatic machinery of platelets, coagulation factors and endothelium is activated in the absence of bleeding.

**Pathogenesis.** Thrombosis is determined by the three primary abnormalities of Virchow triad: endothelial injury, stasis or turbulence of blood flow, and hypercoagulability of the blood. Endothelial integrity is the most important factor. Thrombus formation begins with platelet adhesion and activation, followed by thrombin generation and fibrin deposition. Arterial and cardiac thrombi form at sites of turbulence or endothelial injury and are rich in platelets; venous thrombi form at sites of stasis and are rich in red cells.

**Morphology.** Thrombi may be laminated with lines of Zahn (pale platelet-fibrin layers alternating with red cell-rich layers), which signify formation in flowing blood. Thrombi in the heart or aorta are mural thrombi; on valves they are vegetations. Arterial thrombi are usually occlusive; venous thrombi form a long luminal cast (red or stasis thrombi).

**Fate.** A thrombus may propagate, embolise, dissolve (fibrinolysis), or become organised and recanalised; it may become infected (mycotic aneurysm).

**Consequences.** Thrombi cause tissue injury by local vascular occlusion (infarction in arteries, congestion and oedema in veins) or by distal embolisation (pulmonary embolism from deep vein thrombosis). Thrombosis underlies myocardial infarction, stroke and pulmonary embolism, which are among the most important causes of morbidity and mortality.


## Discuss the role of endothelial injury in thrombus formation.

Endothelial injury is the most important factor in the Virchow triad, and by itself can lead to thrombosis. It is particularly important for thrombus formation in the heart and arterial circulation, where high shear rates impede clot formation unless platelet adherence and activation occur. Injury to endothelial cells also alters local blood flow and coagulability.

**Mechanisms.**

1. **Exposure of subendothelial prothrombotic elements.** Severe endothelial injury (trauma, ulceration of atherosclerotic plaque, vasculitis, damaged valves, myocardial infarct endocardium, catheters) exposes von Willebrand factor and collagen, which cause platelet adhesion and activation, and tissue factor, which initiates the coagulation cascade and thrombin generation.
2. **Endothelial activation or dysfunction.** Even without gross denudation, inflammation and other noxious stimuli shift the pattern of gene expression of endothelium to a prothrombotic one. Stimuli include physical injury, infectious agents, abnormal blood flow, inflammatory mediators, metabolic abnormalities (hypercholesterolaemia, hyperhomocystinaemia, diabetes), and toxins from cigarette smoke and hypertension. The changes are:

- Procoagulant changes: downregulation of thrombomodulin (enhancing the procoagulant and proinflammatory action of thrombin), and of protein C and tissue factor pathway inhibitor, and increased tissue factor.
- Antifibrinolytic effects: secretion of plasminogen activator inhibitors (PAI) and reduced t-PA.
- Loss of antiplatelet agents: reduced prostacyclin (PGI₂), nitric oxide and ADPase.

3. **Altered flow.** Injured endothelium produces local turbulence and stasis.

**Clinical settings.** Ulcerated atheromatous plaques; myocardial infarction (endocardial injury) leading to mural thrombi; damaged or inflamed heart valves (vegetations); hypertensive vascular injury; vasculitis; hypercholesterolaemia; bacterial endotoxins; radiation; and cigarette smoking.


## How does altered blood flow cause thrombosis?

Normal blood flow is laminar: platelets and other cells flow centrally in the lumen, separated from the endothelium by a slower-moving layer of plasma. Turbulence and stasis disrupt this arrangement in the following ways:

1. They **promote endothelial activation**, enhancing procoagulant activity and leukocyte adhesion, partly through flow-induced changes in adhesion molecules and proinflammatory factors.
2. They **disrupt laminar flow and bring platelets into contact with the endothelium.**
3. They **prevent washout and dilution** of activated clotting factors by fresh flowing blood and prevent the inflow of clotting factor inhibitors.

Turbulence contributes mainly to arterial and cardiac thrombosis, by causing endothelial injury or dysfunction and by forming countercurrents that create local pockets of stasis. Stasis is a major contributor to venous thrombosis.

**Clinical settings.**

- Ulcerated atherosclerotic plaques expose subendothelial vWF and tissue factor and also cause turbulence.
- Aneurysms of the aorta and arteries produce local stasis and are fertile sites for thrombosis.
- Acute myocardial infarction (noncontractile myocardium, cardiac aneurysm) causes stasis and abnormal flow that promote cardiac mural thrombi.
- Rheumatic mitral stenosis with left atrial dilation and atrial fibrillation produces profound stasis in the atrium.
- Hyperviscosity (polycythaemia vera) increases resistance to flow and causes small vessel stasis.
- Deformed red cells in sickle cell anaemia impede flow in small vessels.
- Prolonged bed rest, immobilisation, and heart failure cause venous stasis in the legs.


## Write down the pathogenesis of venous thrombus.

Venous thrombi (phlebothrombosis) characteristically occur at sites of **stasis**, and hypercoagulability plays a particularly important role in their pathogenesis, though all three components of Virchow's triad may contribute.

1. **Stasis.** Blood flow in veins is sluggish, particularly in the valve cusp pockets and in the deep veins of the calf. Immobilisation (bed rest, paralysis, surgery), heart failure, obesity, pregnancy (venous compression) and varicosities cause stasis, in which activated clotting factors are not washed away, inhibitors do not reach the site, and platelets and leukocytes contact endothelium, promoting endothelial activation (and hypoxic injury of valve-pocket endothelium).
2. **Hypercoagulability.** Primary (factor V Leiden, prothrombin G20210A mutation, deficiency of antithrombin III, protein C or protein S) or secondary causes (surgery, trauma, burns, malignancy with tissue factor and mucin release, pregnancy and postpartum states, oral contraceptives, nephrotic syndrome, antiphospholipid syndrome, heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, advanced age) enhance coagulation.
3. **Endothelial dysfunction.** Trauma, surgery, venous catheters and inflammation may injure endothelium.
4. **Thrombus formation.** Thrombin generated locally converts fibrinogen to fibrin, which traps large numbers of red cells and relatively few platelets; the thrombus is therefore a red, stasis thrombus. It is firm, attached focally to the vein wall and contains lines of Zahn.
5. **Propagation.** The thrombus extends in the direction of blood flow, toward the heart, usually forming a long luminal cast, and is almost invariably occlusive. The propagating tail is poorly attached and may fragment and embolise.

Ninety percent of cases involve the veins of the lower extremities. Deep vein thrombi at or above the knee are the most dangerous, because they embolise to the lungs; clinically, they cause painful congestion and oedema, though about half are asymptomatic. Superficial thrombi in varicose veins seldom embolise but cause local congestion, pain and varicose ulcers. Cancer-associated migratory thrombophlebitis is called Trousseau syndrome.


## What is Virchow's triad of thrombogenesis?

Virchow's triad comprises the three primary abnormalities that lead to thrombosis: **(1) endothelial injury, (2) stasis or turbulence of blood flow, and (3) hypercoagulability of the blood.** Thrombosis usually results from one or more of these. They may act independently or in combination; endothelial integrity is the most important factor, because injury to endothelium can alter local blood flow and coagulability, and abnormal flow can in turn injure endothelium.

**1. Endothelial injury.** This is the dominant factor, especially in arteries and the heart, where high flow rates impede clot formation, so that platelet adherence and activation is a prerequisite and arterial and cardiac clots are rich in platelets.

- Severe injury exposes subendothelial vWF and collagen (platelet adhesion and activation) and tissue factor (coagulation).
- Endothelial activation or dysfunction (from inflammation, infection, abnormal flow, hypercholesterolaemia, homocystinaemia, hypertension, smoking) produces a prothrombotic state: loss of thrombomodulin, protein C and TFPI; reduced PGI₂, NO and t-PA; increased PAI.
- Examples: ulcerated atherosclerotic plaque, myocardial infarct, damaged valves, vasculitis, catheter injury.

**2. Alterations in normal blood flow (stasis and turbulence).** Turbulence causes endothelial injury or dysfunction and creates countercurrents with local stasis; stasis predominates in veins. Both promote endothelial activation, bring platelets into contact with the endothelium, and prevent washout of activated factors and inflow of inhibitors. Examples: atherosclerotic plaque, aneurysms, myocardial infarct with dyskinetic wall, atrial fibrillation with dilated atrium (mitral stenosis), polycythaemia, sickle cell anaemia, bed rest.

**3. Hypercoagulability.** An abnormally high tendency of the blood to clot, mainly due to alterations in coagulation factors, with special importance in venous thrombosis.

| Primary (genetic) | Secondary (acquired) |
|---|---|
| Factor V Leiden (resistance to protein C), most common | Prolonged bed rest, immobilisation |
| Prothrombin G20210A mutation | Tissue injury (surgery, fracture, burns) |
| Antithrombin III, protein C and protein S deficiency | Cancer; myocardial infarction; atrial fibrillation |
| Homocystinaemia | Oral contraceptives, pregnancy and postpartum |
| Increased factor VIII, IX, XI, fibrinogen | Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia; antiphospholipid syndrome; DIC; nephrotic syndrome; smoking, obesity |

**Fate and significance.** Thrombi propagate, embolise, dissolve or organise and recanalise.


## Mention the causes of hypercoagulability of blood.

Hypercoagulability is divided into primary (genetic) and secondary (acquired) disorders.

**Primary (inherited):**

- Common: factor V Leiden (Arg506Gln mutation, producing resistance to activated protein C; carried by 2% to 15% of people of European ancestry; heterozygotes have a 4- to 8-fold, and homozygotes about a 12-fold, increased risk of venous thrombosis); prothrombin gene mutation G20210A (elevated prothrombin levels, 2- to 4-fold risk in heterozygotes); increased levels of factors VIII, IX, XI or fibrinogen.
- Rare: deficiency of antithrombin III, protein C, protein S (venous thrombosis and recurrent thromboembolism from adolescence or early adulthood).
- Very rare: defects of fibrinolysis; homozygous homocystinuria (cystathionine β-synthase deficiency).

**Secondary (acquired):**

- Strong risk factors: prolonged bed rest or immobilisation, myocardial infarction, atrial fibrillation, tissue injury (surgery, fracture, burn), cancer (release of procoagulants such as tissue factor and mucin), prosthetic cardiac valves, disseminated intravascular coagulation, heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, antiphospholipid antibody syndrome.
- Other risk factors: cardiomyopathy, nephrotic syndrome (loss of antithrombin), hyperoestrogenic states (pregnancy and postpartum, oral contraceptives: increased hepatic synthesis of coagulation factors and reduced anticoagulants), sickle cell anaemia, smoking, obesity, advancing age (reduced endothelial PGI₂), and acquired hyperhomocysteinaemia (deficiency of vitamin B₆, B₁₂, folate).

**Special syndromes.** Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia: antibodies against complexes of heparin and platelet factor 4 activate platelets (via Fc receptors) and cause both thrombocytopenia and thrombosis (venous and arterial in 50%). Antiphospholipid antibody syndrome: antibodies to anionic phospholipids and β₂-glycoprotein I ("lupus anticoagulant") cause arterial and venous thrombosis and recurrent miscarriage; they prolong the PTT in vitro and cause false-positive syphilis serology.

Inherited causes should be considered in patients younger than 50 years who present with thrombosis, even in the presence of acquired risk factors.


## Give the fate of a thrombus.

If a patient survives the initial thrombosis, over days to weeks the thrombus undergoes some combination of four events.

1. **Propagation.** The thrombus accumulates additional platelets and fibrin and enlarges; arterial thrombi grow retrograde and venous thrombi grow in the direction of flow, toward the heart. The propagating portion is poorly attached.
2. **Embolisation.** Thrombi (or fragments) dislodge and travel to other sites in the vasculature; venous thrombi lodge in the lungs, arterial and cardiac thrombi in systemic organs.
3. **Dissolution.** Fibrinolysis, through plasmin, may lead to rapid shrinkage and total disappearance of recent thrombi. Older thrombi, with extensive fibrin cross-linking, are more resistant to lysis, which explains why therapeutic t-PA is effective only in the first few hours of a thrombotic event.
4. **Organisation and recanalisation.** Older thrombi are invaded by endothelial cells, smooth muscle cells and fibroblasts, forming granulation tissue, and capillary channels form that re-establish the continuity of the lumen to a variable degree. With remodelling, only a fibrous lump may remain, incorporated in the vessel wall.

Other possibilities include **infection** of the thrombus in bacteraemia, which may erode the vessel wall and produce a mycotic aneurysm; enzymatic digestion of the centre of the thrombus by lysosomal enzymes of trapped leukocytes; and calcification (phlebolith).

**Embolism**

**Embolism**


## Define embolus.

An embolus is a detached intravascular solid, liquid or gaseous mass that is carried by the blood from its point of origin to a distant site, where it often obstructs blood flow and causes tissue dysfunction or infarction.

Most emboli are dislodged thrombi, hence the term thromboembolism. Rare emboli are composed of fat droplets, air or nitrogen bubbles, atherosclerotic debris (cholesterol emboli), tumour fragments, bone marrow or foreign bodies. Emboli travel through the blood until they encounter vessels too small to permit passage, and cause partial or complete vascular occlusion. The consequences depend on the size and position of the lodged embolus and on the vascular bed involved.


## Classify embolus.

Emboli are classified on the basis of their composition as thromboemboli (the commonest), fat, air or gas, amniotic fluid, atheromatous (cholesterol), tumour, bone marrow, and foreign body emboli; by site as pulmonary (venous) or systemic (arterial), with paradoxical embolism as a special type.

| Basis | Types |
|---|---|
| Composition: solid | Thromboembolus (dislodged thrombus), atheroembolus (cholesterol), tumour embolus, bone marrow embolus, foreign body (bullet, catheter fragment) embolus, parasitic emboli |
| Composition: liquid | Fat embolus, amniotic fluid embolus |
| Composition: gas | Air embolus, nitrogen embolus (decompression sickness) |
| Infection | Bland or septic (infected valve vegetation, infected thrombus) |
| Route | Venous, pulmonary, systemic (arterial), paradoxical (venous embolus crossing an interatrial or interventricular defect) |


## Examples of each type of embolus.

The commonest example is pulmonary thromboembolism from deep vein thrombosis; other examples are fat embolism after long bone fracture, air embolism after neck vein injury, nitrogen embolism in divers, amniotic fluid embolism in labour, and tumour emboli in renal cell carcinoma.

| Type | Example |
|---|---|
| Thromboembolus | Pulmonary embolism from leg DVT; cerebral or limb embolus from left atrial or ventricular mural thrombus |
| Fat embolus | After fracture of long bones (femur), soft tissue trauma, burns |
| Air embolus | Injury to neck or chest veins, central venous catheter, obstetric or laparoscopic procedures, neurosurgery in sitting position |
| Gas (nitrogen) embolus | Decompression sickness in divers (bends, chokes, caisson disease) |
| Amniotic fluid embolus | Complication of labour and the immediate postpartum period |
| Atheroembolus (cholesterol) | After aortic angiography or surgery; ulcerated aortic plaque, causing renal or lower limb emboli |
| Tumour embolus | Renal cell carcinoma into the renal vein and inferior vena cava; hepatocellular carcinoma into hepatic veins |
| Bone marrow embolus | Fractures, cardiopulmonary resuscitation |
| Foreign body | Bullet, broken catheter, talc in intravenous drug users |
| Septic embolus | Infective endocarditis vegetations |


## Common sources of emboli.

The commonest source of emboli is thrombus: deep vein thrombosis of the legs for pulmonary emboli, and cardiac mural thrombi (after myocardial infarction or in atrial fibrillation) for systemic emboli.

- **Pulmonary emboli:** 70% to 80% originate from deep vein thrombosis of the legs (popliteal, femoral and iliac veins); pelvic veins and upper limb veins are less common sources.
- **Systemic emboli:** 80% arise from intracardiac mural thrombi, two-thirds of which are associated with left ventricular wall infarcts and one-fourth with left atrial dilation and fibrillation (as in rheumatic mitral stenosis). The remainder come from aortic aneurysms, atherosclerotic plaques, valvular vegetations, or venous thrombi (paradoxical emboli); 10% to 15% are of unknown origin.


## Other sources of emboli.

Other sources are fractures of long bones (fat and marrow), sudden decompression (nitrogen), intravenous procedures and trauma (air), obstetric tears (amniotic fluid), atherosclerotic plaques (cholesterol), tumours, and foreign bodies.

- **Fat and bone marrow:** fractures of long bones, soft tissue trauma, burns, rarely orthopaedic procedures.
- **Air:** neck and chest wall injuries, intravenous lines, surgery in a sitting position, obstetric and laparoscopic procedures, mechanical ventilation.
- **Nitrogen:** rapid ascent in divers, unpressurised aircraft.
- **Amniotic fluid:** tear in the placental membranes or rupture of uterine veins during labour or delivery.
- **Atheromatous debris:** ulcerated plaques of the aorta, especially after catheterisation or surgery.
- **Tumour fragments:** tumours invading veins (renal cell carcinoma, hepatocellular carcinoma).
- **Foreign bodies:** bullets, catheter fragments, talc and other particles in intravenous drug use.
- **Infected vegetations** of the heart valves (septic emboli), and parasites.


## How does fat embolism occur?

Fat embolism occurs when trauma, usually fracture of long bones, ruptures the vascular sinusoids or small venules of the marrow, allowing droplets of marrow fat (sometimes with haematopoietic marrow) to enter the venous circulation and travel to the lungs.

Fat embolism is the presence of microscopic fat globules, sometimes with haematopoietic bone marrow, in the vasculature, typically after fractures of long bones or, rarely, in soft tissue trauma and burns. It is common, occurring in about 90% of individuals with severe skeletal injuries, but only a minority have the clinical fat embolism syndrome. The injury ruptures vascular sinusoids or small venules in the marrow, allowing marrow and adipose tissue to herniate into the vascular space and travel to the lung. Small globules may pass through pulmonary capillaries to reach the systemic circulation (brain, kidney, skin). The embolic fat also causes biochemical injury, because free fatty acids released from the globules damage endothelium.


## What is fat embolism syndrome?

Fat embolism syndrome is the symptomatic condition seen in a minority of patients with fat embolism, characterised by pulmonary insufficiency, neurological symptoms, anaemia and thrombocytopenia, with a petechial rash, appearing 1 to 3 days after injury and fatal in 5% to 15% of cases.

Typically, 1 to 3 days after injury, there is sudden onset of tachypnoea, dyspnoea and tachycardia, with irritability and restlessness that may progress to delirium or coma. Thrombocytopenia is attributed to platelet adhesion to fat globules and aggregation or splenic sequestration, and anaemia to red cell aggregation or haemolysis. A diffuse petechial rash (20% to 50%) is a useful diagnostic clue.

**Pathogenesis.** Mechanical obstruction by fat microemboli and associated red cell and platelet aggregates occludes the pulmonary and cerebral microvasculature; biochemical injury follows because free fatty acids released from the fat globules cause toxic injury to endothelium, with platelet activation and granulocyte recruitment releasing free radicals, proteases and eicosanoids.

**Diagnosis.** Because paraffin processing dissolves lipids, demonstration of fat microglobules (in the absence of marrow elements) requires frozen sections with fat stains (Oil red O, Sudan).


## What is decompression sickness / caisson disease?

Decompression sickness is a form of gas embolism caused by sudden decrease in atmospheric pressure, in which nitrogen dissolved in blood and tissues at high pressure comes out of solution as bubbles; caisson disease is the chronic form, in which persistent gas emboli in bone cause multiple foci of ischaemic necrosis.

Scuba and deep-sea divers, underwater construction workers and people in unpressurised aircraft who ascend rapidly are at risk. When air is breathed at high pressure, increased amounts of gas (especially nitrogen) dissolve in blood and tissues; with too rapid ascent, nitrogen comes out of solution as bubbles.

- **The bends:** rapid formation of gas bubbles in skeletal muscle and supporting tissues around joints causes severe pain (named from the arched posture of those afflicted, like the "Grecian bend").
- **The chokes:** bubbles in the lung vasculature cause oedema, haemorrhage and focal atelectasis or emphysema, producing respiratory distress.
- **Central nervous system** bubbles cause memory loss, ataxia, visual disturbances, even coma.
- **Caisson disease** (named after the pressurised vessels used in bridge construction) is the chronic form: persistence of gas emboli in the skeletal system leads to multiple foci of ischaemic necrosis, commonly in the femoral heads, tibia and humeri.

Small intravascular bubbles also evoke inflammatory and thrombogenic responses. **Treatment** is recompression in a chamber under high pressure to force the bubbles back into solution, followed by slow decompression.


## How much air is needed to produce a clinical effect?

More than about 100 mL of air is needed to produce a clinical effect in the pulmonary circulation, and 300 to 500 mL introduced over several seconds may be fatal.

A large volume of air, generally more than 100 mL, is necessary to produce a clinical effect in the pulmonary circulation; this volume can inadvertently be introduced during obstetric or laparoscopic procedures, or through chest wall injury. Air in the pulmonary vasculature not only blocks perfusion of downstream regions but also induces an intense inflammatory response with release of cytokines that may injure the alveoli. Air embolism requires communication between the vasculature and outside air and a negative pressure gradient that sucks in air; in the cerebral circulation much smaller volumes can be dangerous.


## Clinical effects of caisson disease.

The clinical effects of decompression sickness and caisson disease are the bends (painful joints and muscles), the chokes (respiratory distress with pulmonary oedema and haemorrhage), neurological manifestations, and, in the chronic form, ischaemic bone necrosis, especially of the femoral heads, tibia and humeri.

- **Acute decompression sickness:** rapid bubble formation in muscles and tissues around joints causes the painful bends; bubbles in the lungs cause oedema, haemorrhage and focal atelectasis or emphysema, leading to respiratory distress (the chokes); bubbles in the central nervous system cause headache, memory loss, ataxia, visual disturbances and the sudden onset of coma; even small bubbles cause inflammatory and thrombogenic responses.
- **Chronic (caisson disease):** persistence of gas emboli in the skeletal system causes multiple foci of ischaemic (avascular) necrosis, most commonly of the femoral heads, tibia and humeri, leading to joint pain and degenerative arthritis.
