Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia is diagnosed by a sustained absolute lymphocytosis of more than 5,000 per µL composed of small mature lymphocytes with smudge cells, confirmed by flow cytometry showing a CD5, CD19, CD20 (weak), CD23 positive monoclonal B-cell population.

1. **Blood count and smear.** An absolute lymphocyte count above 5,000/mm³ (counts exceeding 200,000/mm³ in heavy tumour burden); the smear is flooded with small round lymphocytes with condensed chromatin and scant cytoplasm; characteristically disrupted cells (**smudge cells**) are present; occasional prolymphocytes. Anaemia and thrombocytopenia occur in advanced disease or from autoimmune haemolysis (10–15% have autoimmune haemolytic anaemia or thrombocytopenia); the Coombs test may be positive.
2. **Immunophenotyping (essential).** The cells express the pan-B cell markers CD19 and CD20 (weak), together with **CD5** and **CD23**, low-level surface immunoglobulin (IgM or IgM and IgD) restricted to a single light chain, and high-level BCL2; CD79b and FMC7 are weak or negative, helping to distinguish CLL from mantle cell lymphoma, which is CD5-positive but CD23-negative and cyclin D1 positive.
3. **Bone marrow aspirate and biopsy.** Variable infiltration (diffuse, nodular or interstitial) by small mature lymphocytes, 30% or more of nucleated cells; the marrow involvement is present in almost all cases. Marrow is not required for diagnosis but defines the tumour burden and the cause of cytopenia.
4. **Lymph node biopsy** (for SLL or suspected transformation). Diffuse effacement by small lymphocytes with **proliferation centres** (pseudofollicles), which are pathognomonic; large cell transformation (Richter syndrome) is suspected from a rapidly enlarging node.
5. **Cytogenetics and molecular studies (prognostic).** FISH for del(13q14.3) (favourable if isolated), trisomy 12, del(11q) and del(17p) (TP53; unfavourable); TP53 and NOTCH1 mutation; immunoglobulin heavy chain variable gene (IGHV) mutation status (unmutated is unfavourable); ZAP-70 and CD38 expression.
6. **Other tests.** Serum immunoglobulins (hypogammaglobulinaemia), direct antiglobulin test, LDH, β₂-microglobulin, and clinical staging by the Rai or Binet system.

**Lymphoid Neoplasms**

**Hodgkin and non-Hodgkin lymphoma**


## Classify lymphoma.

Lymphomas are classified into Hodgkin and non-Hodgkin lymphoma; the non-Hodgkin lymphomas are classified by the WHO according to the cell of origin and the stage of differentiation as B-cell, T-cell and NK-cell neoplasms.

Within the large group of lymphomas, Hodgkin lymphoma is segregated from the other forms, which constitute the non-Hodgkin lymphomas (NHLs), because Hodgkin lymphoma has distinctive pathologic features and is treated in a unique fashion. The current WHO scheme uses morphologic, immunophenotypic, genotypic and clinical features to sort the lymphoid neoplasms into five categories according to the cell of origin: precursor B-cell neoplasms, peripheral B-cell neoplasms, precursor T-cell neoplasms, peripheral T-cell and NK-cell neoplasms, and Hodgkin lymphomas. The scheme is summarised below.

| Category | Entities |
|---|---|
| **I. Precursor B-cell neoplasms** | B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukaemia/lymphoma |
| **II. Peripheral B-cell neoplasms** | CLL/SLL; splenic and extranodal marginal zone lymphoma; mantle cell lymphoma; follicular lymphoma; diffuse large B-cell lymphoma; Burkitt lymphoma; lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma; plasma cell neoplasms |
| **III. Precursor T-cell neoplasms** | T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukaemia/lymphoma |
| **IV. Peripheral T-cell and NK-cell neoplasms** | T-cell prolymphocytic leukaemia, T-large granular lymphocytic leukaemia, mycosis fungoides, Sézary syndrome, peripheral T-cell lymphoma NOS, anaplastic large-cell lymphoma, nodal T-follicular helper cell lymphoma, enteropathy-associated T-cell lymphoma, subcutaneous panniculitis-like T-cell lymphoma, hepatosplenic T-cell lymphoma, adult T-cell leukaemia/lymphoma, extranodal NK/T-cell lymphoma, NK-cell leukaemia |
| **V. Hodgkin lymphoma** | Classic: nodular sclerosis, mixed cellularity, lymphocyte-rich, lymphocyte-depleted; nodular lymphocyte predominant |

The terms leukaemia and lymphoma merely reflect the usual tissue distribution at presentation; many entities called lymphoma may present as leukaemia, and vice versa. Approximately two-thirds of NHLs and virtually all Hodgkin lymphomas present as enlarged, nontender lymph nodes. Clinically, NHLs are also grouped as indolent, moderately aggressive or highly aggressive, which determines treatment.


## Differences between Hodgkin and non-Hodgkin lymphoma.

Hodgkin lymphoma is characterised by Reed-Sternberg cells in a reactive background, localised axial nodal origin and contiguous orderly spread, while non-Hodgkin lymphoma shows a monotonous population of neoplastic lymphoid cells, multiple peripheral nodes, frequent extranodal involvement and noncontiguous spread.

| Feature | Hodgkin lymphoma | Non-Hodgkin lymphoma |
|---|---|---|
| **Site of origin** | More often localised to a single axial group of nodes (cervical, mediastinal, para-aortic) | More frequent involvement of multiple peripheral nodes |
| **Spread** | Orderly, by contiguity (nodes, then spleen, liver, marrow) | Noncontiguous and unpredictable, widely disseminated early |
| **Mesenteric nodes and Waldeyer ring** | Rarely involved | Commonly involved |
| **Extranodal presentation** | Rare | Common (about one-third) |
| **Neoplastic cells** | Reed-Sternberg cells and variants, a minority (<10%) of cells | The bulk of the tumour is neoplastic B, T or NK cells (monomorphic) |
| **Background** | Abundant reactive lymphocytes, eosinophils, plasma cells, macrophages | Little or no reactive background |
| **Immunophenotype** | CD15⁺, CD30⁺, PAX5 (weak), CD45⁻ (classic); L&H cells CD20⁺ | Lineage-specific markers, CD45⁺; B-cell (85–90%) or T-cell |
| **Age** | Bimodal: young adults and over 55 years | All ages, incidence rises with age (children: Burkitt, lymphoblastic) |
| **Systemic (B) symptoms** | Common in advanced disease and mixed cellularity and lymphocyte depletion | Variable, more in aggressive types |
| **Staging** | Of great value for therapy and prognosis | Less useful, since disseminated early |
| **Prognosis** | Curable in most; stage I–IIA cure about 90% | Varies from indolent to highly aggressive |

In Hodgkin lymphoma, spread follows a stereotyped sequence (nodal disease first, then spleen, liver and finally marrow); staging is therefore most useful for guiding Hodgkin lymphoma therapy, whereas non-Hodgkin lymphoma disseminates widely and unpredictably early in its course.


## What do you know about Reed-Sternberg cells?

Reed-Sternberg cells are large neoplastic B-cell–derived cells with bilobed or multilobed nuclei and prominent inclusion-like nucleoli that are the diagnostic hallmark of Hodgkin lymphoma; they are CD15 and CD30 positive and are surrounded by a dense reactive infiltrate.

Reed-Sternberg cells are the neoplastic element of Hodgkin lymphoma; their identification, in the proper cellular background, is essential for the diagnosis. The cell is large (45 µm), with abundant cytoplasm, and has a multilobed or two (mirror-image) nuclei, each with a large inclusion-like nucleolus about the size of a small lymphocyte (5–7 µm), giving the "owl-eye" appearance. Variants are the mononuclear (Hodgkin) cell, the lacunar cell of nodular sclerosis, the lymphohistiocytic ("popcorn") cell of nodular lymphocyte predominant type, and the mummified cell.

They derive from germinal centre or post–germinal centre B cells (clonal IGH rearrangement and somatic hypermutation) but lose most B-cell gene expression. They are aneuploid with REL amplification (2p) and gains of the genes for PD-L1 and PD-L2 on 9p; NF-κB is constitutively activated through EBV latent membrane protein 1 (LMP-1) in EBV-positive cases (30–40% overall) or through mutations in IκB and TNFAIP3 in EBV-negative cases. They secrete cytokines (IL-5, IL-10, M-CSF) and chemokines such as eotaxin, which attract eosinophils, T cells and macrophages that form more than 90% of the cellularity. The reactive cells in turn provide survival signals through CD30 and CD40 ligands, while PD-L1 and PD-L2 inhibit antitumour T-cell responses, hence the striking response to PD-1 blockade. IL-10 produced by R-S cells suppresses Th1 responses, accounting for cutaneous anergy.

Immunophenotype of classic R-S cells: CD15⁺, CD30⁺, PAX5 weak⁺, CD45⁻, CD20 variable. R-S–like cells occur in infectious mononucleosis, some NHLs and carcinomas, and so are not diagnostic alone.


## Classification of Hodgkin's lymphoma.

Hodgkin lymphoma is classified by WHO into classic Hodgkin lymphoma, with four subtypes—nodular sclerosis, mixed cellularity, lymphocyte-rich and lymphocyte-depleted—and nodular lymphocyte predominant Hodgkin lymphoma; the older Rye classification recognised lymphocyte predominance, nodular sclerosis, mixed cellularity and lymphocyte depletion.

**WHO classification**

| Type | Subtype | Key features |
|---|---|---|
| Classic Hodgkin lymphoma | Nodular sclerosis (65–70%) | Lacunar cells, collagen bands, nodules; young adults; mediastinal involvement |
| | Mixed cellularity (20–25%) | Diffuse mixed infiltrate with many RS cells; EBV 70%; older males; advanced stage |
| | Lymphocyte-rich | Reactive lymphocytes predominate; classic RS immunophenotype; EBV 40% |
| | Lymphocyte-depleted (<5%) | Few lymphocytes, many RS cells; EBV >90%; elderly, HIV; poor outlook |
| Nodular lymphocyte predominant | (about 5%) | L&H (popcorn) cells, CD20⁺, CD15⁻, CD30⁻; young males; cervical or axillary nodes |

**Rye classification (historical).** Lymphocytic predominance, nodular sclerosis, mixed cellularity, and lymphocytic depletion. The prognosis was formerly considered best in lymphocyte predominance and worst in lymphocyte depletion, but with current treatment protocols tumour **stage**, rather than histologic type, is the most important prognostic variable.

**Staging (Ann Arbor).** Stage I: a single node region or single extralymphatic site; II: two or more regions on the same side of the diaphragm; III: both sides of the diaphragm; IV: diffuse involvement of one or more extranodal organs. Suffix A or B indicates the absence or presence of systemic symptoms (unexplained fever, drenching night sweats, loss of more than 10% of body weight).


## How will you proceed to diagnose a case of lymphoma?

Lymphoid neoplasia can be suspected from the clinical features, but histologic examination of an excised lymph node or other involved tissue, supplemented by immunophenotyping and genetic studies, is required for diagnosis; this is followed by staging.

**1. Clinical evaluation.** Painless, persistent, progressive lymphadenopathy (often more than 2 cm), possibly with hepatosplenomegaly; B symptoms (fever, night sweats, weight loss); pruritus; symptoms from extranodal sites (gastric, skin, brain, mediastinal mass); examination of all node groups, Waldeyer ring, liver and spleen.

**2. Basic laboratory tests.** Complete blood count and smear (anaemia, lymphocytosis, circulating lymphoma cells), ESR, LDH, uric acid, liver and renal function tests, serum immunoglobulins and protein electrophoresis, HIV and hepatitis B/C serology.

**3. Tissue diagnosis (essential).** FNAC is a screening investigation. Excisional biopsy of an entire intact lymph node is the investigation of choice, because architecture is needed for subclassification; core needle biopsy is acceptable when excision is not feasible. Histopathology determines the architecture (diffuse, nodular), cell type and size, and mitotic rate.

**4. Immunohistochemistry and flow cytometry.** Lineage and subtype: CD45, CD20, CD79a, PAX5, CD3, CD5, CD10, CD23, BCL2, BCL6, cyclin D1, CD15, CD30, ALK, Ki-67, and TdT for precursor tumours. Clonality of antigen receptor genes distinguishes reactive (polyclonal) from neoplastic (monoclonal) lymphoid proliferation. Cytogenetics, FISH or PCR for diagnostic translocations: t(14;18) in follicular lymphoma, t(11;14) in mantle cell, MYC t(8;14) in Burkitt, BCL6, ALK; EBV studies (EBER) where relevant.

**5. Staging investigations.** Chest radiograph and CT of the neck, chest, abdomen and pelvis, or PET-CT; bone marrow aspiration and biopsy; CSF examination in high-risk sites and aggressive NHL; Ann Arbor staging with A/B symptom designation.

**6. Pre-treatment assessment.** Cardiac function, pulmonary function tests (before bleomycin or anthracycline therapy), fertility counseling.


## A 20y male has multiple painless cervical/axillary lymph nodes. What is your provisional diagnosis?

The provisional diagnosis is a **lymphoma, most likely Hodgkin lymphoma (nodular sclerosis type)**.

**Reasoning.** Hodgkin lymphoma shows a peak incidence in young adults, and virtually all cases present as painless, enlarged, rubbery, nontender lymph nodes, most often in the cervical (lower cervical and supraclavicular) region, with axillary involvement common; it tends to begin in a single node or chain and spread to contiguous groups. The nodular sclerosis subtype, which is the commonest (65–70%), characteristically involves the lower cervical, supraclavicular and mediastinal nodes of adolescents and young adults. Patients of this type are often free of systemic manifestations, but may have fever, drenching night sweats, weight loss and pruritus, which, if present, define stage B.

**Differential diagnosis.**

1. Non-Hodgkin lymphoma (follicular lymphoma, lymphoblastic lymphoma, Burkitt and diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, anaplastic large-cell lymphoma), which can have a similar presentation but more often involve multiple peripheral and extranodal sites and is noncontiguous.
2. Tuberculous lymphadenitis, which is common in our setting and may present with firm matted nodes, fever and night sweats.
3. Infectious mononucleosis, cytomegalovirus, toxoplasmosis and HIV lymphadenopathy.
4. Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia and metastatic carcinoma (rare at this age).

The diagnosis is established by excision biopsy of a node showing Reed-Sternberg cells and variants in a reactive background with CD15⁺ and CD30⁺ immunophenotype.


## Same: what tests can you do on the lymph nodes?

The tests on the lymph nodes are directed toward obtaining a tissue diagnosis, identifying the lineage and subtype of any lymphoma, and excluding mimics such as tuberculosis.

1. **Fine-needle aspiration cytology (FNAC).** A rapid screening test, which may show Reed-Sternberg cells with a mixed inflammatory background (lymphocytes, eosinophils, plasma cells), caseating granulomas and epithelioid cells (with acid-fast bacilli on Ziehl–Neelsen stain) in tuberculosis, or metastatic carcinoma cells. It is inadequate for definitive diagnosis and subclassification of lymphoma, since the nodal architecture is not evident.
2. **Excision biopsy of an entire intact node (the diagnostic procedure of choice).** Histology with H&E stain shows effacement of the nodal architecture, the Reed-Sternberg cells and variants (diagnostic cells, mononuclear, lacunar), the cellular background (lymphocytes, eosinophils, plasma cells, macrophages), fibrous bands (nodular sclerosis) and necrosis.
3. **Special stains.** Ziehl–Neelsen for acid-fast bacilli; reticulin and PAS where indicated.
4. **Immunohistochemistry.** Classic Hodgkin lymphoma: CD15⁺, CD30⁺, PAX5 weakly positive, CD45⁻, CD20 negative or variable, with EBV-encoded RNA (EBER) or LMP1 in a proportion. Nodular lymphocyte predominant type: CD20⁺, BCL6⁺, CD45⁺, CD15⁻, CD30⁻. Immunostains for CD3, CD20 and other markers help to exclude non-Hodgkin lymphoma and anaplastic large-cell lymphoma (CD30⁺, ALK⁺, EMA⁺).
5. **Flow cytometry, cytogenetic and molecular tests** if non-Hodgkin lymphoma is suspected: monoclonality of immunoglobulin or T-cell receptor genes and specific translocations.
6. **Staging tests.** Complete blood count, ESR, LDH, liver and renal function; chest radiograph; CT or PET-CT of the neck, chest, abdomen and pelvis; bone marrow biopsy; and HIV serology.


## Give the WHO classification of Hodgkin lymphoma.

The WHO classification of Hodgkin lymphoma recognises five subtypes, which are grouped into two categories on the basis of the immunophenotype of the neoplastic cells (Table 13.8).

**I. Classic Hodgkin lymphoma** (Reed-Sternberg cells with a distinctive immunophenotype: CD15⁺, CD30⁺, PAX5 weakly positive, CD45⁻)

1. Nodular sclerosis (65–70%)
2. Mixed cellularity (20–25%)
3. Lymphocyte-rich (uncommon)
4. Lymphocyte-depleted (less than 5%)

**II. Nodular lymphocyte predominant Hodgkin lymphoma** (about 5%; "non-classic"; lymphocytic and histiocytic [L&H, popcorn] cells with a B-cell phenotype: CD20⁺, BCL6⁺, CD15⁻, CD30⁻)

The subtypes differ as follows.

| Subtype | Salient morphology | EBV | Clinical features |
|---|---|---|---|
| Nodular sclerosis | Lacunar cells, birefringent collagen bands dividing node into nodules; polymorphous background | Uncommon | Young adults, both sexes; lower cervical, supraclavicular, mediastinal nodes; stage I–II; excellent prognosis |
| Mixed cellularity | Diffuse effacement; abundant diagnostic RS cells and mononuclear variants; T cells, eosinophils, plasma cells, macrophages | About 70% | Males; older age; systemic symptoms; advanced stage; very good prognosis |
| Lymphocyte-rich | Lymphocytes predominate; frequent mononuclear and diagnostic RS cells of classic phenotype | About 40% | Older males; very good to excellent prognosis |
| Lymphocyte-depleted | Paucity of lymphocytes; many RS cells and pleomorphic variants; immunophenotyping essential | Over 90% | Elderly, HIV-positive, developing countries; advanced stage; less favourable |
| Nodular lymphocyte predominant | Nodules of small lymphocytes and histiocytes, L&H ("popcorn") cells | Rare | Young males; cervical or axillary nodes; excellent prognosis, may recur; 3–5% transform to DLBCL |

In the International Consensus Classification, the last entity is renamed nodular lymphocyte-predominant B-cell lymphoma, dropping the Hodgkin designation.


## Describe in brief the morphological features of Hodgkin's disease.

**Gross.** Involved lymph nodes are enlarged, initially discrete and rubbery, but with progression may become matted. The cut surface is homogeneous, grayish-white to pink and bulging, sometimes with areas of necrosis; in nodular sclerosis the capsule is thickened and the cut surface shows fibrous bands. The disease first involves a single node or chain (most often cervical, then mediastinal, para-aortic) and spreads in a stereotyped fashion to contiguous nodes, then the spleen, liver, bone marrow and other tissues. Involved spleen and liver show irregular tumour nodules, which resemble those seen in lymph nodes.

**Microscopy.** The hallmark is the presence of **Reed-Sternberg cells and variants** scattered in a background of non-neoplastic inflammatory cells, which make up more than 90% of the tumour and usually effaces the normal architecture of the node.

1. Diagnostic Reed-Sternberg cell: a large cell (45 µm) with abundant cytoplasm and a bilobed or multilobed nucleus, each lobe with a thin membrane, open chromatin and a large inclusion-like eosinophilic nucleolus about the size of a small lymphocyte ("owl-eye").
2. Variants: mononuclear (Hodgkin) cells; lacunar cells (nodular sclerosis); L&H "popcorn" cells (lymphocyte predominance); mummified cells; pleomorphic cells (lymphocyte depletion).
3. Background: small lymphocytes (mostly T cells), eosinophils, plasma cells, histiocytes, neutrophils and fibroblasts, in varying proportions that characterise each subtype.
4. Subtypes: nodular sclerosis (collagen bands dividing the node into nodules, lacunar cells); mixed cellularity (diffuse polymorphous infiltrate, plentiful RS cells); lymphocyte-rich (lymphocyte predominance with classic RS cells); lymphocyte-depleted (few lymphocytes, many pleomorphic RS cells, sometimes diffuse fibrosis); nodular lymphocyte predominant (nodules of lymphocytes and histiocytes with L&H cells).
5. Immunohistochemistry: classic RS cells are CD15⁺, CD30⁺, PAX5 weak⁺, CD45⁻; EBV is demonstrable in 30–40% of classic cases. L&H cells are CD20⁺, BCL6⁺, CD15⁻, CD30⁻.


## Describe the Reed-Sternberg cell and its variants.

**Definition and significance.** The Reed-Sternberg (R-S) cell is the neoplastic giant cell of Hodgkin lymphoma. The identification of R-S cells and their variants in a background of non-neoplastic inflammatory cells is essential for the diagnosis. Molecular studies of single isolated R-S cells have revealed clonal immunoglobulin heavy-chain gene rearrangements and somatic hypermutation, establishing derivation from a germinal centre or post–germinal centre B cell; yet the R-S cells of classic Hodgkin lymphoma fail to express most B-cell–specific genes, including immunoglobulin genes, probably through widespread epigenetic reprogramming.

**Morphology of the diagnostic (classical) R-S cell.** The cell is large, about 45 µm in diameter, with abundant, slightly basophilic to amphophilic cytoplasm. The nucleus is multilobed or the cell is binucleate, classically with two mirror-image nuclei or lobes. Each nucleus has a thin, distinct nuclear membrane, vesicular chromatin and a **large, inclusion-like, eosinophilic nucleolus** about the size of a small lymphocyte (5–7 µm), surrounded by a clear halo. The two nuclei with their huge nucleoli produce the "owl-eye" appearance.

**Variants.**

| Variant | Morphology | Association |
|---|---|---|
| **Mononuclear (Hodgkin) cell** | Single nucleus with a large inclusion-like nucleolus | All classic types, particularly mixed cellularity |
| **Lacunar cell** | Delicate, folded or multilobated nucleus; abundant pale cytoplasm retracts in formalin-fixed sections leaving a clear space (lacuna) | Nodular sclerosis |
| **Lymphohistiocytic (L&H, popcorn) cell** | Polypoid, multilobed nucleus with inconspicuous nucleoli, fine chromatin, moderately abundant cytoplasm | Nodular lymphocyte predominant Hodgkin lymphoma |
| **Mummified cell** | Shrunken, pyknotic nucleus and dense eosinophilic cytoplasm resulting from a peculiar form of cell death | Classic Hodgkin lymphoma |
| **Pleomorphic/anaplastic (reticular) variants** | Bizarre, large cells with irregular, multiple nuclei | Lymphocyte-depleted (reticular) type |

**Immunophenotype.** Classic RS cells are positive for CD15 and CD30 and weakly for PAX5, and negative for CD45 (leukocyte common antigen), most other B-cell markers (CD20 negative or variable, CD79a negative) and T-cell markers. About 30–40% are EBV-positive (LMP-1). L&H cells in the lymphocyte predominant type are CD20⁺, CD45⁺, BCL6⁺ and CD15⁻, CD30⁻.

**Pathogenic significance.** NF-κB activation (via EBV LMP-1, or loss-of-function mutations of IκB and TNFAIP3), REL copy number gains and gains of PD-L1 and PD-L2 on 9p contribute to survival and immune evasion. R-S cells secrete IL-5, IL-10, M-CSF and eotaxin, which attract the reactive eosinophils, lymphocytes and macrophages that make up more than 90% of the tumour mass.

**Diagnostic caution.** Cells resembling R-S cells occur in infectious mononucleosis, solid tissue cancers and some non-Hodgkin lymphomas, so diagnosis depends on the characteristic cellular background and immunophenotype.


## Write a short note on Hodgkin's lymphoma.

**Definition and epidemiology.** Hodgkin lymphoma (HL) is a group of lymphoid neoplasms characterised by neoplastic Reed-Sternberg cells and variants surrounded by a large majority (over 90%) of reactive lymphocytes, macrophages, eosinophils and plasma cells. It accounts for 0.7% of cancers in the United States (about 9,000 cases a year), has a bimodal age distribution with peaks in young adults and in persons over 55, and is curable in most cases. It arises in a single node or chain of nodes and spreads in an orderly fashion to contiguous lymphoid tissues.

**Pathogenesis.** R-S cells derive from germinal centre or post–germinal centre B cells; NF-κB is constitutively activated (EBV LMP-1 in the 30–40% of EBV-positive cases; mutations in IκB and TNFAIP3 otherwise), REL is amplified, and PD-L1 and PD-L2 genes on 9p are increased, which suppress the antitumour T-cell response. R-S cells elaborate cytokines and chemokines that recruit the reactive infiltrate.

**Classification.** Classic HL (nodular sclerosis, mixed cellularity, lymphocyte-rich, lymphocyte-depleted) and nodular lymphocyte predominant HL.

**Morphology.** R-S cells (binucleate or multilobed with huge eosinophilic nucleoli) and variants in a reactive background; classic RS cells CD15⁺, CD30⁺.

**Clinical features.** Painless lymphadenopathy, most often cervical, supraclavicular or mediastinal; splenomegaly later; constitutional (B) symptoms (fever, night sweats, weight loss), pruritus, and sometimes alcohol-induced pain in involved nodes. Disseminated disease and mixed cellularity or lymphocyte depletion are more likely to have systemic symptoms. Cutaneous anergy, caused by depressed cell-mediated immunity (IL-10 from R-S cells), is common. Spread follows a stereotyped sequence: nodal, splenic, hepatic, then marrow.

**Staging.** Ann Arbor classification (I to IV; A or B). The stage is the most important prognostic variable with modern treatment.

**Treatment and prognosis.** Combination chemotherapy with or without limited radiotherapy; stage I–IIA cure rates are about 90%, and 5-year disease-free survival in stages IVA and IVB is 60–70%. Second malignancies (lung, breast, melanoma, AML) arising after radiation and alkylating agents have prompted less genotoxic regimens. Immune checkpoint (PD-1) inhibitors produce sustained responses in almost 90% of refractory classic HL.


## Write a short note on nodular sclerosis variety of Hodgkin's disease.

Nodular sclerosis (NS) is the **most common form of Hodgkin lymphoma**, constituting 65% to 70% of cases. It is the one type that occurs with equal frequency in males and females.

**Morphology.** The distinguishing features are (1) the presence of **lacunar variant Reed-Sternberg cells**, and (2) the deposition of **collagen in bands** that divide the involved lymph node into circumscribed nodules (the capsule is usually thickened). The fibrosis may be scant or abundant, and the bands are birefringent under polarised light. The lacunar cells have delicate, folded or multilobated nuclei and abundant pale cytoplasm that retracts during processing, leaving the nucleus in an empty space. The R-S cells lie in a polymorphous background of T cells, eosinophils, plasma cells and macrophages; diagnostic R-S cells are usually uncommon. Involvement of the spleen, liver, marrow and other organs may appear in due course as irregular tumour nodules resembling those in the lymph nodes.

**Immunophenotype and genetics.** The R-S cells are positive for PAX5 (weak), CD15 and CD30, negative for CD45 and other B-cell and T-cell markers, and only uncommonly (usually) associated with EBV.

**Clinical features.** NS has a propensity to involve the **lower cervical, supraclavicular and mediastinal lymph nodes** of adolescents and young adults, so it often presents as a mediastinal mass. It usually presents in stage I or II, with few systemic symptoms, and has an **excellent prognosis**.


## How does Hodgkin lymphoma differ from non-Hodgkin lymphoma?

Hodgkin lymphoma (HL) is segregated from the non-Hodgkin lymphomas (NHLs) because it has distinctive pathologic features, a characteristic pattern of spread, and is treated in a unique fashion. The differences are as follows (Table 13.7).

| Feature | Hodgkin lymphoma | Non-Hodgkin lymphoma |
|---|---|---|
| **Site of presentation** | More often localised to a single axial group of nodes (cervical, mediastinal, para-aortic) | More frequent involvement of multiple peripheral nodes |
| **Pattern of spread** | Orderly, by contiguity | Noncontiguous; disseminates widely and unpredictably early |
| **Mesenteric nodes and Waldeyer ring** | Rarely involved | Commonly involved |
| **Extranodal presentation** | Rare | Common |
| **Marrow involvement** | Late and uncommon | Early and common |
| **Neoplastic cell** | Reed-Sternberg cell and variants | Neoplastic B, T or NK lymphocytes |
| **Proportion of tumour cells** | Few (usually under 10%) in a reactive infiltrate of lymphocytes, eosinophils, plasma cells, macrophages | Monotonous infiltrate; tumour cells are the majority |
| **Architecture** | Partial or total effacement with fibrosis (nodular sclerosis) | Diffuse or follicular effacement, capsular invasion |
| **Immunophenotype** | CD15⁺, CD30⁺, PAX5 (weak), CD45⁻ (classic) | B-cell (85–90%) or T-cell markers; CD45⁺ |
| **Clonality** | Clonal IGH rearrangement in micro-dissected R-S cells | Clonal antigen receptor rearrangement in whole tissue |
| **EBV** | 30–40% (classic) | Burkitt (subset), immunodeficiency-associated lymphomas |
| **Age** | Bimodal: young adults and over 55 | All ages; increases with age (DLBCL median 60 years) |
| **Systemic symptoms** | Fever, night sweats, weight loss in advanced disease; pruritus; cutaneous anergy | Variable |
| **Staging** | Highly informative for prognosis and therapy | Less useful, since widely disseminated early |
| **Prognosis** | Curable in most (stage I–IIA about 90%) | Varies with type from indolent to highly aggressive |

**Plasma Cell Disorders**

**Myeloma and paraproteinaemia**


## What is paraproteinaemia?

Paraproteinaemia, or monoclonal gammopathy, is the presence in the blood or urine of a homogeneous monoclonal immunoglobulin or immunoglobulin fragment—the M component or paraprotein—secreted by a single clone of plasma cells or B lymphocytes.

Plasma cell neoplasms and related B-cell proliferations virtually always secrete monoclonal immunoglobulin or immunoglobulin fragments, which serve as tumour markers and often have pathologic consequences. A monoclonal immunoglobulin identified in the blood is referred to as an **M component**, in reference to myeloma. Complete M components have molecular weights of 160,000 or more and are therefore restricted to plasma and extracellular fluid, being excluded from the urine in the absence of glomerular damage. Neoplastic plasma cells, however, often synthesise excess light chains along with complete immunoglobulin, occasionally only light chains, and rarely only heavy chains. In most patients, the level of free light chains in the blood is elevated and markedly skewed toward one light chain (κ or λ); because free light chains are small, they are excreted in the urine as **Bence Jones proteins**.

The paraprotein appears on serum protein electrophoresis as a sharp, narrow band ("M spike") in the γ or β region, in contrast to the broad polyclonal band of normal immunoglobulins, and its isotype is determined by immunofixation. Clinical associations include multiple myeloma, MGUS, Waldenström macroglobulinaemia, heavy-chain disease and AL amyloidosis. The paraprotein may cause disease by tissue infiltration by the plasma cell clone, by the physicochemical properties of the protein (hyperviscosity, cryoglobulinaemia, amyloid deposition, renal tubular toxicity), and by suppression of normal immunoglobulins.


## Give 4 common causes of paraproteinaemia.

The four commonest causes of paraproteinaemia are monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance, multiple myeloma, Waldenström macroglobulinaemia, and AL amyloidosis.

1. **Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS)** is the most common plasma cell disorder, occurring in about 3% of persons over 50 and 5% of those over 70. The M protein is below 3 g/dL, there are no symptoms, and about 1% a year progress to myeloma or another symptomatic plasma cell neoplasm.
2. **Multiple myeloma**, the most important plasma cell neoplasm, usually has more than 3 g/dL of serum immunoglobulin and/or Bence Jones protein in the urine, with lytic bone lesions, hypercalcaemia, renal failure and anaemia.
3. **Waldenström macroglobulinaemia (lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma)**, with a monoclonal IgM paraprotein causing hyperviscosity.
4. **Primary (AL) amyloidosis**, caused by monoclonal plasma cells secreting light chains (usually λ) that deposit as amyloid.

Other causes include smoldering myeloma, solitary plasmacytoma, heavy-chain disease, chronic lymphocytic leukaemia and other B-cell lymphomas, cryoglobulinaemia, and transient paraproteins in infections, autoimmune diseases and solid tumours.


## What is myeloma?

Multiple myeloma, or plasma cell myeloma, is a malignant clonal proliferation of plasma cells in the bone marrow, characterised by lytic bone lesions, hypercalcaemia, renal failure, anaemia, and a monoclonal immunoglobulin in serum and/or urine with suppression of normal humoral immunity.

Multiple myeloma is a plasma cell neoplasm commonly associated with lytic bone lesions, hypercalcaemia, renal failure and acquired immune abnormalities. The disease is chiefly one of older adults, with a peak age at onset of 65 to 70 years, and is more common in males and in persons of African descent. It causes about 1% of cancer deaths in Western countries and accounts for the largest share of deaths from plasma cell neoplasms. The neoplastic cells are post–germinal centre plasma cells with frequent translocations involving the IGH locus on 14q32 (to cyclin D1 and D3 genes and others) and deletions of 13q and 17p, with dependence on IL-6 and the marrow stroma. Bony disease dominates, but the disease can spread late to lymph nodes and extranodal sites. Variants include solitary plasmacytoma, smoldering myeloma and plasma cell leukaemia. The diagnosis requires clonal marrow plasma cells with myeloma-defining events (CRAB criteria: hypercalcaemia, renal dysfunction, anaemia and bone lesions).


## Pathophysiological and biochemical features of myeloma.

The pathophysiology of myeloma stems from plasma cell growth in the marrow and bone, from the excess monoclonal immunoglobulin and light chains with abnormal physicochemical properties, and from suppression of normal immunoglobulin production; biochemically there is an M spike, Bence Jones proteinuria, hypercalcaemia and renal impairment.

**A. Pathophysiology**

1. **Bone destruction.** Myeloma cells secrete factors, notably MIP-1α (CCL3), that augment osteoclast formation (with RANKL up-regulation), while other factors, such as inhibitors of the Wnt pathway (DKK1), inhibit osteoblast function. The net effect is marked bone resorption, producing punched-out lytic lesions, osteopenia, bone pain, pathologic fractures and hypercalcaemia. Hypercalcaemia causes confusion, weakness, constipation, polyuria and contributes to renal dysfunction.
2. **Marrow replacement.** Normocytic normochromic anaemia (and sometimes leukopenia and thrombocytopenia) from replacement of marrow and from IL-6 and inflammatory suppression of erythropoiesis; reduced erythropoietin in renal failure.
3. **Immune suppression.** Decreased production of normal immunoglobulins (immunoparesis) leads to recurrent bacterial infections (pneumococcus, Haemophilus); cellular immunity is relatively unaffected.
4. **Renal failure** (up to 50%; second only to infections as a cause of death): the single most important factor is Bence Jones proteinuria, since light chains are toxic to tubular epithelium and form obstructing casts with Tamm-Horsfall protein (myeloma kidney, cast nephropathy). Contributing factors include hypercalcaemia, hyperuricaemia, amyloid (AL), dehydration, hyperviscosity and nephrotoxic drugs.
5. **Amyloidosis.** Certain light chains (λ6 and λ3 families) are prone to cause AL amyloid deposition.
6. **Hyperviscosity** (about 7%): aggregation of IgA or IgG₃ M protein, with visual, neurologic and bleeding symptoms.

**B. Biochemical features**

- Serum protein electrophoresis: sharp M spike (more than 3 g/dL in most), most often IgG (55%), then IgA (25%); light chains only in about 20%; nonsecretory in about 1%; reduced polyclonal immunoglobulins (immunoparesis).
- Urine: free light chains (Bence Jones proteins; more than 6 mg/dL in most), usually with proteinuria that is not detected by dipstick.
- Serum free light chain assay with an abnormal κ/λ ratio.
- Raised serum calcium (hypercalcaemia), with normal serum alkaline phosphatase (pure lytic lesions), raised urea and creatinine, hyperuricaemia.
- Raised β₂-microglobulin (a prognostic index, with albumin), LDH, and CRP; low serum albumin in advanced disease; **low anion gap** because the paraprotein is cationic; pseudohyponatraemia.
- Markedly raised ESR with rouleaux formation on the smear.


## Laboratory diagnosis of myeloma.

Myeloma is diagnosed by demonstrating clonal plasma cells in the bone marrow, a monoclonal protein in the serum and/or urine on electrophoresis and immunofixation, and evidence of end-organ damage by the CRAB criteria—hypercalcaemia, renal dysfunction, anaemia and lytic bone lesions.

1. **Blood count and smear.** Normocytic normochromic anaemia, **rouleaux formation** (red cells stacked in linear arrays), markedly raised ESR, sometimes leukopenia or thrombocytopenia; plasma cells in the blood in plasma cell leukaemia.
2. **Serum and urine protein studies.** Serum protein electrophoresis shows an M spike; immunofixation identifies the heavy-chain class and the light-chain type; quantitative immunoglobulins show suppression of the uninvolved immunoglobulins; serum free light chain assay and ratio; urine protein electrophoresis and immunofixation for Bence Jones protein (24-hour urine). Most myelomas have more than 3 g/dL of serum immunoglobulin and/or more than 6 mg/dL of urinary Bence Jones protein; in 99% there is an M protein in serum or urine. About 20% have only free light chains and about 1% are nonsecretory, so absence of M protein does not exclude the diagnosis.
3. **Bone marrow aspirate and biopsy (essential).** Increased plasma cells, usually more than 30% of cellularity, in sheets or clusters, with CD138⁺, CD56⁺ (often), and cytoplasmic κ or λ light-chain restriction on immunophenotyping.
4. **Biochemistry.** Serum calcium, creatinine and urea, uric acid, albumin, β₂-microglobulin, LDH.
5. **Radiology.** Skeletal survey—punched-out osteolytic lesions of the skull, vertebrae, ribs, pelvis and long bones, osteopenia, pathologic fractures; MRI, low-dose CT or PET-CT for more sensitive assessment.
6. **Cytogenetics and FISH.** t(11;14), t(4;14), t(14;16), del(17p), del(13q), gain 1q for risk stratification.
7. **Diagnostic criteria.** In Robbins' summary, the diagnosis relies on identification of clonal plasma cells in the marrow and the presence of CRAB criteria. In the IMWG criteria, 10% or more clonal marrow plasma cells (or a biopsy-proven plasmacytoma) plus one or more myeloma-defining events (CRAB; or 60% or more marrow plasma cells; or a serum free light chain ratio of 100 or more; or more than one focal lesion on MRI).


## What is Bence-Jones protein?

Bence Jones protein consists of monoclonal free immunoglobulin light chains (κ or λ) that are small enough to be filtered by the glomerulus and excreted in the urine; it is found in multiple myeloma and other plasma cell neoplasms.

Neoplastic plasma cells often synthesise an excess of light chains relative to heavy chains. Because free light chains are small (molecular weight about 22,000 for monomers and 44,000 for dimers), they pass through the glomerular filter and are excreted in the urine, where they are called Bence Jones proteins; the intact immunoglobulin (160,000 or more) is retained in the circulation unless there is glomerular damage. The proteins were described by Henry Bence Jones in 1847.

**Significance.** Bence Jones proteinuria occurs in a majority of patients with multiple myeloma, including the roughly 20% with light-chain–only disease, and in Waldenström macroglobulinaemia and AL amyloidosis. The excreted light chains are toxic to renal tubular epithelial cells and form casts with Tamm-Horsfall protein, causing **myeloma kidney**, the single most important factor in the renal failure of myeloma. Certain light chains (λ6 and λ3 families) cause AL-type amyloidosis. Its demonstration has diagnostic and monitoring value. Ordinary dipsticks, which detect mostly albumin, may be negative, so specific tests are needed.


## Classify immunoproliferative disorders.

Immunoproliferative disorders, which are proliferations of immunoglobulin-producing B-cell and plasma cell clones, are classified as plasma cell dyscrasias—multiple myeloma and its variants, MGUS, Waldenström macroglobulinaemia, heavy-chain diseases and AL amyloidosis—and the secretory B-cell lymphomas.

**I. Plasma cell neoplasms and related disorders (monoclonal gammopathies)**

1. Multiple myeloma (plasma cell myeloma), with its variants: smoldering (asymptomatic) myeloma, solitary plasmacytoma of bone or extraosseous (soft tissue) plasmacytoma, plasma cell leukaemia, and nonsecretory myeloma.
2. Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS), a premalignant state.
3. Lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma/Waldenström macroglobulinaemia, with IgM paraprotein.
4. Heavy-chain diseases (α—the immunoproliferative small intestinal disease or Mediterranean lymphoma; γ; μ), with free heavy-chain fragments.
5. Immunoglobulin-related (AL) amyloidosis, and light-chain deposition disease.
6. POEMS syndrome and cryoglobulinaemia associated with clonal proliferations.

**II. Other B-cell lymphoproliferative disorders that may secrete monoclonal protein.** CLL, marginal zone lymphomas, and other non-Hodgkin lymphomas, with a small M spike in some.

**III. Secondary (reactive) gammopathies.** Polyclonal increases in immunoglobulins in chronic infections, autoimmune disorders and liver disease, which must be distinguished from monoclonal disorders by the broad (not narrow) band on electrophoresis.


## Waldenström's macroglobulinaemia (in short).

Waldenström macroglobulinaemia is a syndrome of hyperviscosity caused by high levels of monoclonal IgM secreted by a lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma in older adults, without lytic bone lesions.

**Definition and pathogenesis.** Waldenström macroglobulinaemia is a syndrome in which high levels of IgM lead to symptoms related to hyperviscosity of the blood. It occurs in older adults (sixth to seventh decade), most commonly in association with **lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma**, a B-cell neoplasm that resembles CLL/SLL but in which a substantial fraction of tumour cells undergo terminal differentiation into plasma cells. Virtually all cases harbor acquired mutations in MYD88, an adaptor protein that activates NF-κB and promotes tumour growth and survival.

**Morphology.** The marrow contains lymphocytes, plasma cells and plasmacytoid lymphocytes with mast cell hyperplasia; PAS-positive inclusions of immunoglobulin are seen in the cytoplasm (Russell bodies) or nucleus (Dutcher bodies). The lymph nodes, spleen and liver are involved at diagnosis. The lymphoid cells express CD20 and surface IgM.

**Clinical features.** Weakness, fatigue, weight loss; lymphadenopathy, hepatomegaly and splenomegaly in about half; anaemia from marrow infiltration. Because of its large size, IgM increases blood viscosity, producing **hyperviscosity syndrome**: visual impairment from retinal venous engorgement (sausage-link veins, haemorrhages); neurologic symptoms such as headache, dizziness, deafness and stupor; bleeding from complexes of IgM with clotting factors and platelet dysfunction; and cryoglobulinaemia with Raynaud phenomenon and cold urticaria. About 10% have autoimmune haemolysis from cold agglutinins. Unlike multiple myeloma, **bone destruction does not occur**, and renal failure and amyloidosis from light chains are relatively rare.

**Treatment and prognosis.** Plasmapheresis relieves the hyperviscosity (most IgM is intravascular); tumour growth is controlled by low-dose chemotherapy, anti-CD20 antibody (rituximab) and BTK inhibitors. It is indolent, with a median survival of more than 10 years, and transformation to large-cell lymphoma is uncommon.


## How will you diagnose a case of multiple myeloma?

Multiple myeloma can be strongly suspected when the characteristic clinical picture and radiographic changes are present, but definitive diagnosis requires bone marrow examination and tests assessing calcium levels, renal function, blood counts, and serum and urine immunoglobulins. The diagnosis rests on clonal plasma cells in the marrow and the CRAB criteria (hypercalcaemia, renal dysfunction, anaemia and bone lesions).

**1. Clinical suspicion.** An older adult (peak 65–70 years), with bone pain (back, ribs), pathologic fractures, fatigue (anaemia), recurrent bacterial infections, symptoms of hypercalcaemia (confusion, constipation, polyuria), renal failure, and sometimes hyperviscosity, neuropathy or amyloid features.

**2. Haematology.** Normocytic normochromic anaemia; **rouleaux formation** on the smear; markedly raised ESR; sometimes leukopenia and thrombocytopenia; circulating plasma cells in plasma cell leukaemia.

**3. Serum and urine protein studies (key).** Serum protein electrophoresis (a sharp M spike), immunofixation (class of heavy chain and type of light chain), quantitative serum immunoglobulins (reduced uninvolved immunoglobulins), serum free light chain assay with an abnormal ratio, urine electrophoresis and immunofixation for **Bence Jones protein**. The M protein is IgG in about 55%, IgA in 25%, light chains only in about 20%, and nonsecretory in about 1%. Most patients have more than 3 g/dL of serum immunoglobulin and/or more than 6 mg/dL of urine Bence Jones protein.

**4. Bone marrow aspiration and biopsy.** Plasma cells constituting more than 30% of cellularity (10% or more by modern criteria), with atypical and multinucleate forms, immunostaining for CD138, CD56 and monotypic light chains.

**5. Biochemistry.** Raised calcium, creatinine and urea; uric acid; low albumin; β₂-microglobulin and LDH for prognosis; normal alkaline phosphatase.

**6. Imaging.** Skeletal survey showing punched-out lytic lesions 1–4 cm in diameter (skull, vertebrae, ribs, pelvis, femur), osteopenia, or compression fractures; MRI or PET-CT where indicated.

**7. Cytogenetics and FISH.** IGH translocations [t(11;14), t(4;14), t(14;16)], del(17p), del(13q), for risk stratification.

**Diagnostic criteria.** Clonal marrow plasma cells (10% or more) or a biopsy-proven plasmacytoma, plus at least one myeloma-defining event: hypercalcaemia, renal insufficiency, anaemia, or bone lesions (CRAB), or biomarkers of malignancy (marrow plasma cells 60% or more, free light chain ratio of 100 or more, or more than one focal lesion on MRI). Smoldering myeloma (10–30% marrow plasma cells, M protein above 3 g/dL, no symptoms) and MGUS (M protein below 3 g/dL, no symptoms) must be distinguished.


## Give the bone marrow findings of multiple myeloma.

Even away from overt tumour masses, the marrow contains an increased number of plasma cells, which usually constitute **more than 30% of the cellularity** (a diagnostic threshold of 10% clonal plasma cells is used in current criteria, together with a myeloma-defining event). They may infiltrate subtly or completely replace the normal marrow elements.

**Cytologic features.** Like benign plasma cells, malignant plasma cells have an eccentrically placed nucleus and perinuclear clearing (hof) because of a prominent Golgi apparatus. The cells vary from relatively normal-appearing plasma cells, through plasmablasts with vesicular nuclear chromatin and a prominent single nucleolus, to bizarre, multinucleated cells. Dysregulated synthesis and secretion of immunoglobulin leads to intracellular accumulation of intact or partially degraded protein, producing variants: **flame cells** with fiery red cytoplasm, **Mott cells** with multiple grape-like cytoplasmic droplets, and cells containing other inclusions such as fibrils, crystalline rods and globules. The globular inclusions are called **Russell bodies** if cytoplasmic and **Dutcher bodies** if nuclear.

**Other features.** The normal haematopoietic cells are reduced; erythrocytes show rouleaux in the marrow smear. The biopsy shows interstitial, nodular or diffuse (packed marrow) patterns, with bone destruction and lytic lesions consisting of soft, gelatinous red tumour masses. **Immunophenotype:** CD138 (syndecan-1)-positive, often CD56-positive, with cytoplasmic κ or λ light chain restriction. In advanced disease plasma cell infiltrates may be present in the spleen, liver, kidneys, lungs, lymph nodes and other soft tissues.


## Why is ESR sky-high in multiple myeloma?

The erythrocyte sedimentation rate depends mainly on the degree of **rouleaux formation**—the stacking of red cells like coins—because aggregates sediment faster than single cells. Normally red cells repel one another because of the negative charge (zeta potential) on their surface sialic acid residues, and this keeps them separated.

In multiple myeloma the plasma contains large amounts of **monoclonal immunoglobulin (M protein)**. These large, asymmetric, positively charged proteins coat the red cell surface and neutralise its negative charge, so the cells lose their mutual repulsion and adhere in linear stacks. High M protein levels in the blood cause red cells to stick to one another in linear arrays on smears, a finding called rouleaux formation. This increases the rate of sedimentation of red cells in the Westergren tube to sometimes more than 100 mm in the first hour. Increased fibrinogen and acute-phase proteins from inflammation, and anaemia (fewer red cells per unit volume, which favours faster sedimentation), contribute additionally.

Rouleaux formation is characteristic but not specific, since it may be seen in other conditions in which immunoglobulin levels are elevated, such as lupus erythematosus and early HIV infection.


## An elderly patient has low back/bone pain, punched-out lesions, sky-high ESR. What is your probable diagnosis?

The probable diagnosis is **multiple myeloma** (plasma cell myeloma).

**Reasoning.** Multiple myeloma is chiefly a disease of older adults, with a peak age of 65 to 70 years. The back and bone pain results from destructive plasma cell tumours, which involve the axial skeleton—the vertebral column, ribs, skull, pelvis and femur—and cause pathologic fractures, such as vertebral compression fractures. The radiographic hallmark is **punched-out lytic lesions** of 1 to 4 cm in diameter, best seen in the skull. These lesions result from myeloma-derived MIP-1α and Wnt pathway inhibitors, which increase osteoclast activity and inhibit osteoblasts. The very high ESR results from the M protein-induced rouleaux formation.

**Confirmation.** (1) Serum and urine electrophoresis with immunofixation, to demonstrate an M spike and Bence Jones protein; (2) bone marrow aspirate and biopsy showing an increased number of plasma cells (usually above 30%); (3) serum calcium, creatinine, haemoglobin (CRAB features); (4) skeletal survey or MRI/PET-CT; (5) serum free light chains and β₂-microglobulin.

**Differential diagnosis.** Metastatic carcinoma (breast, prostate, lung, kidney, thyroid), which also causes lytic lesions but without an M spike (prostate metastases are typically sclerotic); lymphoma involving bone; hyperparathyroidism (brown tumours, raised parathyroid hormone); MGUS and solitary plasmacytoma; osteoporotic fractures; tuberculosis of the spine.


## Write a short note on Bence-Jones protein and its detection in urine.

**Nature.** Bence Jones protein consists of monoclonal free immunoglobulin light chains (κ or λ) produced in excess by neoplastic plasma cells. Because free light chains are small, they are filtered by the glomerulus and excreted in the urine, whereas intact immunoglobulin (molecular weight 160,000 or more) is not. They occur in most patients with multiple myeloma (more than 6 mg/dL of urinary Bence Jones protein is typical), in light-chain–only myeloma, and in Waldenström macroglobulinaemia, AL amyloidosis and light-chain deposition disease.

**Clinical significance.** Bence Jones proteins are toxic to renal tubular epithelial cells and form obstructing casts with Tamm-Horsfall protein (myeloma kidney); this is the single most important factor in the renal failure of myeloma. Certain light chains (λ6, λ3) cause AL amyloidosis. Their detection helps in diagnosis and in monitoring the response to therapy.

**Detection in urine.**

1. **Heat test (classic).** An acidified urine sample (pH about 5, acetate buffer) is slowly heated. Bence Jones protein precipitates when heated to about 40–60 °C, redissolves partly or completely on boiling at 100 °C, and reappears on cooling to about 60 °C. The test is insensitive and subject to false results.
2. **Sulfosalicylic acid or acid precipitation test.** Positive precipitation in a urine that is **negative on dipstick** suggests non-albumin protein, because dipsticks detect albumin principally and miss light chains.
3. **Urine protein electrophoresis** of a concentrated 24-hour specimen shows a sharp monoclonal band.
4. **Immunofixation electrophoresis (definitive).** It identifies the protein as κ or λ free light chain and confirms its monoclonality.
5. **Serum free light chain assay** (κ/λ ratio) is the most sensitive test and is also used in monitoring.

**Myeloproliferative and Myelodysplastic Disorders**

**Myeloproliferative disorders**


## What do you know about myelodysplastic syndrome?

Myelodysplastic syndrome, now called myelodysplastic neoplasm, is a group of clonal stem cell disorders characterised by ineffective and dysplastic haematopoiesis, producing peripheral cytopenias with a hypercellular marrow, and carrying a high risk of transformation to acute myeloid leukaemia.

**Definition.** The term myelodysplastic neoplasm (MDS) refers to a group of clonal stem cell disorders in which the bone marrow is partly or wholly replaced by the clonal progeny of a neoplastic multipotent stem cell that retains the capacity to differentiate, but does so in an ineffective and disordered fashion. Because the "birthing process" of blood cells is defective, patients have peripheral blood cytopenias of varying severity. MDS may be primary (idiopathic) or therapy-related (t-MDS), appearing 2 to 8 years after genotoxic exposure (alkylating agents, radiation).

**Pathogenesis.** Driver mutations partly overlap with those of AML, and affect (1) epigenetic regulators (DNA methylation, histone modification), (2) RNA splicing factors (SF3B1, SRSF2, U2AF1), and (3) transcription factors such as RUNX1; about 10% have TP53 mutations, associated with complex karyotype and very poor outcome. Recurrent chromosomal abnormalities include monosomy 5 and 7, deletions of 5q, 7q and 20q, and trisomy 8. The loss of one copy of the ribosomal protein gene RPS14 in the 5q region contributes to ineffective erythropoiesis. Clonal haematopoiesis with splicing factor mutations is a precursor.

**Morphology.** The marrow is usually hypercellular (sometimes normo- or hypocellular), with dysplasia in the erythroid, granulocytic, monocytic and megakaryocytic lineages: ring sideroblasts, megaloblastoid maturation and nuclear budding in erythroid cells; hypogranular neutrophils with **pseudo–Pelger-Hüet cells** (bilobed nuclei); and micromegakaryocytes, with single nuclear lobes or multiple separate nuclei (pawn-ball megakaryocytes). Marrow blasts are increased but fewer than 20%. The blood shows macrocytes, poikilocytes, giant platelets, and cytopenias; blasts under 10% of leukocytes.

**Clinical features.** A disease of older adults (mean age 70), often discovered incidentally; when symptomatic there is weakness, infections and bleeding from pancytopenia. Prognosis varies by blast count, cytopenias and cytogenetics, with survival from under 6 months to over 5 years. Progression to AML occurs more rapidly in poor-risk groups and in t-MDS (median survival 4 to 8 months). Management includes supportive care (transfusion, antibiotics), hypomethylating agents, lenalidomide in del(5q), and allogeneic stem cell transplantation, the only curative option.


## What are myeloproliferative disorders?

Myeloproliferative neoplasms are clonal disorders of haematopoietic stem or progenitor cells in which there is increased production of one or more mature myeloid elements—red cells, granulocytes or platelets—driven by constitutively activated tyrosine kinases, leading to high blood counts, splenomegaly, and a tendency to transform to marrow fibrosis or acute leukaemia.

**Definition and pathogenesis.** The common pathogenic feature of the myeloproliferative neoplasms (MPNs) is the presence of mutated, constitutively activated tyrosine kinases or other acquired aberrations in signalling pathways that lead to growth factor independence. Haematopoietic growth factors act on normal progenitors by binding to surface receptors and activating tyrosine kinases, which turn on pathways that promote growth and survival. The mutated kinases circumvent these controls, and because they do not impair differentiation, the usual result is an increase in one or more mature blood elements. Most MPNs originate in multipotent myeloid progenitors, while others arise in pluripotent stem cells.

**Common features.**

1. Increased proliferative drive in the bone marrow.
2. Variable homing of the neoplastic stem cells to secondary haematopoietic organs, producing extramedullary haematopoiesis (splenomegaly, hepatomegaly).
3. Variable transformation to a "spent phase" characterised by marrow fibrosis and peripheral cytopenias.
4. Variable transformation to acute leukaemia.

**Principal entities and their driver lesions.**

| Disorder | Mutation | Main feature |
|---|---|---|
| Chronic myeloid leukaemia | BCR::ABL1 (Ph chromosome) | Granulocytosis, splenomegaly |
| Polycythaemia vera | JAK2 (V617F in >95%) | Erythrocytosis |
| Essential thrombocythaemia | JAK2 (50–60%), CALR (25–35%), MPL (5–10%) | Thrombocytosis |
| Primary myelofibrosis | JAK2, CALR, MPL | Marrow fibrosis, extramedullary haematopoiesis |
| Systemic mastocytosis | KIT | Mast cell proliferation |
| Chronic eosinophilic leukaemia | FIP1L1::PDGFRA | Eosinophilia |

There is considerable clinical and morphologic overlap among MPNs, and they are classified on clinical, laboratory and molecular criteria. Effective kinase inhibitors (imatinib for BCR-ABL and PDGFRA, ruxolitinib for JAK2) have made molecular diagnosis important.


## Classify myeloproliferative disorder.

Myeloproliferative neoplasms are classified, on the basis of clinical, laboratory and molecular criteria, into chronic myeloid leukaemia (BCR::ABL1-positive) and the BCR::ABL1-negative group of polycythaemia vera, essential thrombocythaemia and primary myelofibrosis, plus rarer entities.

| Group | Entities | Driver mutation |
|---|---|---|
| **A. BCR::ABL1-positive** | Chronic myeloid leukaemia | BCR::ABL1 fusion (Philadelphia chromosome, t(9;22)) |
| **B. BCR::ABL1-negative (classic or "non-CML")** | Polycythaemia vera | JAK2 (V617F or exon 12) |
| | Essential thrombocythaemia | JAK2, CALR, MPL |
| | Primary myelofibrosis | JAK2, CALR, MPL |
| **C. Rarer MPNs** | Chronic neutrophilic leukaemia | CSF3R |
| | Chronic eosinophilic leukaemia and myeloid/lymphoid neoplasms with eosinophilia and tyrosine kinase gene rearrangement | FIP1L1::PDGFRA, PDGFRB, FGFR1, JAK2 fusions |
| | Systemic mastocytosis | KIT |
| | MPN, unclassifiable | — |

Related myeloid neoplasms are acute myeloid leukaemia and myelodysplastic neoplasms; some tumours have features intermediate between myelodysplastic and myeloproliferative neoplasms (e.g., chronic myelomonocytic leukaemia).


## What do you mean by polycythaemia?

Polycythaemia is an increase in the haemoglobin concentration, haematocrit and red cell count above the normal range; it may be relative, due to a reduced plasma volume, or absolute, due to a true increase in red cell mass, which is either primary (polycythaemia vera) or secondary.

In men, polycythaemia is a haemoglobin above about 16.5 g/dL or a haematocrit above 49% (in women, above 16.0 g/dL or 48%).

**Classification.**

1. **Relative (spurious) polycythaemia:** a decrease in plasma volume with a normal red cell mass—dehydration, diarrhoea and vomiting, burns, diuretic use, and stress polycythaemia (Gaisböck syndrome).
2. **Absolute polycythaemia:** a true increase in red cell mass.

- Primary: **polycythaemia vera**, a clonal myeloproliferative neoplasm with JAK2 mutation, low serum erythropoietin and growth factor–independent proliferation; and rare familial erythropoietin receptor mutations.
- Secondary (erythropoietin-driven): appropriate, due to hypoxia (high altitude, chronic lung disease, cyanotic congenital heart disease, hypoventilation, sleep apnoea, heavy smoking with carboxyhaemoglobin, high-affinity haemoglobins); and inappropriate, due to autonomous erythropoietin production by tumours (renal cell carcinoma, hepatocellular carcinoma, cerebellar haemangioblastoma, uterine leiomyoma) and renal disease (cysts, hydronephrosis, post-transplant).

Distinguishing among these categories is the first step in evaluating polycythaemia, since PV must be differentiated from relative polycythaemia and other causes of absolute polycythaemia.


## Clinical features of polycythaemia.

The clinical features of polycythaemia, taking polycythaemia vera as the prototype, arise from the increased red cell mass and blood viscosity—plethora, headache, dizziness and hypertension—together with thrombosis and bleeding, pruritus, peptic ulceration, gout and splenomegaly.

PV is uncommon (1 to 3 per 100,000 a year), usually appears insidiously in adults of late middle age, and most symptoms relate to the increased red cell mass and haematocrit; total blood volume is also increased.

1. **Hyperviscosity and abnormal blood flow.** The low-pressure venous side becomes greatly distended; patients are plethoric (ruddy complexion, conjunctival injection) and cyanotic from stagnation and deoxygenation of blood in peripheral vessels. Headache, dizziness, tinnitus, visual disturbances, hypertension, and gastrointestinal symptoms are common.
2. **Thrombosis.** Abnormal blood flow and platelet function lead to an increased risk of both thrombosis and bleeding. About 25% of patients present with deep venous thrombosis, myocardial infarction or stroke; thromboses occur in the hepatic veins (Budd-Chiari syndrome) and the portal and mesenteric veins (bowel infarction); thrombosis may precede the haematologic findings. Erythromelalgia (burning pain in the hands and feet) may occur.
3. **Bleeding.** Minor haemorrhages (epistaxis, bleeding gums) are common, and life-threatening haemorrhages occur in 5% to 10%.
4. **Basophil histamine effects.** Intense pruritus (often after a hot bath) and peptic ulceration, possibly from histamine release by basophils.
5. **Hypermetabolism and cell turnover.** Hyperuricaemia with symptomatic secondary gout in 5% to 10%.
6. **Organomegaly.** Mild splenomegaly and hepatomegaly, from congestion early and from extramedullary haematopoiesis later.
7. **Progression.** After about 10 years, 15% to 20% enter a spent phase with marrow fibrosis and massive splenomegaly; about 2% transform to AML.


## Differences between polycythaemia vera and secondary polycythaemia.

In polycythaemia vera the erythropoietin level is low, JAK2 is mutated, and there is a panmyelosis with splenomegaly, whereas in secondary polycythaemia the erythropoietin level is high, JAK2 is normal, and only red cells are increased in response to hypoxia or an erythropoietin-secreting tumour.

| Feature | Polycythaemia vera | Secondary polycythaemia |
|---|---|---|
| **Nature** | Clonal myeloproliferative neoplasm | Reactive; erythropoietin-driven |
| **Cause** | Activating JAK2 mutation (V617F in more than 95%) | Hypoxia (altitude, lung disease, cardiac shunt, smoking), erythropoietin-secreting tumours, renal disease |
| **Serum erythropoietin** | **Low** (constitutive JAK/STAT signalling) | **High** (or inappropriately normal) |
| ***JAK2* mutation** | Present | Absent |
| **Cell lines involved** | Panmyelosis: red cells, granulocytes and platelets | Red cells only |
| **White cells and platelets** | Leukocytosis (12,000–50,000) with basophilia; thrombocytosis, giant platelets | Normal |
| **Spleen** | Splenomegaly (in about 70%) | Not enlarged |
| **Pruritus, gout, thrombosis** | Common | Uncommon |
| **Arterial oxygen saturation** | Normal | Often reduced (hypoxic causes) |
| **LAP score and vitamin B₁₂** | Raised | Normal |
| **Bone marrow** | Hypercellular; trilineage proliferation with pleomorphic megakaryocytes | Erythroid hyperplasia only |
| **Course** | Thrombosis and bleeding; spent phase with myelofibrosis (15–20%); AML (2%) | Resolves with correction of cause |


## Laboratory diagnosis of polycythaemia.

The laboratory work-up first confirms a true absolute erythrocytosis by haemoglobin and haematocrit, then separates polycythaemia vera from secondary causes by serum erythropoietin and JAK2 mutation testing, supported by marrow examination.

**1. Complete blood count and smear.** Haemoglobin above 16 g/dL (above 16.5 in men), haematocrit above 49% (48% in women), often 55% or more in PV; raised red cell count; leukocytosis (12,000–50,000/µL) and thrombocytosis (often above 500,000/µL) with large or abnormal platelets, basophilia, and increased red cell mass. Note that chronic bleeding with iron deficiency may suppress erythropoiesis enough to bring the haematocrit into the normal range.

**2. Confirm absolute polycythaemia.** Red cell mass by radioisotope (⁵¹Cr-labelled red cells) together with plasma volume ¹³¹I-albumin, when needed; this excludes relative polycythaemia (high haematocrit, normal red cell mass).

**3. Serum erythropoietin.** Low in PV; high in secondary polycythaemia.

**4. Molecular tests.** JAK2 V617F (more than 95% of PV), or JAK2 exon 12 mutation in the remainder.

**5. Bone marrow aspirate and biopsy.** Hypercellularity for age with trilineage growth (panmyelosis), prominent erythroid, granulocytic and megakaryocytic proliferation, pleomorphic mature megakaryocytes; increased reticulin in about 10% at diagnosis; stainable iron reduced.

**6. Tests to exclude secondary causes.** Arterial oxygen saturation (and P₅₀), carboxyhaemoglobin, ultrasound/CT of the abdomen (renal or hepatic tumour, polycystic disease), chest radiograph, sleep study.

**7. Other findings in PV.** Raised leukocyte alkaline phosphatase and serum vitamin B₁₂, hyperuricaemia, abnormal platelet function tests.


## Non-CML myeloproliferative disorders.

The non-CML myeloproliferative neoplasms, also called the Philadelphia chromosome–negative or classic MPNs, are polycythaemia vera, essential thrombocythaemia and primary myelofibrosis, which are driven by JAK2, CALR or MPL mutations.

The BCR::ABL1 fusion distinguishes CML from all other myeloproliferative neoplasms. The BCR::ABL1-negative group comprises the following.

| Disease | Mutation | Predominant feature | Salient points |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Polycythaemia vera** | JAK2 (>95%) | Erythrocytosis (panmyelosis) | Low erythropoietin; thrombosis; pruritus; spent phase 15–20%; AML about 2%; phlebotomy and aspirin; median survival about 10 years |
| **Essential thrombocythaemia** | JAK2 (50–60%), CALR (25–35%), MPL (5–10%) | Sustained thrombocytosis | Thrombosis, bleeding, erythromelalgia; absence of polycythaemia and marrow fibrosis; survival 12–15 years |
| **Primary myelofibrosis** | JAK2, CALR, MPL (about 90%) | Marrow fibrosis, extramedullary haematopoiesis | Anaemia, massive splenomegaly, leukoerythroblastosis, teardrop cells; median survival 3–5 years |

Less common examples are chronic neutrophilic leukaemia (CSF3R), chronic eosinophilic leukaemia (FIP1L1::PDGFRA), and systemic mastocytosis (KIT). All of these disorders have increased proliferative drive in the marrow, variable extramedullary haematopoiesis, and variable transformation to a spent phase of marrow fibrosis or to acute leukaemia. Unlike CML, transformation to ALL is rarely seen in PV, as the cell of origin is a progenitor committed to myeloid differentiation.


## WHO diagnostic criteria for polycythaemia vera.

The WHO criteria for polycythaemia vera require either all three major criteria, or the first two major criteria plus the minor criterion; the major criteria are raised haemoglobin or haematocrit, a hypercellular marrow with trilineage growth, and the JAK2 V617F or exon 12 mutation, and the minor criterion is a subnormal serum erythropoietin.

**Major criteria**

1. Haemoglobin above 16.5 g/dL in men or above 16.0 g/dL in women, or haematocrit above 49% in men or above 48% in women (the earlier WHO scheme also allowed an increased red cell mass above 25% of the predicted mean).
2. Bone marrow biopsy showing hypercellularity for age with trilineage growth (panmyelosis), including prominent erythroid, granulocytic and megakaryocytic proliferation with pleomorphic, mature megakaryocytes (differing in size).
3. Presence of JAK2 V617F or JAK2 exon 12 mutation.

**Minor criterion**

- Subnormal serum erythropoietin level.

**Rule.** The diagnosis of PV requires **all three major criteria**, or the **first two major criteria and the minor criterion**. The bone marrow biopsy (major criterion 2) may not be required in patients with sustained absolute erythrocytosis (haemoglobin above 18.5 g/dL in men or above 16.5 g/dL in women, corresponding to haematocrits above 55.5% and 49.5%) when the JAK2 mutation and the low erythropoietin are present.


## Define myelofibrosis.

Myelofibrosis is a disorder in which the bone marrow is progressively replaced by fibrous tissue, leading to cytopenias, extramedullary haematopoiesis with splenomegaly, and a leukoerythroblastic blood picture.

The hallmark of primary myelofibrosis is the development of obliterative marrow fibrosis. The replacement of the marrow by fibrous tissue reduces bone marrow haematopoiesis, leading to cytopenias and extensive extramedullary haematopoiesis, principally in the spleen, liver and lymph nodes. The fibroblasts are non-neoplastic; the fibrosis is caused by inappropriate release of fibrogenic factors, platelet-derived growth factor and TGF-β, from neoplastic megakaryocytes. TGF-β also promotes collagen deposition and angiogenesis. The disease may arise as a primary myeloproliferative neoplasm (about 90% have JAK2, CALR or MPL mutations), or the same histologic picture may represent the spent phase of polycythaemia vera, essential thrombocythaemia or CML, or result from other marrow-injuring processes (secondary myelofibrosis).


## Laboratory diagnosis of myelofibrosis.

Myelofibrosis is suspected from anaemia with a leukoerythroblastic blood picture and teardrop red cells in a patient with splenomegaly, and is confirmed by a bone marrow biopsy showing fibrosis with atypical megakaryocytes and by the finding of a JAK2, CALR or MPL mutation.

**Peripheral blood**

- Moderate to severe **normochromic normocytic anaemia**.
- **Leukoerythroblastosis:** premature release of nucleated red cell precursors and early granulocyte precursors (myelocytes, metamyelocytes, occasional blasts), caused by marrow distortion and by immature cells entering the blood from sites of extramedullary haematopoiesis.
- **Teardrop-shaped red cells (dacryocytes)**, probably damaged during their passage from the fibrotic marrow.
- The white cell count is usually normal or mildly reduced but may be markedly elevated (80,000 to 100,000/µL) early; the platelet count is usually normal or elevated at diagnosis, with large platelets (and basophilia), and thrombocytopenia may supervene with progression.
- These findings are not specific; leukoerythroblastosis and teardrop cells are also seen in other infiltrative marrow disorders, including granulomatous diseases and metastatic tumours.

**Bone marrow**

- Aspiration: often a **dry tap** because of the fibrosis. The **trephine biopsy is essential for diagnosis**.
- Early (prefibrotic) phase: hypercellular marrow with increased maturing cells of all lineages; erythroid and granulocytic precursors appear normal, but megakaryocytes are large, with bulbous, hyperchromatic or "cloud-like" nuclei, and are abnormally clustered; minimal fibrosis.
- Fibrotic phase: the marrow becomes hypocellular and diffusely fibrotic (reticulin and then collagen); atypical megakaryocytes in clusters; haematopoietic cells in dilated sinusoids; very late osteosclerosis (new bone formation).

**Molecular and other tests.** JAK2 V617F in 50–60%, CALR in 25–35% and MPL in 5–10% (about 90% overall); absence of BCR::ABL1 excludes CML. Serum uric acid, LDH and alkaline phosphatase are raised; the LAP score is variable. Imaging shows splenomegaly (up to 4,000 g), with extramedullary haematopoiesis and infarcts. Marrow cytogenetics may show del(13q), del(20q), trisomy 8 and 9.


## Types of myelofibrosis.

Myelofibrosis is of two types: primary (idiopathic) myelofibrosis, a myeloproliferative neoplasm, and secondary myelofibrosis, which follows other myeloproliferative neoplasms or other marrow-injuring diseases.

**1. Primary myelofibrosis (chronic idiopathic myelofibrosis, agnogenic myeloid metaplasia).** A myeloproliferative neoplasm in which about 90% of cases have activating JAK2, CALR or MPL mutations. It occurs mostly after 60 years of age and passes through a prefibrotic (early) phase of marrow hypercellularity with atypical megakaryocytes and an overt fibrotic phase with marrow fibrosis, massive splenomegaly and cytopenias.

**2. Secondary myelofibrosis.** Fibrosis resulting from another disease, in which the marrow fibroblasts are reactive.

- Post-polycythaemia vera and post–essential thrombocythaemia myelofibrosis (the "spent phase" of myeloproliferative neoplasms, which is histologically identical to primary myelofibrosis; spent phase of PV in 15–20% after about 10 years), and the fibrotic transformation of CML.
- Myelofibrosis secondary to other disorders, such as metastatic carcinoma, lymphomas and other haematologic malignancies, granulomatous infections, toxins and radiation, and metabolic bone disease.

**3. Acute (malignant) myelofibrosis (acute panmyelosis with myelofibrosis).** A rare, rapidly progressive form with pancytopenia and fibrosis, often overlapping with megakaryoblastic leukaemia, without splenomegaly.

It is not clear whether primary myelofibrosis is truly distinct from polycythaemia vera and essential thrombocythaemia or merely reflects unusually rapid progression to the spent phase.


## Conditions associated with secondary myelofibrosis.

Secondary myelofibrosis occurs in other myeloproliferative neoplasms, in marrow infiltration by tumour or granulomas, in other haematologic malignancies, and with toxic, infectious and autoimmune injury to the marrow.

| Category | Conditions |
|---|---|
| **Other myeloid neoplasms** | Polycythaemia vera, essential thrombocythaemia, chronic myeloid leukaemia (spent phase), myelodysplastic neoplasms, acute megakaryoblastic leukaemia (AML with megakaryocytic differentiation) |
| **Other haematologic malignancies** | Hairy cell leukaemia, acute lymphoblastic leukaemia, Hodgkin and non-Hodgkin lymphomas, multiple myeloma, systemic mastocytosis |
| **Metastatic and infiltrative disease** | Metastatic carcinoma (breast, prostate, lung, stomach), Gaucher disease |
| **Infections and granulomatous disease** | Tuberculosis, sarcoidosis, fungal infection, HIV |
| **Toxins, drugs, radiation** | Benzene, thorium dioxide, ionising radiation |
| **Metabolic and bone disease** | Hyperparathyroidism, renal osteodystrophy, vitamin D deficiency (rickets), osteopetrosis, Paget disease |
| **Autoimmune and other** | Systemic lupus erythematosus, systemic sclerosis, pulmonary hypertension, gray platelet syndrome |

Marrow fibrosis in these settings arises from the inappropriate release of fibrogenic cytokines (PDGF, TGF-β) by abnormal megakaryocytes or inflammatory and malignant cells. Metastatic cancer and granulomatous disease induce local marrow fibrosis, in which the marrow usually cannot be aspirated, and the lesions are best seen in biopsy.


## Essential thrombocythaemia (in short).

Essential thrombocythaemia is a myeloproliferative neoplasm characterised by a sustained, marked increase in platelet number, driven by JAK2, CALR or MPL mutations, with thrombosis and bleeding as the main complications, and without polycythaemia or marrow fibrosis.

**Definition and pathogenesis.** Essential thrombocythaemia (ET) is associated with diverse mutations that increase JAK-STAT signalling and mimic constitutive growth factor receptor signalling. Over 90% of cases have activating mutations in JAK2 (approximately 50–60%), MPL (5–10%), the thrombopoietin receptor, or CALR (calreticulin, approximately 25–35%). The mutated CALR proteins are secreted and bind and activate the thrombopoietin receptor, an oncogenic autocrine loop. Constitutive signalling renders the progenitors thrombopoietin-independent.

**Morphology.** The marrow is mildly hypercellular with markedly increased, large megakaryocytes; delicate reticulin only, without the overt fibrosis of myelofibrosis. The blood smear shows large to giant platelets, up to the size of red cells, often with mild leukocytosis. Mild organomegaly in about 50%.

**Clinical features.** Incidence 1 to 3 per 100,000 per year; usually over 60 years but also in young adults. Platelets are increased and functionally abnormal, leading to **thrombosis** (deep veins, portal and hepatic veins, myocardial infarction) and **haemorrhage**; up to one-third have acquired von Willebrand disease. **Erythromelalgia** (burning pain in the hands and feet from occlusion of small arterioles by platelet aggregates) is characteristic.

**Diagnosis.** Persistent platelet count of 450,000/µL or more, with JAK2, CALR or MPL mutation or exclusion of reactive thrombocytosis (iron deficiency, inflammation); exclusion of PV, primary myelofibrosis and CML.

**Course.** Indolent with long asymptomatic periods punctuated by thrombotic or haemorrhagic crises; median survival 12–15 years; rare spent phase or transformation to AML. Treatment: low-dose aspirin and "gentle" cytoreduction (hydroxyurea).


## What do you mean by sub-leukaemic leukaemia (marrow picture)?

**Meaning.** Subleukaemic leukaemia is a form of leukaemia, usually acute, in which the total leukocyte count in the peripheral blood is normal or only slightly increased (or low) and blasts are few or absent in the blood, whereas the bone marrow is heavily infiltrated by leukaemic cells. When the leukocyte count is low and no blasts are seen, the term aleukaemic leukaemia is used. In acute myeloid leukaemia the number of blasts in the blood is variable; blasts are under 10,000/µL in about 50% of patients and occasionally absent altogether, which is why a marrow examination is essential to exclude acute leukaemia in a pancytopenic patient.

**Peripheral blood.** Pancytopenia or bicytopenia, with anaemia, thrombocytopenia and neutropenia; very few or no blasts; normal or slightly raised total count; the peripheral smear may be misleading.

**Marrow picture (diagnostic).**

- The marrow is **hypercellular** (occasionally normocellular), with replacement of the normal fat and haematopoietic elements by **blasts that constitute 20% or more** of nucleated cells (WHO), or fewer if a defining genetic abnormality is present.
- Residual erythroid, granulocytic and megakaryocytic cells are markedly reduced, and may show dysplasia.
