- The blasts are identified by cytochemistry (myeloperoxidase, Sudan black positive in myeloblasts; PAS positive in lymphoblasts) and immunophenotyping; Auer rods suggest AML.
- The biopsy confirms hypercellularity with sheets of blasts and shows fibrosis if present (an aspiration "dry tap" may occur in AML with megakaryocytic differentiation and in hairy cell leukaemia).
- Cytogenetics and molecular studies identify the type and prognosis.

The importance of recognising the entity is that, without a marrow examination, the pancytopenia may be misdiagnosed as aplastic anaemia, myelodysplasia or megaloblastic anaemia.


## How will you differentiate sub-leukaemic leukaemia from aplastic anemia?

Both conditions present with pancytopenia (anaemia, neutropenia and thrombocytopenia) and may have a "normal" leukocyte count with no blasts in the blood, and therefore cannot be separated by the peripheral smear alone; the distinction depends on the bone marrow examination, particularly the trephine biopsy.

| Feature | Subleukaemic leukaemia | Aplastic anaemia |
|---|---|---|
| **Nature** | Clonal neoplasm of haematopoietic progenitors | Marrow failure from stem cell injury (often immune-mediated; drugs, viruses, idiopathic) |
| **Clinical findings** | Pallor, fever, bleeding, **bone pain, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly** | Pallor, fever, bleeding; **no organomegaly** and no lymphadenopathy |
| **Peripheral blood** | Pancytopenia with few or occasional blasts; hiatus leukaemicus | Pancytopenia without blasts or abnormal cells |
| **Bone marrow aspirate** | Hypercellular with **20% or more blasts** | Hypocellular, with fatty replacement, scanty haematopoietic cells, relative lymphocyte, plasma cell and stromal cell predominance; no blasts |
| **Trephine biopsy** | Packed marrow, loss of fat spaces, infiltration by blasts | Markedly hypocellular, with the proportion of fat greatly increased |
| **Cytochemistry / flow cytometry** | MPO, SBB, TdT or myeloid/lymphoid markers positive | No blast population |
| **Cytogenetics** | Clonal abnormalities (t(8;21), t(15;17), etc.) | Normal karyotype |
| **LDH and uric acid** | Raised | Normal |
| **Spleen** | Enlarged (often) | Not enlarged |
| **Treatment and prognosis** | Chemotherapy, transplant | Immunosuppression, transplant; supportive care |

The aspirate in aplastic anaemia is typically dilute and haemodilute, and the trephine biopsy settles the question, since the proportion of fat is greatly increased in hypoplastic states, whereas fat cells are largely replaced when the marrow is infiltrated by haematopoietic tumours.


## Write a short note on polycythaemia rubra vera.

**Definition.** Polycythaemia rubra vera (polycythaemia vera, PV) is a clonal myeloproliferative neoplasm characterised by increased marrow production of red cells, granulocytes and platelets (panmyelosis), though it is the increase in red cells (polycythaemia) that is responsible for most of the clinical symptoms. It must be differentiated from relative polycythaemia due to haemoconcentration and from other causes of absolute polycythaemia.

**Pathogenesis.** The transformed progenitor cells have markedly decreased requirements for erythropoietin and other growth factors because of activating mutations in the tyrosine kinase JAK2, which lies downstream of the erythropoietin, thrombopoietin and G-CSF receptors. More than 97% of cases have the JAK2 V617F mutation (valine to phenylalanine at residue 617); the rest have other JAK2 mutations such as those in exon 12. In 25% to 30% the tumour cells have two mutated copies of JAK2, associated with higher white counts, greater splenomegaly, pruritus and progression to the spent phase. Because the pathway is constitutively active, **serum erythropoietin levels are low**, in contrast to secondary polycythaemia. Elevated haematocrit causes hyperviscosity and sludging, and together with thrombocytosis and abnormal platelet function predisposes to both thrombosis and bleeding.

**Morphology.** The marrow is hypercellular with residual fat; red cell, granulocyte and megakaryocyte precursors are increased. Reticulin fibres are moderately to markedly increased in about 10% of marrows at diagnosis. Mild organomegaly early, from congestion. The blood often contains increased basophils and abnormally large platelets. Late in the course, a **spent phase** with extensive marrow fibrosis, massive splenomegaly and extramedullary haematopoiesis occurs in 15–20% after an average of 10 years. Transformation to AML occurs in about 2%.

**Clinical features.** Insidious onset in adults of late middle age (1–3 per 100,000 a year). Plethora and cyanosis, headache, dizziness, hypertension, gastrointestinal symptoms, intense pruritus and peptic ulceration (histamine from basophils), and hyperuricaemia with gout in 5–10%. About 25% present with thrombosis (deep vein thrombosis, myocardial infarction, stroke, Budd-Chiari syndrome, mesenteric thrombosis); haemorrhage in 5–10% is life-threatening.

**Laboratory findings.** Haemoglobin above 16 g/dL, often haematocrit above 55%; white cell count 12,000–50,000/µL; platelets often above 500,000/µL with giant forms and defective aggregation; low erythropoietin; JAK2 mutation. Iron deficiency from chronic bleeding can lower the haematocrit into the normal range, masking the disease.

**Treatment and prognosis.** Untreated, death from bleeding or thrombosis occurs within months. Maintaining the haematocrit at nearly normal levels by phlebotomy with low-dose aspirin extends median survival to about 10 years; cytoreduction (hydroxyurea) in high-risk patients; JAK2 inhibitors (ruxolitinib) for the spent phase.

**Spleen and Hypersplenism**

**Splenomegaly and hypersplenism**


## Causes of hypersplenism.

Hypersplenism is enlargement of the spleen with cytopenias caused by increased sequestration and destruction of blood cells, and it complicates any cause of splenomegaly, the commonest being portal hypertension from cirrhosis, haematologic disorders such as haemolytic anaemias and myeloproliferative neoplasms, lymphomas and chronic infections.

Hypersplenism is a syndrome characterised by anaemia, leukopenia and/or thrombocytopenia in the presence of splenomegaly. The probable cause of the cytopenias is increased sequestration of formed elements with enhanced phagocytosis by splenic macrophages. The normal spleen holds 30% to 40% of the platelet mass, and with splenomegaly up to 80% to 90% may be sequestered in the red pulp. In congestive splenomegaly, the increased portal pressure causes collagen deposition in the sinusoidal basement membranes and slows the flow of blood from the cords to the sinusoids, prolonging exposure of the blood cells to macrophages. An expanded plasma volume contributes by dilution.

**Causes** (any condition causing significant splenomegaly may produce hypersplenism):

| Category | Examples |
|---|---|
| **Congestive (portal hypertension)** | Cirrhosis (the main cause of massive congestive splenomegaly), schistosomiasis, portal vein or splenic vein thrombosis, Budd-Chiari syndrome, right heart failure |
| **Haematologic** | Hereditary spherocytosis, autoimmune haemolytic anaemia, thalassaemia major, sickle cell disease (early); myeloproliferative neoplasms (CML, primary myelofibrosis, polycythaemia vera); extramedullary haematopoiesis |
| **Lymphoproliferative** | Non-Hodgkin lymphomas and lymphocytic leukaemias (CLL, hairy cell leukaemia), Hodgkin lymphoma |
| **Infections** | Malaria, visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar), tuberculosis, typhoid, brucellosis, infective endocarditis, infectious mononucleosis, HIV |
| **Infiltrative and storage disorders** | Gaucher disease, Niemann-Pick disease, amyloidosis, sarcoidosis |
| **Autoimmune** | Felty syndrome (rheumatoid arthritis with splenomegaly and neutropenia), systemic lupus erythematosus |
| **Primary (idiopathic)** | Rare; splenomegaly with cytopenias and no demonstrable cause |


## Causes of splenomegaly.

Splenomegaly results from infections, congestion from portal hypertension, haematologic and lymphoid disorders, immunologic and inflammatory diseases, storage diseases and neoplasms; the spleen is involved secondarily in all systemic inflammations, generalised haematopoietic disorders and many metabolic disturbances.

Splenomegaly is the major manifestation of splenic disorders, which are only rarely primary. When sufficiently enlarged, the spleen causes a dragging sensation in the left upper quadrant, discomfort after eating from pressure on the stomach, and may produce hypersplenism. Disorders associated with splenomegaly are as follows.

| Mechanism | Examples |
|---|---|
| **Infections (acute splenitis)** | Any blood-borne infection, particularly infective endocarditis; infectious mononucleosis; typhoid, tuberculosis, brucellosis, septicaemia; malaria; kala-azar; schistosomiasis; HIV |
| **Congestive** | Cirrhosis (the main cause of massive congestive splenomegaly), schistosomal "pipestem" fibrosis, portal or splenic vein thrombosis, Budd-Chiari syndrome, right heart failure |
| **Lymphohaematogenous neoplasms** | Non-Hodgkin lymphomas and lymphocytic leukaemias (CLL, hairy cell), Hodgkin lymphoma, multiple myeloma; myeloproliferative neoplasms (CML, polycythaemia vera, primary myelofibrosis) with extramedullary haematopoiesis |
| **Haemolytic anaemias** | Hereditary spherocytosis, thalassaemia, autoimmune haemolytic anaemia, sickle cell disease (early), with red cell destruction and compensatory extramedullary haematopoiesis |
| **Immunoinflammatory** | Rheumatoid arthritis (Felty syndrome), systemic lupus erythematosus, sarcoidosis, serum sickness |
| **Storage and infiltrative diseases** | Gaucher disease, Niemann-Pick disease, mucopolysaccharidoses, amyloidosis |
| **Primary splenic lesions** | Cysts, haemangioma, lymphangioma, other rare tumours; metastases rare |

**Weights.** The normal adult spleen weighs 150 g. Acute nonspecific splenitis gives 200–400 g; systemic (right heart) congestion rarely exceeds 500 g; long-standing portal congestion gives 1,000–5,000 g; myeloproliferative neoplasms may reach 4,000 g or more.


## Diagnostic criteria of hypersplenism.

The classical diagnostic criteria of hypersplenism are splenomegaly, one or more cytopenias in the blood with a normocellular or hypercellular marrow, and correction of the cytopenias after splenectomy; evidence of increased splenic sequestration supports the diagnosis.

1. **Splenomegaly.** Clinically or by imaging.
2. **Cytopenia of one or more cell lines**—anaemia, leukopenia (neutropenia), thrombocytopenia, or pancytopenia. Robbins describes hypersplenism as a syndrome characterised by anaemia, leukopenia and/or thrombocytopenia.
3. **Normal or hyperplastic (cellular) bone marrow** with normal or increased precursors, reflecting a compensatory response to peripheral destruction, with no other cause of cytopenia (such as marrow failure, infiltration or drug effect).
4. **Evidence of increased destruction or pooling.** Shortened survival of red cells or platelets, with increased splenic uptake demonstrated by radioisotope studies (⁵¹Cr-labelled red cells or ¹¹¹In-labelled platelets, with excess counting over the spleen), and increased plasma volume; reticulocytosis if haemolysis is present.
5. **Response to splenectomy.** Correction of cytopenias after removal of the spleen. This is retrospective but diagnostic; splenectomy is reserved for severe cases as it increases the risk of overwhelming sepsis by encapsulated bacteria (pneumococci, meningococci, Haemophilus influenzae), so asplenic patients must be vaccinated.

## Elderly man (55 or 65 years) with bone/back pain, punched-out skull lesions or osteolytic lesions, high ESR, vertebral fracture — Most probable diagnosis? How will you establish / confirm the diagnosis?

The most probable diagnosis is multiple myeloma, and I would confirm it with serum and urine protein electrophoresis and immunofixation to show a monoclonal protein, a bone marrow aspirate and biopsy showing clonal plasma cells, and tests for the CRAB features—calcium, creatinine, haemoglobin—and skeletal imaging.

**Diagnosis.** The age (peak 65 to 70 years), bone and back pain, punched-out lytic lesions of the skull (1 to 4 cm, sharply demarcated), pathologic vertebral fracture and markedly raised ESR (from rouleaux formation due to the M protein) are characteristic of **multiple myeloma**. The lesions are destructive plasma cell tumours resulting from increased osteoclast activity (MIP-1α) and inhibition of osteoblasts (Wnt inhibitors), and involve the axial skeleton in decreasing order of frequency: vertebral column, ribs, skull, pelvis and femur.

**How to establish the diagnosis.**

1. **Blood:** haemoglobin (normocytic normochromic anaemia), blood film with **rouleaux**, ESR, serum calcium (hypercalcaemia), urea and creatinine (renal impairment), uric acid, albumin, β₂-microglobulin, LDH; alkaline phosphatase is typically normal.
2. **Serum protein electrophoresis** (a sharp M spike, usually IgG or IgA), immunofixation to type the immunoglobulin, quantitative immunoglobulins (reduced normal immunoglobulins), and serum free light chain assay with κ/λ ratio.
3. **Urine:** 24-hour urine protein electrophoresis and immunofixation for **Bence Jones protein** (the dipstick may be negative).
4. **Bone marrow aspirate and biopsy:** increased plasma cells (typically above 30%; 10% or more clonal plasma cells with a myeloma-defining event for diagnosis), atypical and multinucleate forms, flame cells, Mott cells, with CD138⁺, CD56⁺ and light-chain restriction.
5. **Imaging:** skeletal survey, or MRI/low-dose CT/PET-CT; MRI of the spine for cord compression if neurologic signs.
6. **Cytogenetics/FISH** for prognosis: t(4;14), del(17p), t(11;14), del(13q).

**Diagnostic criteria.** Clonal plasma cells in the marrow plus CRAB features (hypercalcaemia, renal dysfunction, anaemia, bone lesions) or other myeloma-defining events. Distinguish from MGUS (M protein below 3 g/dL, no end-organ damage), smoldering myeloma and solitary plasmacytoma, and from metastatic carcinoma (lytic bone lesions but no M protein).


## 40-year-old man with massive splenomegaly and total WBC count 2,50,000/cu.mm — Diagnosis?

This is most probably chronic myeloid leukaemia in the chronic phase, and I would confirm it by peripheral smear, marrow examination and demonstration of the Philadelphia chromosome or BCR::ABL1 fusion gene.

**Reasoning.** A middle-aged adult (peak incidence in the fifth to sixth decades) with a very high white cell count, well above 100,000/µL, and **massive splenomegaly** from extensive extramedullary haematopoiesis, is the typical presentation of CML. The onset is insidious, with fatigue, weight loss, anorexia and a dragging sensation in the left upper quadrant, and occasionally acute pain from splenic infarction.

**Confirmation.**

1. **Peripheral smear:** neutrophils, bands, metamyelocytes and myelocytes (the full spectrum of granulocytic maturation), basophilia and eosinophilia, blasts below 10%; platelets often increased; mild anaemia.
2. **Leukocyte alkaline phosphatase score:** low or absent.
3. **Bone marrow:** markedly hypercellular with granulocytic hyperplasia, increased megakaryocytes (small, hypolobated), sea-blue histiocytes.
4. **Cytogenetic and molecular tests:** Philadelphia chromosome t(9;22)(q34;q11), or BCR::ABL1 by FISH or RT-PCR.
5. **Other:** uric acid, LDH, vitamin B₁₂ raised; blasts and basophils to define phase.

**Differential diagnosis.** Leukaemoid reaction (high LAP, toxic changes, no basophilia, no massive splenomegaly, Ph negative); primary myelofibrosis (leukoerythroblastosis, teardrop cells, fibrotic marrow, lower WBC); chronic neutrophilic leukaemia, chronic myelomonocytic leukaemia, chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (lymphocytes), hairy cell leukaemia (pancytopenia), and the other BCR::ABL1-negative myeloproliferative neoplasms.

**Management note.** With a count of 250,000/µL there is a risk of leukostasis and tumour lysis; hydration, allopurinol and cytoreduction are needed, and BCR-ABL tyrosine kinase inhibitors induce sustained haematologic remission in over 90% of patients and reduce the risk of progression to blast crisis.


## 10-year-old boy with weakness, fever, joint pain and gum bleeding — Clinical diagnosis? Expected PBF findings?

This is most likely acute leukaemia—acute lymphoblastic leukaemia being the commonest in a child—and the peripheral blood film would show anaemia, thrombocytopenia and circulating blasts.

**Clinical diagnosis.** The combination of weakness (anaemia), fever (neutropenia with infection, or the disease itself), joint and bone pain (marrow expansion and subperiosteal infiltration by leukaemic cells) and gum bleeding (thrombocytopenia) in a child suggests **acute leukaemia**: the stormy onset over days to weeks, the marrow failure triad and the bone pain are characteristic. ALL is the most common cancer of children and is more likely (peak at about 3 years, with a second adolescent peak for T-ALL), but AML can present identically; prominent **gum hypertrophy** and bleeding would suggest AML with monocytic differentiation. Other features sought are lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, testicular enlargement, mediastinal mass and CNS signs.

**Expected peripheral blood findings.**

- **Normocytic normochromic anaemia**, with a low reticulocyte count.
- **Thrombocytopenia**, often severe.
- **White cell count** variable: raised in most, but normal or low in some; neutropenia.
- **Blasts** in the smear: in ALL, lymphoblasts of high nuclear-cytoplasmic ratio, condensed finely stippled chromatin, small nucleoli and scant agranular cytoplasm; in AML, myeloblasts with delicate chromatin, prominent nucleoli, fine granules and **Auer rods**.
- **Hiatus leukaemicus** (blasts and mature cells without intermediate stages); smudge cells may be present.

**Confirmation.** Bone marrow aspiration and biopsy showing 20% or more blasts; cytochemistry (MPO negative and PAS positive in ALL); flow cytometry (TdT, CD19, CD10, CD3); cytogenetics; CSF examination.

**Differential diagnosis.** Aplastic anaemia (no blasts, hypocellular marrow); idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura (isolated thrombocytopenia); juvenile idiopathic arthritis and rheumatic fever (joint pain, but normal blood counts and no marrow failure); infectious mononucleosis (atypical lymphocytes); scurvy (gum bleeding and bone pain).


## What is haemopoiesis?

Haemopoiesis is the continuous, regulated process by which all the cellular elements of blood (red cells, white cells and platelets) are produced from a small population of self-renewing pluripotent haemopoietic stem cells.

Haemopoietic stem cells (HSCs) reside in specialised niches of the bone marrow. They have two cardinal properties: self-renewal, which preserves the stem cell pool, and multipotent differentiation, which gives rise to progressively committed progenitors. The first major branch separates a common myeloid progenitor (the CFU-GEMM, giving rise to erythroid, granulocytic, monocytic and megakaryocytic lineages) from a common lymphoid progenitor (giving rise to B cells, T cells and NK cells). Committed progenitors such as the burst-forming unit–erythroid (BFU-E) and colony-forming unit–erythroid (CFU-E) then differentiate into recognisable precursors that mature into the cells found in the circulation.

Haemopoiesis is controlled by the marrow microenvironment (stromal cells, extracellular matrix, adhesion molecules) and by lineage-specific growth factors. Erythropoietin, produced by peritubular interstitial cells of the kidney in response to hypoxia, drives erythroid progenitors; G-CSF and GM-CSF drive granulocytic and monocytic development; thrombopoietin, made mainly in the liver, drives megakaryocytes and platelets; and stem cell factor, IL-3 and IL-6 act on early progenitors. The output is exquisitely matched to need: red cell production rises several-fold in haemolysis or after haemorrhage, and neutrophil production rises in infection. Failure of the process produces cytopenias (aplastic anaemia, marrow infiltration), while uncontrolled clonal proliferation produces leukaemias and myeloproliferative neoplasms.


## Sites of normal haemopoiesis.

Haemopoiesis moves between sites during development: the yolk sac in early foetal life, then the liver and spleen, then the bone marrow, which is the sole site of haemopoiesis after birth and throughout normal adult life.

The sites change with age as follows.

| Period | Site of haemopoiesis |
|---|---|
| Embryonic (about 3 to 10 weeks) | Yolk sac (mesoblastic phase), producing primitive nucleated red cells with embryonic haemoglobins |
| Foetal (about 6 weeks to birth) | Liver is the main site (peak at 3 to 6 months of gestation), with a contribution from the spleen, thymus and lymph nodes; the bone marrow takes over from about the fifth month |
| Infancy and childhood | All marrow cavities (central and peripheral skeleton) contain red, haemopoietically active marrow |
| From about 5 to 7 years onward | Red marrow in the shafts of long bones is progressively replaced by fat |
| Adult | Red marrow is confined to the axial skeleton and proximal ends of long bones: vertebrae, ribs, sternum, skull, pelvis and the proximal femur and humerus |

Lymphocytes additionally mature and proliferate in the thymus, lymph nodes, spleen and mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue, but their progenitors originate in the marrow. Fatty (yellow) marrow retains the capacity to revert to haemopoietic marrow when demand is sustained, as in chronic haemolysis.


## Where does extramedullary haemopoiesis occur?

Extramedullary haemopoiesis is blood cell formation outside the bone marrow, occurring mainly in the liver and spleen and also in the lymph nodes, when the marrow cannot meet the demand or has been replaced or damaged.

In the foetus the liver and spleen are the normal sites. In postnatal life they can resume this function whenever there is marked, sustained erythropoietic drive or marrow failure. The conditions in which it appears include severe chronic haemolytic anaemias, particularly β-thalassaemia major (where ineffective erythropoiesis produces massive erythroid expansion and the spleen may reach 1500 g), and sickle cell disease; myelofibrosis and the spent phase of myeloproliferative neoplasms; myelophthisic anaemia due to metastatic cancer or granulomatous disease; and, rarely, severe megaloblastic anaemia. The liver, spleen and lymph nodes are enlarged, and in extreme cases extraosseous masses develop in the thorax (paravertebral), abdomen and pelvis. Because the foci release immature cells prematurely, the blood film shows nucleated red cells and immature granulocytes (a leukoerythroblastic picture), and teardrop cells appear when the marrow is fibrotic.


## Write the developmental stages of RBC.

Red cell development (erythropoiesis) begins with the pluripotent haemopoietic stem cell, which passes through the common myeloid progenitor and the committed erythroid progenitors, the burst-forming unit–erythroid (BFU-E) and the colony-forming unit–erythroid (CFU-E). The latter is the target of erythropoietin. These progenitors cannot be recognised morphologically. The first recognisable cell is the proerythroblast, and the sequence of morphologically identifiable stages is:

1. **Proerythroblast (pronormoblast):** a large cell (14 to 20 µm) with a large round nucleus, fine chromatin, one to two nucleoli and deeply basophilic, agranular cytoplasm.
2. **Basophilic (early) normoblast:** slightly smaller, with coarser chromatin, nucleoli no longer visible and intensely basophilic cytoplasm owing to abundant ribosomal RNA.
3. **Polychromatic (intermediate) normoblast:** the nucleus becomes smaller and the chromatin clumped; haemoglobin synthesis gives the cytoplasm a mixed blue-pink (polychromatic) colour. This is the last stage capable of mitosis.
4. **Orthochromatic (late) normoblast:** a small cell with a dense pyknotic nucleus and pink, fully haemoglobinised cytoplasm, which loses its nucleus by extrusion.
5. **Reticulocyte:** an anucleate cell that retains ribosomal RNA; it is slightly larger than a mature red cell, polychromatic on Romanowsky stains and shows a reticulum with supravital stains. It spends about one to two days in the marrow and one day in the circulation maturing.
6. **Mature erythrocyte:** a biconcave, anucleate disc about 7 to 8 µm in diameter with a central pallor of about one-third of its diameter, surviving about 120 days before removal by macrophages of the spleen, liver and marrow.

As the cell matures, its size decreases, nuclear chromatin condenses, basophilia gives way to haemoglobinisation, and the nucleus is lost. The whole sequence from proerythroblast to reticulocyte takes about 5 to 7 days and is accelerated by erythropoietin. Each proerythroblast produces about 8 to 16 red cells.


## What are the essential nutrients for haemopoiesis?

Effective erythropoiesis, and haemopoiesis generally, requires an adequate supply of the following.

- **Iron:** essential for the synthesis of haem; dietary iron is carried by transferrin to erythroid precursors, which take it up through transferrin receptors. Deficiency causes hypochromic microcytic anaemia.
- **Vitamin B₁₂ (cobalamin) and folic acid:** cofactors required for the synthesis of thymidylate and hence DNA. Deficiency impairs nuclear maturation and produces megaloblastic anaemia with ineffective haemopoiesis.
- **Protein and amino acids:** required for globin synthesis. Protein-energy malnutrition causes anaemia.
- **Vitamin B₆ (pyridoxine):** a cofactor for δ-aminolevulinic acid synthase, the first and rate-limiting enzyme of haem synthesis; deficiency, or isoniazid antagonism, causes sideroblastic anaemia.
- **Vitamin C (ascorbic acid):** promotes the absorption of nonhaem iron and the mobilisation of iron stores, and is involved in folate metabolism.
- **Copper:** required for ceruloplasmin and hephaestin, the oxidases that allow iron to be loaded onto transferrin; deficiency causes an iron-refractory anaemia.
- **Others in smaller roles:** vitamin E (protects the red cell membrane from oxidant injury), riboflavin, pantothenic acid, cobalt (a component of B₁₂), vitamin A, and trace elements such as zinc.

Non-nutrient requirements include erythropoietin, thyroid and androgenic hormones, a normal marrow microenvironment and an adequate stem cell pool.


## What is reticulocyte?

A reticulocyte is a young, newly released, anucleate red cell that has just extruded its nucleus but still contains residual ribosomal RNA. It is slightly larger than a mature red cell, and on a Romanowsky-stained smear it has a bluish-red (polychromatophilic) cytoplasm because of the RNA. With supravital stains such as new methylene blue or brilliant cresyl blue, the RNA precipitates to form a blue reticulum or granules, from which the cell takes its name. The reticulocyte matures into an erythrocyte over about one day in the circulation.

The reticulocyte count is the most useful bedside index of effective marrow erythropoietic activity. The reference range is 0.5% to 1.5% of red cells (an absolute count of about 25 to 75 × 10⁹/L). The count is expressed as a percentage, which should be corrected for the degree of anaemia (corrected reticulocyte count = observed % × patient Hct/normal Hct), because in anaemia the percentage rises simply because there are fewer red cells.

Reticulocytosis occurs in haemolytic anaemias, after acute haemorrhage (reaching 10% to 15% after about 7 days) and a few days after starting specific therapy for iron, B₁₂ or folate deficiency (the reticulocyte response, about 5 to 7 days). Reticulocytopenia, in the presence of anaemia, indicates underproduction, as in aplastic anaemia, pure red cell aplasia, marrow infiltration and deficiency states.


## Mention the cells in the steps of granulopoiesis.

Granulopoiesis proceeds from the myeloid stem cell through the colony-forming unit–granulocyte/monocyte (CFU-GM) to the following sequence of morphologically recognisable cells:

1. **Myeloblast:** a large cell with a high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio, fine chromatin, prominent nucleoli and a thin rim of agranular basophilic cytoplasm.
2. **Promyelocyte:** larger, with a few nucleoli and the appearance of primary (azurophilic, nonspecific) granules in the cytoplasm.
3. **Myelocyte:** the stage at which secondary (specific) granules appear and the cell can be identified as neutrophil, eosinophil or basophil; the nucleus is round to oval, nucleoli disappear, and this is the last stage capable of division.
4. **Metamyelocyte:** the nucleus becomes indented (kidney-shaped); the cell no longer divides.
5. **Band (stab) form:** the nucleus is elongated and horseshoe-shaped without distinct lobes.
6. **Segmented (mature) granulocyte:** the nucleus has two to five lobes joined by thin filaments.

Dividing cells (myeloblast to myelocyte) form the mitotic pool, and the nondividing cells (metamyelocyte to mature neutrophil) form the maturation and storage pool of the marrow. The process takes about 10 to 14 days from myeloblast to release, and the cells are driven by G-CSF and GM-CSF. In the circulation neutrophils are divided into a freely circulating pool and a marginal pool attached to the endothelium; adrenergic stimulation, as in massive haemorrhage, mobilises the marginal pool and causes leukocytosis.


## Information you can get from a stained peripheral blood film.

A stained peripheral blood film gives direct information on the size, shape, colour and inclusions of red cells, the differential count and morphology of white cells, the number and morphology of platelets, and the presence of abnormal cells or parasites, and it is the single most useful starting point for diagnosing a haematological disorder.

Red cells: size (normocytic, microcytic, macrocytic) and variation in size (anisocytosis); degree of haemoglobinisation (normochromic or hypochromic) and polychromasia (young cells, reticulocytosis); shape and variation in shape (poikilocytosis), including spherocytes, elliptocytes, target cells, sickle cells, teardrop cells, schistocytes (fragmented cells that point to microangiopathic or mechanical haemolysis), bite cells and burr cells; inclusions such as basophilic stippling, Howell-Jolly bodies (as in asplenia), Pappenheimer bodies, and Heinz bodies (with supravital stain); rouleaux formation and agglutination; and circulating nucleated red cells. Together with the red cell indices, these features allow classification of the anaemia and often point to the cause.

White cells: the differential count; morphology of neutrophils (hypersegmentation in megaloblastic anaemia, toxic granulation and Döhle bodies in sepsis, left shift); presence of immature cells, blasts or atypical lymphocytes; and smear cells in chronic lymphocytic leukaemia.

Platelets: an estimate of number, which must be correlated with the electronic count since clumping causes spurious thrombocytopenia, and morphology such as giant platelets in accelerated thrombopoiesis.

Parasites and other findings: malaria parasites, microfilariae, babesia and trypanosomes.


## What are red cell indices?

Red cell indices are calculated or measured values that describe the average size, haemoglobin content and haemoglobin concentration of red cells, together with the variation in their size, and they are used to classify anaemias.

They are derived from three primary measurements: the haemoglobin concentration (Hb), the red cell count (RBC) and the haematocrit or packed cell volume (Hct/PCV); modern analysers measure the MCV and RBC directly and calculate the Hct.

- **Mean cell volume (MCV):** the average volume of a red cell in femtolitres. MCV = Hct (%) × 10 ÷ RBC (× 10¹²/L). Reference range 82 to 96 fL.
- **Mean cell haemoglobin (MCH):** the average mass of haemoglobin per red cell in picograms. MCH = Hb (g/dL) × 10 ÷ RBC (× 10¹²/L). Reference range 27 to 33 pg.
- **Mean cell haemoglobin concentration (MCHC):** the average concentration of haemoglobin in a given volume of packed red cells, in g/dL. MCHC = Hb (g/dL) × 100 ÷ Hct (%). Reference range 33 to 37 g/dL.
- **Red cell distribution width (RDW):** the coefficient of variation of red cell volume, a numerical expression of anisocytosis. Reference range 11.5% to 14.5%.

Reference ranges vary among laboratories, and the range of the laboratory issuing the result should be used.


## Importance of red cell indices.

Red cell indices allow the morphological classification of anaemia into microcytic hypochromic, normocytic normochromic and macrocytic types, which narrows the differential diagnosis and directs further investigation.

Their value lies in the following. The MCV and MCH classify anaemia: a low MCV and MCH (microcytic hypochromic) point to disorders of haemoglobin synthesis, namely iron deficiency, thalassaemia, anaemia of chronic inflammation and sideroblastic anaemia; a normal MCV (normocytic, normochromic) is seen in acute blood loss, most haemolytic anaemias, aplastic anaemia, renal failure and many chronic diseases; and a high MCV (macrocytic) is seen in megaloblastic anaemia and in nonmegaloblastic causes such as liver disease, alcohol excess, hypothyroidism and reticulocytosis. The RDW separates conditions with uniform red cells (such as thalassaemia trait, where the RDW is relatively normal) from those with heterogeneous populations (iron deficiency, where it is raised, and mixed deficiencies). The MCHC is raised in hereditary spherocytosis because of cellular dehydration, a useful clue, and in cold agglutinin disease as an artefact. The indices help to monitor response to treatment, for example the appearance of a normocytic population in a patient with iron deficiency who is responding to iron, and may reveal a problem before anaemia develops. A simple derived index, the Mentzer index (MCV ÷ RBC count), is below 13 in thalassaemia trait and above 13 in iron deficiency.


## Normal haemoglobin level in different age groups / influence of age and sex on Hb estimation.

The normal haemoglobin is about 13.6 to 17.2 g/dL in adult males and 12.0 to 15.0 g/dL in adult females, and it is high at birth, falls to a nadir in infancy, and then rises gradually to adult values at puberty, where the sex difference appears.

Approximate reference values (laboratory-specific) are:

| Group | Haemoglobin (g/dL) |
|---|---|
| Cord blood / newborn | 14 to 20 (mean about 17 to 18) |
| 2 to 3 months (physiological nadir) | 9.5 to 12.5 |
| 6 months to 6 years | 11 to 14 |
| 6 to 12 years | 11.5 to 15.5 |
| Adult female | 12.0 to 15.0 |
| Adult male | 13.6 to 17.2 |

Factors influencing the value:

- **Age:** the newborn has a high Hb with predominant foetal haemoglobin, produced in the hypoxic intrauterine environment; the postnatal fall (physiological anaemia of infancy) reflects the switch from foetal to adult haemoglobin, suppression of erythropoietin when oxygen supply improves, and shortened survival of foetal red cells. Values are slightly lower in the very old.
- **Sex:** after puberty males have higher values because androgens stimulate erythropoietin production and erythropoiesis, while females lose iron in menstruation and have lower iron stores.
- **Other factors:** altitude and smoking (raise Hb); pregnancy (physiological fall caused by plasma volume expansion, with anaemia defined as Hb below 11 g/dL); hydration and plasma volume changes, since Hb correlates with red cell mass only when plasma volume is normal; posture and time of day.

For diagnosing anaemia the WHO uses thresholds of below 13 g/dL in men, below 12 g/dL in nonpregnant women and below 11 g/dL in pregnant women and young children.


## What information can you get from a stained PBF?

A Romanowsky-stained peripheral blood film (PBF) provides morphological information on all three cell lines and is a cornerstone of haematological diagnosis.

**Red cells.** The film shows size (microcytes, macrocytes, macro-ovalocytes) and anisocytosis; the degree of haemoglobinisation (hypochromia, with an enlarged zone of central pallor, or hyperchromic cells such as spherocytes that lack central pallor); polychromasia (reticulocytes); and poikilocytosis, with specific shapes that point to a diagnosis: spherocytes (hereditary spherocytosis, autoimmune haemolytic anaemia), elliptocytes and pencil cells (iron deficiency), target cells (thalassaemia, liver disease, haemoglobin C, post-splenectomy), sickle cells, teardrop cells (myelofibrosis, thalassaemia, myelophthisis), schistocytes (microangiopathic haemolysis, mechanical valves), bite cells and blister cells (G6PD deficiency) and burr cells. Inclusions include basophilic stippling (thalassaemia, lead poisoning), Howell-Jolly bodies (asplenia), Pappenheimer bodies and malarial parasites, and the film shows rouleaux and agglutination, and nucleated red cells.

**White cells.** The differential count, hypersegmented neutrophils (five or more lobes) in megaloblastic anaemia, toxic changes in infection, left shift, myelocytes and blasts (leukaemia, leukoerythroblastosis), atypical lymphocytes (infectious mononucleosis), eosinophilia and basophilia.

**Platelets.** Their number is estimated and morphology assessed (giant platelets, clumps), which serves to confirm or refute the automated platelet count.

**Other information.** Haemoparasites (malaria, filaria, trypanosomes), and, in combination with indices and the reticulocyte count, a morphological classification of the anaemia and a lead to the cause of any cytopenia or leukocytosis.


## Define ESR / write a short note on ESR.

**Definition.** The erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) is the rate at which red cells settle out of anticoagulated blood in a vertical tube under the influence of gravity, measured as the length in millimetres of the clear plasma column above the red cells at the end of one hour.

**Method.** The Westergren method is standard: venous blood is mixed with 3.8% (or 3.2%) sodium citrate in the ratio 4:1, drawn into a 200 mm long, 2.5 mm bore tube, held exactly vertical at room temperature and read after one hour. The Wintrobe method uses a shorter tube with undiluted EDTA blood, and automated methods are increasingly used.

**Principle and mechanism.** Sedimentation occurs in three stages: an initial lag phase in which rouleaux form, a phase of rapid, constant-rate fall (decantation) and a final slow packing phase. The principal determinant is rouleaux formation, the stacking of red cells like coins. Normally red cells repel each other because of the negative surface charge (zeta potential). Positively charged acute-phase proteins, particularly fibrinogen, and immunoglobulins neutralise this charge, promoting rouleaux. Aggregates are heavier relative to their surface area and settle faster.

**Reference values (Westergren).** Males up to 15 mm/h and females up to 20 mm/h in the first hour, rising with age (an approximate upper limit is age ÷ 2 in men and (age + 10) ÷ 2 in women). It is very low in the newborn.

**Clinical significance.**

- Raised: infections (tuberculosis, chronic infections), chronic inflammatory diseases (rheumatoid arthritis, giant cell arteritis, polymyalgia rheumatica), malignancy (especially multiple myeloma, where it may exceed 100 mm/h), anaemia, pregnancy, nephrotic syndrome, tissue necrosis such as myocardial infarction.
- Low: polycythaemia, sickle cell disease, hereditary spherocytosis (cells cannot form rouleaux), congestive cardiac failure, hypofibrinogenaemia.

The ESR is a nonspecific test, useful for screening and for monitoring disease activity of inflammatory conditions, and a normal ESR does not exclude disease.


## Mention the major physiological factors affecting ESR.

The ESR is influenced by several physiological conditions in a healthy person.

- **Age:** it is very low at birth (0 to 2 mm/h), rises through childhood and tends to rise gradually in older adults.
- **Sex:** it is higher in women than men, partly because of the lower haematocrit and higher fibrinogen.
- **Pregnancy:** the ESR begins to rise from about the third month, may reach 40 to 50 mm/h at term and returns to normal about four weeks after delivery, because of the increase in fibrinogen and globulins and the fall in haematocrit from plasma volume expansion.
- **Menstruation:** a slight rise.
- **Meals and exercise:** a mild, short-lived rise after a meal, and variation by time of day, with higher values in the afternoon than the morning.

Technical factors that influence the value, though not physiological, include the temperature (higher at higher temperature), tilting of the tube (which increases the rate), the dilution of blood and the time between blood collection and the test (blood should be tested within 2 to 4 hours).


## How do changes in blood components influence ESR?

The ESR depends on the balance between factors that promote rouleaux formation and those that oppose it.

**Plasma factors.** Increased fibrinogen (the single most important factor) and other acute-phase reactants, and increased globulins, including immunoglobulins and paraproteins in myeloma and the polyclonal rise in chronic infection, neutralise the negative surface charge of red cells and increase rouleaux, raising the ESR. Hypercholesterolaemia also raises it. Albumin has the opposite effect, so hypoalbuminaemia accelerates sedimentation, while hypofibrinogenaemia (for example in afibrinogenaemia) lowers it.

**Red cell factors.**

- Number: in anaemia, the lower red cell mass means less interference between settling cells and relatively more plasma protein per cell, so the ESR rises; in polycythaemia it falls.
- Shape: spherocytes, sickle cells, acanthocytes and other poikilocytes cannot form rouleaux, so the ESR is low in hereditary spherocytosis and sickle cell disease. Macrocytes settle faster because they have a smaller surface area-to-volume ratio, and microcytes slower.
- Agglutination: in cold agglutinin disease the clumping of red cells may produce spurious values.

**Other factors.** Bile salts and high plasma viscosity (lowering the rate) and a markedly raised white cell count (a small effect on the ESR) can also modify the result.


## What are the iron profile tests?

The iron profile (iron studies) assesses body iron status and distinguishes iron deficiency from other causes of microcytic anaemia. The tests are:

1. **Serum iron:** the iron bound to transferrin; it is low in iron deficiency and anaemia of chronic inflammation and high in iron overload and haemolysis. Reference values average about 120 µg/dL in males and 100 µg/dL in females and are subject to diurnal variation (highest in the morning).
2. **Total iron-binding capacity (TIBC):** a measure of transferrin, the iron transport protein; it is raised in iron deficiency, as the liver increases transferrin synthesis, and reduced in chronic inflammation, malnutrition and iron overload.
3. **Transferrin saturation:** serum iron ÷ TIBC × 100. Normally about one-third; below 15% in iron deficiency.
4. **Serum ferritin:** the best single index of storage iron, since plasma ferritin correlates with body iron stores. It is below 12 µg/L in iron deficiency, and may reach several thousand in iron overload. As an acute-phase reactant it may be raised in inflammation, liver disease and malignancy, which can mask iron deficiency.
5. **Additional tests:** soluble transferrin receptor (raised in iron deficiency, not influenced by inflammation), free erythrocyte protoporphyrin or zinc protoporphyrin (raised), reticulocyte haemoglobin content, hepcidin (low in iron deficiency, high in inflammation), and Prussian blue staining of the bone marrow for stainable iron, absent in iron deficiency.

| Test | Iron deficiency | Chronic inflammation | β-Thalassaemia trait |
|---|---|---|---|
| Serum iron | Low | Low | Normal |
| TIBC | High | Low/normal | Normal |
| Transferrin saturation | Low (<15%) | Low/normal | Normal |
| Ferritin | Low | Normal/high | Normal |
| Marrow iron | Absent | Present (in macrophages) | Normal/increased |


## Enumerate the laboratory methods of assessing iron stores.

The methods for assessing body iron stores are as follows.

1. **Serum ferritin:** the most practical and widely used noninvasive method, because plasma ferritin correlates with body iron stores; a level below 12 µg/L indicates depleted stores. It must be interpreted with caution in inflammation, infection, liver disease and malignancy.
2. **Bone marrow iron:** Prussian blue (Perls) staining of an aspirate smear reveals haemosiderin in macrophages; absence of stainable iron is diagnostic of iron deficiency and increased iron is seen in iron overload and chronic inflammation. It has been considered the gold standard but is invasive.
3. **Transferrin saturation, serum iron and TIBC:** these reflect iron supply to tissues, and are altered once stores are depleted.
4. **Soluble transferrin receptor and zinc protoporphyrin:** indicate functional iron deficiency in erythropoiesis.
5. **Liver biopsy or MRI:** quantitation of hepatic iron concentration in suspected iron overload (haemochromatosis, transfusional siderosis).
6. **Desferrioxamine test and quantitative phlebotomy:** historical methods; urinary iron excretion after desferrioxamine, or the amount of iron removed by phlebotomy to depletion.
7. **Therapeutic trial:** a reticulocyte response and rise in haemoglobin after oral iron supports iron deficiency.


## Define PCV.

The packed cell volume (PCV), also called the haematocrit (Hct), is the ratio of the volume occupied by packed red cells to the total volume of whole blood, expressed as a percentage or as a fraction (L/L). It is a direct reflection of the red cell mass except where the plasma volume is altered by fluid retention or dehydration.

It is measured by centrifuging anticoagulated blood in a capillary tube (microhaematocrit method, about 12,000 g for 5 minutes) or a Wintrobe tube, and reading the height of the red cell column relative to the whole column. Modern automated analysers calculate it (Hct = MCV × RBC ÷ 10). A small amount of plasma (about 1% to 3%) is trapped between the packed cells. Reference ranges (Robbins) are 39% to 49% in males and 33% to 43% in females. A rule of thumb is that the Hct is about three times the haemoglobin in g/dL. PCV is needed to calculate MCV and MCHC. It is reduced in anaemia and raised in polycythaemia and dehydration (relative polycythaemia).


## Name the red cell (absolute) indices with values.

The absolute red cell indices (Wintrobe indices) are the mean cell volume, mean cell haemoglobin and mean cell haemoglobin concentration, derived from the haemoglobin, red cell count and haematocrit.

| Index | Definition | Formula | Reference range |
|---|---|---|---|
| MCV (mean cell volume) | Average volume of a red cell | Hct (%) × 10 ÷ RBC (× 10¹²/L) | 82–96 fL |
| MCH (mean cell haemoglobin) | Average haemoglobin mass per red cell | Hb (g/dL) × 10 ÷ RBC (× 10¹²/L) | 27–33 pg |
| MCHC (mean cell haemoglobin concentration) | Average haemoglobin concentration in packed cells | Hb (g/dL) × 100 ÷ Hct (%) | 33–37 g/dL |
| RDW (red cell distribution width) | Coefficient of variation of red cell volume | Automated | 11.5–14.5% |

The MCV classifies anaemias as microcytic (below 82 fL), normocytic or macrocytic (above 96 fL), while the MCH and MCHC indicate hypochromia (low values) or, in the case of MCHC, spherocytosis (high value).


## Write a short note on MCV.

The mean cell volume (MCV) is the average volume of the red cells in a blood sample, expressed in femtolitres (fL; 10⁻¹⁵ L). The reference range for adults is 82 to 96 fL. It is measured directly by automated analysers (from the electrical impedance or light scatter produced by each cell) and can be calculated as MCV = Hct (%) × 10 ÷ red cell count (× 10¹²/L).

The MCV is the most useful of the indices in classifying anaemias. A low MCV (microcytosis) is found in iron deficiency, thalassaemia, anaemia of chronic inflammation (sometimes) and sideroblastic anaemia. A normal MCV is found in acute blood loss, most haemolytic anaemias, aplastic anaemia, renal failure, and in anaemias of chronic disease. A high MCV (macrocytosis) is found in megaloblastic anaemia (often more than 110 fL), alcohol excess, liver disease, hypothyroidism, myelodysplastic neoplasms, aplastic anaemia, drug therapy (hydroxyurea, zidovudine, methotrexate) and with marked reticulocytosis, since reticulocytes are larger than mature red cells.

Limitations: the MCV is an average and can be normal when microcytic and macrocytic populations coexist (as in combined iron and B₁₂ deficiency); the RDW and the blood film should be examined. MCV is falsely high with cold agglutinins and marked hyperglycaemia, and normally higher in newborns.


## Indications of bone marrow biopsy / aspiration / examination.

Bone marrow examination is indicated to investigate unexplained abnormalities of the peripheral blood, particularly cytopenias, to diagnose and stage haematological malignancies, and to detect marrow infiltration and certain infections or storage diseases.

The main indications are:

1. **Unexplained cytopenias:** pancytopenia, unexplained anaemia, leukopenia or thrombocytopenia not explained by other tests, to distinguish aplastic anaemia (hypocellular marrow) from marrow replacement or ineffective haemopoiesis.
2. **Suspected or known haematological malignancy:** acute leukaemia, chronic myeloid leukaemia, myelodysplastic neoplasms, myeloproliferative neoplasms and multiple myeloma; also for subclassification by cytochemistry, flow cytometry, cytogenetics and molecular tests, and for monitoring remission or relapse and minimal residual disease.
3. **Staging of lymphomas** and detection of marrow infiltration by metastatic carcinomas, which gives a myelophthisic picture.
4. **Megaloblastic anaemia** when the diagnosis is uncertain, and assessment of iron stores when other tests are inconclusive.
5. **Infections:** visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar), miliary tuberculosis, disseminated fungal infections, enteric fever and pyrexia of unknown origin, for culture and demonstration of organisms.
6. **Storage disorders** such as Gaucher disease, and haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis.
7. **Idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura** in selected situations, mainly to exclude marrow failure or other primary marrow disease in older patients or before splenectomy, rather than for routine diagnosis.
8. **Myelofibrosis and other conditions** where trephine biopsy is necessary because aspiration yields a dry tap.


## How is trephine biopsy done?

Trephine biopsy is performed by inserting a wide-bore Jamshidi needle through the posterior iliac crest under local anaesthesia and removing a core of bone and marrow, which is then fixed, decalcified and sectioned.

After explaining the procedure and obtaining informed consent, the patient is placed in the lateral or prone position. The site, usually the posterior superior iliac spine, is cleaned and draped, and local anaesthetic is infiltrated down to the periosteum. A small skin incision is made and the biopsy needle, with its stylet locked in place, is advanced through the soft tissue to the cortex. The stylet is removed, and the needle is advanced with a gentle rotating (clockwise-anticlockwise) movement for about 2 cm into the marrow cavity. The needle is rotated several times to cut the base of the core and then withdrawn, and the core is expelled with a probe through the back of the needle. A core at least 1.5 to 2 cm long is needed for adequate evaluation. Firm pressure is applied until bleeding stops and a dressing is placed.

When both procedures are done, the aspirate is taken first and the trephine second, from a different site on the same bone. The core is used to make touch imprints, fixed in formalin or Zenker's solution, decalcified and processed. Sections are stained with haematoxylin and eosin, reticulin (for fibrosis), and Prussian blue where appropriate, and immunohistochemistry may be performed. Trephine biopsy gives information on cellularity, architecture, fibrosis, focal infiltrates and the megakaryocytes, which an aspirate cannot reliably provide.


## What do you mean by blood tap and dry tap?

A dry tap is a failure to obtain any marrow cells on aspiration despite a correctly performed procedure, while a blood tap is an aspirate that is diluted with or consists mainly of peripheral blood and so is unsuitable for assessing the marrow.

A **dry tap** means that no marrow can be aspirated even though the needle is correctly placed. It points to a marrow in which the cells are packed so tightly or entangled in fibres that they cannot be sucked out, or to an almost empty marrow. The common causes are myelofibrosis, aplastic anaemia (the marrow is replaced by fat, a "dry tap" being typical, so that aplasia is best assessed on trephine biopsy), hairy cell leukaemia, packed marrow in acute leukaemia and lymphoma, and marrow infiltration by metastatic carcinoma. A technical failure, such as the needle not being in the marrow cavity, must be excluded. A trephine biopsy should always follow.

A **blood tap** (or "haemodiluted" aspirate) is one that is contaminated or diluted with peripheral blood, either because of a too-large volume being aspirated (more than 0.5 to 1 mL at a time), or because the marrow is very vascular. It shows no marrow particles (spicules), and the proportions of cells are not reliable. The procedure should be repeated from another site or with a smaller aspirate volume.


## How can bone marrow be examined?

Bone marrow can be examined by aspiration and by trephine biopsy, which are complementary.

**Bone marrow aspiration** uses a needle introduced into the marrow cavity under local anaesthesia to withdraw a small volume (0.2 to 0.5 mL) of liquid marrow. The usual sites are the posterior superior iliac spine (preferred), the anterior iliac crest and the sternum (at the level of the second intercostal space) in adults, and the anteromedial surface of the upper tibia in infants below 2 years. Smears are made at the bedside, air-dried and stained with a Romanowsky stain, and the aspirate may also be used for iron staining (Perls), cytochemistry, immunophenotyping by flow cytometry, cytogenetics and molecular studies, and culture. It gives excellent cytological detail, allows a differential count of marrow cells and the myeloid to erythroid ratio (normally about 2:1 to 4:1), and indicates the erythroid maturation (normoblastic or megaloblastic).

**Trephine biopsy** takes a core of bone with marrow, usually from the posterior iliac crest using a Jamshidi needle. It shows overall cellularity, the architecture and spatial relationships, the megakaryocytes, the extent of fibrosis, and focal lesions such as lymphomatous infiltrates, granulomas, metastatic tumour and amyloid deposits. It is essential when aspiration is a dry tap.

Additional preparations are **touch imprints** of the core and **clot sections** from aspirate particles.


## What are the indications of bone marrow examination/aspiration?

Bone marrow examination is indicated in the following situations.

**Haematological disorders**

- Unexplained anaemia, leukopenia or thrombocytopenia, and especially pancytopenia, to differentiate aplastic anaemia from marrow infiltration, megaloblastic anaemia and hypersplenism.
- Suspected leukaemia: diagnosis and classification of acute leukaemias, and chronic leukaemias in unclear cases; evaluation of blast crisis.
- Myelodysplastic neoplasms and myeloproliferative neoplasms (including myelofibrosis, with trephine biopsy).
- Multiple myeloma and other plasma cell disorders, to quantify plasma cells.
- Megaloblastic anaemia of uncertain cause, sideroblastic anaemia and refractory anaemias, and the assessment of iron stores in doubtful cases.
- Monitoring of treatment: confirmation of remission, detection of relapse and of minimal residual disease; assessment of marrow recovery after chemotherapy or transplantation.

**Nonhaematological disorders**

- Staging of lymphomas and detection of marrow metastases from solid tumours (neuroblastoma, breast, lung and prostate carcinoma).
- Infections: kala-azar (Leishman-Donovan bodies), miliary tuberculosis, histoplasmosis, enteric fever and fever of unknown origin, for culture.
- Lipid storage disorders (Gaucher disease, Niemann-Pick disease).


## Name the white cell disorders for which bone marrow aspiration is done.

Bone marrow aspiration is performed in the following white cell disorders:

1. Acute leukaemias (acute myeloid and acute lymphoblastic leukaemia), for diagnosis, subclassification and follow-up.
2. Chronic myeloid leukaemia, for diagnosis, assessment of phase and blast crisis, and cytogenetics (Philadelphia chromosome).
3. Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia and other chronic lymphoproliferative disorders, when the diagnosis is doubtful or to assess marrow involvement.
4. Hairy cell leukaemia (trephine biopsy is needed because the tap is usually dry).
5. Myelodysplastic neoplasms and myeloproliferative neoplasms.
6. Multiple myeloma and other plasma cell neoplasms.
7. Lymphomas, for staging.
8. Unexplained leukopenia or agranulocytosis, to assess the cause (maturation arrest or drug-induced) and leukaemoid reactions versus leukaemia.
9. Haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis and Langerhans cell histiocytosis.


## Mention the site of marrow puncture in a child below 2 years.

In a child below 2 years the preferred site of bone marrow puncture is the anteromedial surface of the upper end (proximal shaft) of the tibia, about 1 to 2 cm below and medial to the tibial tuberosity, where the bone is flat and subcutaneous and the cortex thin. The posterior iliac crest may also be used. The sternum is avoided in children because of the risk of injury to the heart and great vessels.


## What is trephine biopsy?

Trephine biopsy is a procedure in which a core of bone together with its marrow is removed from the iliac crest, usually the posterior superior iliac spine, using a specialised wide-bore needle (Jamshidi or Islam needle). A core at least 1.5 to 2 cm long is obtained, fixed, decalcified, sectioned and stained with haematoxylin and eosin, reticulin and, if required, Prussian blue stain and immunohistochemical stains.

Its advantages over aspiration are that it preserves the marrow architecture and shows the overall cellularity, the distribution of haemopoietic cells, the megakaryocytes and the presence of fibrosis, granulomas or focal infiltrates by tumour or lymphoma. It is the investigation of choice for aplastic anaemia (hypocellular marrow with fat), myelofibrosis, hairy cell leukaemia, marrow metastases, lymphoma staging and whenever the aspirate is a dry tap. Its disadvantages are that it is more painful, requires decalcification (limiting cytogenetic studies) and gives less cytological detail than a smear.


## What is dry tap?

A dry tap is the failure to aspirate any marrow material, despite proper placement of the needle in the marrow cavity and correct technique. It indicates either an excessively cellular, packed marrow, or marrow in which fibrosis or fat prevents the cells from being aspirated. The common causes are myelofibrosis, aplastic anaemia, hairy cell leukaemia, acute leukaemia, lymphoma and marrow infiltration by metastatic tumour. Faulty technique, such as an incorrect needle position, must be excluded by repeating the procedure. A trephine biopsy should be done in every case of dry tap.


## What is blood tap?

A blood tap is an aspirate in which the sample is mainly peripheral blood and not marrow, so that the smears contain no marrow fragments (spicules) and few marrow precursors, and are therefore not suitable for reliable assessment. It results from aspiration of an excessive volume of material (more than about 0.5 mL), slow aspiration with dilution, or an unusually vascular marrow, or from the needle being in a vessel or the soft tissues. The procedure is repeated, using a small volume and rapid, firm aspiration, or at another site. A trephine biopsy should be considered if blood taps persist.


## Mention 4 conditions where dry tap is frequent.

Dry taps are frequent in the following conditions:

1. **Myelofibrosis** (primary myelofibrosis and the spent phase of other myeloproliferative neoplasms), in which fibrosis traps the marrow cells.
2. **Aplastic anaemia**, in which the marrow is largely replaced by fat and aspirates yield little or no material.
3. **Hairy cell leukaemia**, because of reticulin fibrosis and infiltration by hairy cells.
4. **Marrow infiltration or packed marrow**, as in acute leukaemias, lymphomas, multiple myeloma and metastatic carcinoma (myelophthisic anaemia).

Others include chronic myeloid leukaemia and polycythaemia vera with marrow fibrosis and Gaucher disease.

**Anaemia: General**

**Classification and investigation**


## What is anemia?

Anaemia is a reduction in the total circulating red cell mass below normal limits, which in practice is diagnosed by a haemoglobin concentration or haematocrit below the reference range for the age and sex of the patient, and which leads to reduced oxygen-carrying capacity of the blood and tissue hypoxia.

Because direct measurement of the red cell mass is not easy, anaemia is diagnosed from reductions in the haemoglobin concentration and the haematocrit, which correlate with the red cell mass except when the plasma volume is altered by fluid retention (as in pregnancy, causing a dilutional fall) or dehydration (which masks anaemia). The working thresholds are a haemoglobin below 13 g/dL in men, below 12 g/dL in nonpregnant women and below 11 g/dL in pregnant women and young children (Robbins reference ranges: males 13.6 to 17.2 g/dL, females 12.0 to 15.0 g/dL).

Anaemia may result from blood loss, increased red cell destruction (haemolysis) or decreased red cell production (Table of mechanisms), and may be further described by red cell size (microcytic, normocytic, macrocytic), haemoglobinisation (hypochromic, normochromic) and shape. When severe enough, anaemia causes weakness, malaise, easy fatigability and dyspnoea on mild exertion; pallor; fatty change in the liver, myocardium and kidney; angina in patients with coronary disease; and headache, dimness of vision and faintness from central nervous system hypoxia. Acute massive blood loss additionally causes hypovolaemic shock, and in intravascular and extravascular haemolysis jaundice and splenomegaly appear respectively.


## Morphological types of anaemia.

On the basis of red cell size and haemoglobin content, anaemia is classified morphologically into microcytic hypochromic, normocytic normochromic and macrocytic types.

The classification rests on the red cell indices (MCV, MCH, MCHC) and the peripheral blood film.

| Type | MCV | MCH / MCHC | Underlying defect |
|---|---|---|---|
| Microcytic hypochromic | Low (below 80 fL) | Low | Disorders of haemoglobin synthesis (iron, globin or haem) |
| Normocytic normochromic | Normal (82–96 fL) | Normal | Acute blood loss, haemolysis, marrow failure, renal disease, many chronic diseases |
| Macrocytic | High (above 96–100 fL) | MCH raised, MCHC normal | Impaired DNA synthesis (megaloblastic) or increased red cell membrane lipid / young cells (non-megaloblastic) |

A fourth, "dimorphic" pattern, with two populations of red cells (for example, combined iron and B₁₂ deficiency or treated iron deficiency), is recognised by a raised RDW and a film showing both microcytic and macrocytic cells. Characteristic abnormalities of red cell shape on the film frequently give a further clue to the cause.


## Examples of each morphological type.

Iron deficiency and thalassaemia are the commonest microcytic hypochromic anaemias, acute blood loss and most haemolytic anaemias are normocytic normochromic, and megaloblastic anaemia due to B₁₂ or folate deficiency is the classical macrocytic anaemia.

- **Microcytic hypochromic:** iron deficiency anaemia (the most common), thalassaemia syndromes (α and β), anaemia of chronic inflammation (often normocytic but may be slightly microcytic and hypochromic), sideroblastic anaemia, lead poisoning, and the rare iron-refractory iron deficiency anaemia from TMPRSS6 mutations.
- **Normocytic normochromic:** acute blood loss, haemolytic anaemias (hereditary spherocytosis, G6PD deficiency, sickle cell disease, autoimmune haemolytic anaemia, microangiopathic haemolysis), aplastic anaemia (usually slightly macrocytic), pure red cell aplasia, anaemia of chronic inflammation, anaemia of renal failure, endocrine disorders (such as hypothyroidism), marrow infiltration (myelophthisic anaemia) and the dilutional anaemia of pregnancy.
- **Macrocytic:** megaloblastic anaemias (vitamin B₁₂ deficiency including pernicious anaemia, folate deficiency, drugs interfering with DNA synthesis such as methotrexate); and non-megaloblastic causes, namely chronic liver disease, alcohol excess, hypothyroidism, myelodysplastic neoplasms, aplastic anaemia, and reticulocytosis in haemolysis or haemorrhage.


## Pathophysiological categories of anaemia.

Anaemia is classified by mechanism into three broad groups: blood loss, increased red cell destruction (haemolysis), and decreased red cell production.

| Mechanism | Subtypes and examples |
|---|---|
| Blood loss | Acute (trauma); chronic (gastrointestinal lesions, gynaecological disturbances, which usually lead to iron deficiency anaemia) |
| Increased red cell destruction (haemolysis) | Inherited: membrane defects (hereditary spherocytosis, elliptocytosis); enzyme deficiencies (G6PD, pyruvate kinase); haemoglobin abnormalities (thalassaemia, sickle cell disease and other haemoglobinopathies). Acquired: paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria; antibody-mediated (immunohaemolytic anaemia, haemolytic disease of the newborn, transfusion reactions); mechanical trauma (microangiopathic haemolysis in DIC, HUS, TTP; defective cardiac valves); infections (malaria, babesiosis); toxic injury (clostridial sepsis, snake venom, lead); membrane lipid abnormalities; hypersplenism |
| Decreased red cell production | Inherited: stem cell defects (Fanconi anaemia, telomerase defects); erythroblast maturation defects (thalassaemia). Nutritional: B₁₂ and folate deficiency (DNA synthesis), iron deficiency (haemoglobin synthesis). Other: erythropoietin deficiency (renal failure), immune-mediated progenitor injury (aplastic anaemia, pure red cell aplasia), inflammation-mediated iron sequestration (anaemia of chronic inflammation), primary haematopoietic neoplasms, space-occupying marrow lesions (myelophthisis), parvovirus B19 infection, endocrine and liver disease |


## Causes of anaemia.

The causes of anaemia are blood loss, increased destruction of red cells, and decreased production of red cells, and in many patients more than one mechanism contributes.

Blood loss. Acute haemorrhage (trauma, surgery, obstetric haemorrhage) produces a normocytic anaemia once the blood volume has been restored by shift of interstitial fluid. Chronic blood loss (peptic ulcer, gastrointestinal malignancy, haemorrhoids, hookworm infestation, menorrhagia) depletes iron stores and leads to iron deficiency anaemia.

Increased destruction (haemolysis). The red cell lifespan is shortened below 120 days owing to intrinsic defects (hereditary spherocytosis, G6PD deficiency, pyruvate kinase deficiency, sickle cell disease, thalassaemia, PNH) or extrinsic factors (autoantibodies and alloantibodies, mechanical injury by prosthetic valves or microangiopathy, malaria, drugs, toxins and hypersplenism). Marrow compensation produces reticulocytosis, but anaemia develops when the destruction outpaces production.

Decreased production. Deficiency of iron, vitamin B₁₂ or folate; marrow failure (aplastic anaemia, pure red cell aplasia, marrow replacement by leukaemia, lymphoma, metastases or granulomas); myelodysplastic neoplasms; decreased erythropoietin in chronic renal failure; chronic inflammation, infection and malignancy (inflammatory cytokines raise hepcidin and trap iron in macrophages); endocrine disorders (hypothyroidism); chronic liver disease; and drugs, toxins and radiation.

Dilutional. Expansion of plasma volume in pregnancy and in splenomegaly lowers the haemoglobin concentration without a true fall in the red cell mass.


## How will you investigate a case of anaemia?

I would take a detailed history and examine the patient, confirm anaemia and classify it morphologically with a complete blood count, red cell indices, reticulocyte count and peripheral blood film, and then perform specific tests directed by the type of anaemia to determine the underlying cause.

History and examination. Duration and tempo, diet, drugs (NSAIDs, anticonvulsants, antimalarials), alcohol, bleeding (gastrointestinal, menstrual, urinary), pregnancy, previous surgery (gastrectomy, ileal resection), family history and ethnic origin, and symptoms of the underlying cause. Examination looks for pallor, jaundice, glossitis, koilonychia, neurological signs, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly and bone tenderness.

First-line investigations.

1. Complete blood count: Hb, PCV, RBC count, red cell indices (MCV, MCH, MCHC, RDW), total and differential white cell count, platelet count.
2. Peripheral blood film: size, colour, shape, inclusions, white cell and platelet abnormalities, parasites.
3. Reticulocyte count, to distinguish underproduction from increased destruction or loss.

Investigations directed by the findings.

- **Microcytic hypochromic:** serum iron, TIBC, transferrin saturation, ferritin; if iron studies are normal, haemoglobin electrophoresis/HPLC (HbA₂), and in iron deficiency a search for the source of blood loss (stool for occult blood, endoscopy, parasites).
- **Macrocytic:** serum vitamin B₁₂ and folate (red cell folate), antibodies to intrinsic factor, homocysteine and methylmalonic acid, liver and thyroid function; bone marrow if megaloblastic changes or dysplasia are suspected.
- **Normocytic with high reticulocytes (haemolysis):** serum bilirubin (unconjugated), LDH, haptoglobin, urine haemoglobin and haemosiderin, direct Coombs test, osmotic fragility, G6PD assay, haemoglobin electrophoresis, and tests for PNH by flow cytometry.
- **Normocytic with low reticulocytes:** renal function, ferritin and inflammatory markers (anaemia of chronic inflammation), thyroid function, and bone marrow aspiration with trephine biopsy in suspected aplasia, infiltration or neoplasm.


## Write the morphological/red-cell-indices classification of anemia with examples.

Anaemia is classified morphologically on the basis of the red cell indices, chiefly the MCV, MCH and MCHC, supported by examination of the blood film. This classification is clinically useful because the indices identify the underlying defect: disordered haemoglobin synthesis gives small pale cells, disordered DNA synthesis gives large cells, and a normal red cell phenotype points to blood loss, haemolysis, marrow failure or systemic disease.

| Morphological type | Indices | Blood film | Causes (examples) |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Microcytic hypochromic** | MCV <80 fL; MCH <27 pg; MCHC <32 g/dL | Small, pale red cells with enlarged central pallor, pencil cells | Iron deficiency anaemia; thalassaemia syndromes; anaemia of chronic inflammation (some cases); sideroblastic anaemia; lead poisoning |
| **Normocytic normochromic** | MCV 82–96 fL; MCH and MCHC normal | Cells of normal size and colour; polychromasia in haemolysis | Acute blood loss; haemolytic anaemias (hereditary spherocytosis, G6PD deficiency, sickle cell disease, immune haemolysis); aplastic anaemia; anaemia of chronic inflammation; renal failure; endocrine disease; marrow infiltration |
| **Macrocytic** | MCV >96–100 fL; MCH raised; MCHC normal | Megaloblastic: macro-ovalocytes, hypersegmented neutrophils. Non-megaloblastic: round macrocytes | Megaloblastic: vitamin B₁₂ deficiency (pernicious anaemia), folate deficiency, drugs (methotrexate). Non-megaloblastic: chronic liver disease, alcoholism, hypothyroidism, myelodysplastic neoplasm, reticulocytosis |
| **Dimorphic** | MCV may be normal; RDW raised | Two populations | Combined iron and B₁₂/folate deficiency; partially treated iron deficiency; sideroblastic anaemia |

The red cell distribution width (RDW) adds a further dimension: it is raised when anisocytosis is marked (iron deficiency, megaloblastic anaemia) and normal or near normal in thalassaemia trait.


## Write a short note on investigations for morphological classification of anemia.

The morphological classification of anaemia depends on a small set of laboratory tests performed on a venous blood sample.

1. **Haemoglobin and haematocrit (PCV):** establish the presence and degree of anaemia.
2. **Red cell count:** needed to calculate the indices.
3. **Red cell indices:** MCV = PCV × 10 ÷ RBC; MCH = Hb × 10 ÷ RBC; MCHC = Hb × 100 ÷ PCV; and RDW. Modern automated analysers report these directly.
4. **Peripheral blood film:** the examination of the size, shape and staining of red cells, white cell morphology and platelet number gives information that the indices cannot, for instance spherocytes, target cells, sickle cells, schistocytes, hypersegmented neutrophils and parasites.
5. **Reticulocyte count:** an assessment of marrow response.

According to these results, anaemia is typed as microcytic hypochromic, normocytic normochromic or macrocytic, and further investigations are chosen: iron studies and haemoglobin electrophoresis for microcytic anaemia; vitamin B₁₂, folate and bone marrow for macrocytic anaemia; and haemolysis screen, bone marrow, renal, hepatic and thyroid tests for normocytic anaemia.


## Define polycythemia.

Polycythaemia denotes an abnormally high number of circulating red cells, usually with a corresponding rise in haemoglobin concentration and haematocrit (for example, haemoglobin above 16.5 g/dL in men and 16.0 g/dL in women, or haematocrit above 49% and 48%, respectively).

It is classified as **relative**, when there is haemoconcentration from reduced plasma volume (dehydration due to water deprivation, prolonged vomiting or diarrhoea, or diuretic excess) with a normal red cell mass, and **absolute**, when the total red cell mass is increased. Absolute polycythaemia is **primary** when it results from an intrinsic abnormality of haemopoietic precursors, the most common cause being polycythaemia vera, a myeloproliferative neoplasm with mutations (most often JAK2) that cause erythropoietin-independent growth of red cell progenitors, and rarely familial erythropoietin receptor mutations. It is **secondary** when it is a response to raised erythropoietin, which may be appropriate (chronic hypoxia: high altitude, chronic lung disease, cyanotic heart disease, smoking, haemoglobin variants with high oxygen affinity, Chuvash polycythaemia from VHL mutations stabilising HIF) or inappropriate (erythropoietin-secreting tumours such as renal cell carcinoma, hepatocellular carcinoma and cerebellar haemangioblastoma).

**Iron Deficiency and Microcytic Anaemia**

**Iron deficiency anaemia**


## Causes of iron deficiency anaemia.

Iron deficiency anaemia results from a negative iron balance, which arises from dietary lack, impaired absorption, increased requirement, or chronic blood loss, with chronic blood loss being the commonest cause in developed countries.

Normal iron balance depends on absorbing about 1 mg of iron daily to replace the 1 to 2 mg lost in shed epithelial cells, since there is no regulated pathway of excretion. The causes are as follows.

1. **Chronic blood loss:** gastrointestinal bleeding (peptic ulcer, gastrointestinal cancers, haemorrhoids, hookworm infestation, NSAIDs, angiodysplasia, varices), menorrhagia and other genital tract bleeding, haematuria, and repeated blood donation.
2. **Dietary lack:** infants, the impoverished, older adults, vegans, and populations eating mainly inorganic (nonhaem) iron, which is poorly absorbed (often <5%) compared with haem iron (about 20%).
3. **Impaired absorption:** sprue and other malabsorption syndromes with steatorrhoea, chronic diarrhoea, gastrectomy (reduced acidity and rapid transit), and diets rich in tannates, phytates or oxalates.
4. **Increased requirement:** growing infants and children, adolescents, pregnancy and lactation, particularly with closely spaced pregnancies.

Rarely, iron-refractory iron deficiency anaemia occurs from TMPRSS6 mutations that cause inappropriately high hepcidin.


## Causes of IDA in relation to different age groups.

The cause of iron deficiency varies with age: inadequate intake and rapid growth in infants and children, increased demands and menstrual loss in adolescent girls and women of reproductive age, and chronic gastrointestinal blood loss in adult men and postmenopausal women.

| Age group | Principal causes |
|---|---|
| Infants (6 months to 2 years) | Low iron in breast milk (about 0.3 mg/L) and poorly bioavailable iron in cow's milk, prematurity and low birth stores, rapid growth, delayed weaning to iron-rich foods, cow's-milk-induced intestinal blood loss |
| Children | Nutritional inadequacy, rapid growth, hookworm and other intestinal parasites, malabsorption, Meckel diverticulum |
| Adolescents | Rapid growth, poor diet, onset of menstruation (especially girls) |
| Women of reproductive age | Menorrhagia, repeated pregnancies and lactation, poor diet |
| Adult men | Gastrointestinal blood loss until proven otherwise (peptic ulcer, malignancy, hookworm, haemorrhoids) |
| Postmenopausal women | Gastrointestinal blood loss until proven otherwise (cancer, gastritis, NSAID use), malabsorption, poor diet |
| Older adults | Poor diet with little meat, poor dentition, occult gastrointestinal bleeding, chronic NSAID or aspirin use |


## Causes of IDA in adult males.

In an adult male, iron deficiency is almost always due to chronic gastrointestinal blood loss until proven otherwise, because dietary lack is rare and men have no physiological iron losses other than the minimal obligatory ones.

The average Western diet provides more than enough iron for men, so dietary insufficiency is rarely responsible. The sources of occult bleeding to be investigated include peptic ulcer disease and erosive gastritis (aspirin or NSAID use), carcinoma of the stomach, caecum or colon, oesophagitis, hiatus hernia, oesophageal varices, angiodysplasia, haemorrhoids, inflammatory bowel disease, and, in endemic regions such as Bangladesh, hookworm infestation (Ancylostoma duodenale, Necator americanus). Less commonly, malabsorption (coeliac disease), previous gastrectomy, urinary tract bleeding (haematuria) and frequent blood donation are responsible. To ascribe iron deficiency prematurely to another cause risks missing a gastrointestinal cancer or other bleeding lesion, and an alert clinician who investigates unexplained iron deficiency anaemia may thereby save a life.


## Causes of IDA in post-menopausal women.

After the menopause, menstrual loss and pregnancy are no longer relevant, so iron deficiency anaemia in a postmenopausal woman must be attributed to gastrointestinal blood loss until proven otherwise.

The same causes as in adult males therefore apply: bleeding peptic ulcer, erosive gastritis from NSAIDs or aspirin, gastric and colorectal carcinoma, angiodysplasia, haemorrhoids and hookworm infestation.
